2 Part 1: Conceptual Questions

2.1 Question 1: What is Regression?
Simple linear regression is used to:
Compare two groupsPredict one variable from another using a linear equationTest for differences before and afterDetermine if variables are categorical
In regression, the predictor variable is also called:
The dependent variableThe independent variable (IV) or X variableThe outcomeThe residual
The outcome variable is also called:
The predictorThe dependent variable (DV) or Y variableThe independent variableThe slope


2.2 Question 2: The Regression Equation
The regression equation is: Y = a + bX. In this equation:
‘a’ (the intercept) represents:
The slope of the lineThe predicted Y value when X = 0The correlation coefficientThe sample size
‘b’ (the slope) represents:
The Y-interceptThe change in Y for each one-unit increase in XThe total varianceThe residual


2.3 Question 3: Regression vs Correlation
How is regression different from correlation?
They are exactly the sameRegression allows prediction and has a specific direction (X predicts Y)Correlation is more accurateRegression only works with experiments
If the correlation between X and Y is strong, the regression will:
Fail to workMake more accurate predictionsAlways predict perfectlyHave a slope of zero


2.4 Question 4: R-Squared in Regression
R-squared (R2) tells us:
The significance levelThe proportion of variance in Y explained by XThe slope of the lineThe sample size needed
If R2 = .36, this means:
The correlation is .3636% of participants showed the effect36% of the variance in Y is explained by XThe prediction is 36% accurate
The remaining variance (1 - R2) is called:
Explained varianceUnexplained or residual varianceTotal varianceThe intercept


2.5 Question 5: Residuals
A residual is:
The predicted valueThe slopeThe difference between the actual Y value and the predicted Y valueThe correlation coefficient
If a residual is positive, the actual score was:
Lower than predictedHigher than predictedExactly as predictedCannot determine


2.6 Question 6: Assumptions of Regression
Linear regression assumes:
A linear relationship between X and YA curvilinear relationshipNo relationship at allCategorical variables only
If the relationship is clearly curved (nonlinear), we should:
Use linear regression anywayConsider transforming variables or using nonlinear methodsIgnore the patternCollect more data

ImportantKey Distinction



Correlation tells us about the strength and direction of a relationship. Regression goes further by providing a specific equation for prediction and quantifying how much variance is explained. However, regression (like correlation) still cannot establish causation without an experimental design.

2 Part 1: Conceptual Questions

2.1 Question 1: The Logic of Hypothesis Testing
We test the null hypothesis (H0) because:
The null hypothesis is what we want to proveWe can calculate the probability of our data if the null were trueThe null hypothesis is always correctIt is easier than testing the alternative hypothesis
The null hypothesis typically states:
There is a significant effectThere is no effect or no differenceOur prediction is correctThe sample is representative


2.2 Question 2: What is a p-Value?
A p-value tells us:
The probability that the null hypothesis is trueThe probability that our hypothesis is correctThe probability of obtaining results this extreme (or more) if the null hypothesis were trueThe size of the effect
A p-value of .03 means:
There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is trueThere is a 3% probability of getting these results if there were no real effect3% of participants showed the effectThe effect is 3%


2.3 Question 3: Statistical Significance
The conventional alpha level in psychology is:
.01.05.10.50
We reject the null hypothesis when:
p > .05p < .05p = .05 exactlyThe effect size is large
A result with p = .07 is:
Statistically significantNot statistically significant at alpha = .05Definitely not a real effectA large effect


2.4 Question 4: Types of t-Tests
An independent samples t-test is used when:
The same participants are measured twiceDifferent participants are in each conditionWe are measuring a correlationData are not normally distributed
A paired samples t-test is used when:
The same participants are measured twice (or matched pairs)Different participants are in each conditionWe have three or more groupsVariables are categorical


2.5 Question 5: One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed Tests
A one-tailed hypothesis:
Tests for any differencePredicts a specific direction of effectIs always more powerfulShould never be used
A two-tailed hypothesis:
Is weaker than one-tailedTests for a difference in either directionRequires a larger sampleIs inappropriate for t-tests
When should you use a one-tailed test?
When you want a significant resultWhen theory strongly predicts a specific direction and the opposite would be meaninglessAlwaysNever


2.6 Question 6: t-Test Assumptions
Which assumption applies to both independent and paired t-tests?
Equal group sizesData should be approximately normally distributedPerfect random samplingCorrelation between conditions
The independent t-test also assumes:
Same participants in both groupsHomogeneity of variance (similar SDs in both groups)Exactly equal meansLarge effect sizes

2 Why Literature Reviews Matter
A good literature review does several things:

Establishes context: Shows what’s already known in the field
Identifies gaps: Reveals what hasn’t been studied or remains unclear
Justifies your study: Explains why your research question is worth investigating
Informs methodology: Shows how others have approached similar questions







ImportantYour Goal



Your introduction should create a “funnel” — starting broad (the general topic), narrowing to specific previous findings, and concluding with your specific research question and hypothesis.

title: Chapter 12: Project Groups - Literature Review
text:
5 Evaluating Sources
Not all papers are equally useful. Ask yourself:

5.1 Is it relevant?

Does it address your research question directly?
Does it study a similar population?
Are the methods applicable to your study?



5.2 Is it credible?

Is it peer-reviewed? (Check: is it in a journal?)
Who are the authors? (Do they have relevant expertise?)
Is it published in a reputable journal?
Has it been cited by others?



5.3 Is it current?

How old is the research?
Is this a rapidly changing field where older studies might be outdated?
Are there more recent replications or meta-analyses?







WarningRed Flags



Be cautious of:

Non-peer-reviewed sources (blogs, news articles, opinion pieces)
Predatory journals (poor quality control)
Studies with very small samples
Single studies that haven’t been replicated
Sources that cite only themselves

title: Chapter 12: Project Groups - Literature Review
text:
6 Reading Research Papers Efficiently
You don’t need to read every paper in full. Use a strategic approach:

6.1 1. Screen by Abstract
Read the abstract first. Does this paper:

Address your topic?
Use relevant methods?
Study a similar population?

If not, move on.


6.2 2. Skim the Introduction and Discussion

Introduction: What’s their research question? What do they cite?
Discussion: What did they find? What do they recommend for future research?



6.3 3. Deep Read Key Papers
For highly relevant papers, read carefully:

What exactly did they measure and how?
What were the limitations?
How does this inform your own study?

title: Chapter 12: Project Groups - Literature Review
text:
8 From Notes to Narrative
Your literature review should tell a story, not just list studies. Compare:
Poor (list-style): > Smith (2020) found that social media use affected sleep. Jones (2019) also studied social media and sleep. Brown (2021) looked at screen time.
Better (narrative): > Recent research has established a link between social media use and sleep quality. Smith (2020) found that students who used social media for more than two hours daily reported significantly worse sleep quality. This relationship may be explained by blue light exposure (Jones, 2019) or by the emotionally arousing nature of social content (Brown, 2021).

8.1 Synthesis Tips

Group by theme, not by paper
Compare and contrast findings across studies
Identify patterns and inconsistencies
Build toward your specific question

title: Chapter 12: Project Groups - Literature Review
section: 9 Common Errors and How to Avoid Them
text:
9 Common Errors and How to Avoid Them

9.1 Relying too heavily on Google Scholar
Problem: Google Scholar includes non-peer-reviewed sources and doesn’t filter by quality.
Solution: Use Google Scholar to find papers, but verify they’re peer-reviewed. Cross-reference with PsycINFO.


9.2 Using only recent papers
Problem: Missing foundational/classic studies that established the field.
Solution: Follow citation trails — what papers do recent articles cite? Include seminal works.


9.3 Over-quoting
Problem: Too many direct quotes make your writing feel disjointed.
Solution: Paraphrase whenever possible. Direct quotes should be rare and used for particularly important or well-phrased points.


9.4 Not being critical
Problem: Treating all studies as equally valid.
Solution: Note limitations. A study with n = 20 is less reliable than n = 200. Self-report measures have different limitations than objective measures.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
2 What Is Correlation?
Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables.

Strength: How tightly the data points cluster around a line (from weak to strong)
Direction: Whether variables increase together (positive) or one increases as the other decreases (negative)


2.1 The Correlation Coefficient (r)
The correlation coefficient r ranges from -1 to +1:



Value
Interpretation




r = +1
Perfect positive relationship


r = +0.7
Strong positive relationship


r = +0.3
Weak positive relationship


r = 0
No linear relationship


r = -0.3
Weak negative relationship


r = -0.7
Strong negative relationship


r = -1
Perfect negative relationship









ImportantDirection vs Strength



The sign tells you direction; the absolute value tells you strength. r = -0.8 is a stronger relationship than r = +0.3.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
3 Reading Scatterplots

3.1 Why Visualise?
Before looking at numbers, always examine a scatterplot. It reveals:

The direction of the relationship (positive, negative, or none)
The strength of the relationship (tight cluster vs spread out)
The shape (linear vs curved)
Any unusual patterns or outliers



3.2 What to Look For
Each point represents one participant:

X-axis: One variable
Y-axis: The other variable

Pattern Guide:



Pattern
Meaning




Upward slope
Positive relationship


Downward slope
Negative relationship


No clear slope
No relationship


Tight cluster around line
Strong relationship


Wide scatter
Weak relationship





3.3 Visual Examples
Strong Positive (r ≈ 0.8)    Weak Positive (r ≈ 0.3)    No Relationship (r ≈ 0)

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
4 Interpreting Correlation Output
When you run a correlation test, you’ll see output like this:
    Pearson's product-moment correlation

    data:  reaction_time and time_estimate
    t = 3.12, df = 48, p-value = 0.003
    95 percent confidence interval:
     0.15  0.63
    sample estimates:
          cor
         0.42

4.1 What Each Part Means







Output
Meaning




t = 3.12
The test statistic


df = 48
Degrees of freedom (sample size - 2)


p-value = 0.003
Probability of this r if there’s truly no relationship


95 percent confidence interval
Plausible range for the true correlation


cor = 0.42
The sample correlation coefficient





4.2 Key Questions to Answer

What is r? → 0.42 (medium positive correlation)
Is it significant? → Yes, p = 0.003 < 0.05
What’s the CI? → [0.15, 0.63] - the true r is likely in this range
What does it mean? → Higher reaction times are associated with higher time estimates







TipInterpreting the Confidence Interval



A 95% CI of [0.15, 0.63] means we’re fairly confident the true population correlation is somewhere in this range. Since it doesn’t include 0, the correlation is statistically significant.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
5 Correlation Strength Guidelines
Cohen (1988) suggested these benchmarks:




r




.10 - .29
Small/weak


.30 - .49
Medium/moderate


.50+
Large/strong









WarningContext Matters



These are rough guidelines. In some research areas, r = .30 is typical and meaningful. In others, r = .50 might be expected.



5.1 Understanding r-squared
Squaring r tells you the proportion of variance explained:



r
r²
Interpretation




.10
.01
1% shared variance


.30
.09
9% shared variance


.50
.25
25% shared variance


.70
.49
49% shared variance









ImportantReality Check



A correlation of r = .42 sounds reasonable. But r² = .18 means one variable explains only 18% of the variance in the other. The remaining 82% is due to other factors!

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
6 Pearson vs Spearman

6.1 Pearson’s r (Most Common)
Use when:

Both variables are continuous
Relationship is approximately linear
Data are roughly normally distributed



6.2 Spearman’s rho (ρ)
Use when:

Data are ordinal (ranked)
Relationship is monotonic but not linear
Data have outliers or are skewed

Both are interpreted the same way — they range from -1 to +1 with the same strength guidelines.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
7 Correlation Does NOT Mean Causation






WarningCritical Point



A correlation between X and Y does NOT mean X causes Y. This is possibly the most important lesson in research methods.



7.1 Why Not?
Three possible explanations for any correlation:

X causes Y: More sleep → better performance
Y causes X: Better performance → more sleep (less stress)
Z causes both: Good health → more sleep AND better performance

Without experimental manipulation, we cannot determine which explanation is correct.


7.2 Classic Example
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated.
Does ice cream cause drowning? No! A third variable (hot weather) causes both:

Hot weather → more ice cream sales
Hot weather → more swimming → more drowning



7.3 DataLab Example
Self-rating and throwing performance might be correlated.
Does thinking you’re good make you perform better? Possible alternatives:

Past experience → higher self-rating AND better performance
Natural ability → higher self-rating AND better performance

We can’t determine causation from correlation alone.

NoteWhat You’ll Learn

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
This reading prepares you for the lab session where you’ll interpret t-test output. The t-test is one of the most widely used statistical tests in psychology, allowing us to compare means and determine whether observed differences are likely to reflect real effects or just random variation.






NoteWhat You’ll Learn



By the end of this lab, you’ll be able to:

Interpret t-test output including t-values, p-values, and confidence intervals
Understand the difference between independent and paired samples t-tests
Choose the appropriate type of t-test for your research question

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
2 When to Use a t-test
The t-test answers the question: Is the difference between two means larger than we’d expect by chance?
Use a t-test when you have:

A continuous outcome variable (e.g., reaction time, mood score)
Two groups to compare OR two measurements from the same people
Reasonably normally distributed data (or a large enough sample)


2.1 Types of t-tests








Type
When to Use
Example




Independent samples
Different people in each group
Room A vs Room B


Paired samples
Same people measured twice
Pre vs Post mood


One sample
Compare to a known value
Sample mean vs 50%

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
3 Independent Samples t-test
Use this when comparing different people in two groups.

3.1 Example: Comparing Rooms
Did Room A and Room B differ in reaction time?


3.2 Understanding the Output
    Welch Two Sample t-test

    data:  reaction_time by room
    t = -2.34, df = 45.2, p-value = 0.024
    alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
    95 percent confidence interval:
     -42.5  -3.2
    sample estimates:
    mean in group A   mean in group B
              265.3             288.1


3.3 What Each Part Means







Output
Meaning




t = -2.34
The t-statistic: how many standard errors the difference is from 0


df = 45.2
Degrees of freedom


p-value = 0.024
Probability of this difference (or larger) if null hypothesis is true


95 percent confidence interval
Range of plausible values for the true difference


sample estimates
The actual group means





3.4 Key Questions to Answer

What are the means? → Room A: 265.3 ms, Room B: 288.1 ms
What is t? → -2.34
Is it significant? → Yes, p = 0.024 < 0.05
What’s the CI? → [-42.5, -3.2] - the true difference is likely in this range
What does it mean? → Room A was faster than Room B







ImportantInterpreting the p-value



A p-value of 0.024 means: if there were truly no difference between rooms, we’d see a difference this large (or larger) about 2.4% of the time. Since this is less than 0.05, we conclude the difference is statistically significant.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
4 Paired Samples t-test
Use this when comparing the same people measured at two time points.

4.1 Example: Pre-Post Mood
Did mood change after DataLab?


4.2 Understanding the Output
    Paired t-test

    data:  mood_pre and mood_post
    t = -3.45, df = 29, p-value = 0.002
    alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
    95 percent confidence interval:
     -1.82  -0.45
    sample estimates:
    mean difference
              -1.13


4.3 Key Questions to Answer

What is the mean difference? → -1.13 (mood increased by 1.13 points)
Is it significant? → Yes, p = 0.002 < 0.05
What’s the CI? → [-1.82, -0.45] - the true change is likely in this range
What does it mean? → Mood significantly improved after DataLab



4.4 Why Paired Tests Are More Powerful
Paired tests account for individual differences. Consider:

Person A: Pre = 5, Post = 7 (change = +2)
Person B: Pre = 8, Post = 10 (change = +2)

Both people increased by 2 points, even though their baseline scores differ. The paired test focuses on the change within each person, not the raw scores.






TipRule of Thumb



If the same individuals provide both measurements, use a paired test. It’s more sensitive because it removes between-person variability.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
5 One Sample t-test
Use this to compare your sample mean to a specific value.

5.1 Example: Comparing to Chance
Is staring detection accuracy different from 50% (chance)?


5.2 Understanding the Output
    One Sample t-test

    data:  staring_accuracy
    t = 1.87, df = 29, p-value = 0.072
    alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0.5
    95 percent confidence interval:
     0.48  0.61
    sample estimates:
    mean of x
        0.545


5.3 Key Questions to Answer

What is the sample mean? → 54.5%
Is it significantly different from 50%? → No, p = 0.072 > 0.05
What does it mean? → Performance is not significantly better than chance

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
6 Effect Size: Cohen’s d
The p-value tells you whether a difference is statistically significant, but not whether it’s practically meaningful. For that, we use effect sizes.
Cohen’s d expresses the difference in standard deviation units:



d value
Interpretation




0.2
Small effect


0.5
Medium effect


0.8
Large effect




6.1 Example Output
    Cohen's d

    d estimate: 0.62
    95% CI: [0.15, 1.09]

    Interpretation: medium






ImportantWhy Effect Size Matters



A study with n = 1000 might find p < .001 for a tiny effect (d = 0.1). The effect is “real” but practically meaningless. Always report and interpret effect sizes alongside p-values.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
7 Choosing the Right Test








Research Question
Design
Test




Do two different groups differ?
Between-subjects
Independent t-test


Does the same group change over time?
Within-subjects
Paired t-test


Does a sample differ from a known value?

One-sample t-test




7.1 DataLab Examples



Question
Test Type

One-sample


Did word type (abstract/concrete) affect memory?

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
8 Assumptions of the t-test

8.1 1. Independence
Observations should be independent (one person’s score doesn’t influence another’s). This is about study design.


8.2 2. Normality
The data should be approximately normally distributed, especially for small samples.






TipRobustness



The t-test is quite robust to violations of normality, especially with larger samples (n > 30 per group). Don’t worry too much unless your data are severely skewed.




8.3 3. Homogeneity of Variance (for independent samples)
Groups should have similar variability. The Welch’s t-test (default in most software) handles unequal variances automatically.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
9 Reporting t-tests (APA Style)

9.1 Template

[Group 1] (M = XX.X, SD = X.X) [were/was] [significantly/not significantly] [higher/lower/different] than [Group 2] (M = XX.X, SD = X.X), t(df) = X.XX, p = .XXX, d = X.XX.



9.2 Independent Samples Example

Participants in Room A (M = 265.3 ms, SD = 45.2) had significantly faster reaction times than those in Room B (M = 288.1 ms, SD = 52.1), t(45.2) = -2.34, p = .024, d = 0.47.



9.3 Paired Samples Example

Mood significantly increased from pre-session (M = 5.2, SD = 1.8) to post-session (M = 6.3, SD = 1.6), t(29) = 3.45, p = .002, d = 0.62.



9.4 Elements to Include

Group means and SDs
The t-value and df
The p-value
Effect size (Cohen’s d)
Direction of the difference

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
10 Common Interpretation Errors

10.1 Error 1: “p > .05 means no difference”
Wrong! A non-significant result means we can’t rule out chance — not that there’s definitely no effect. The study might lack power.


10.2 Error 2: “p < .001 means a huge effect”
Wrong! Statistical significance depends on sample size. Large samples can detect tiny effects. Always check effect size.


10.3 Error 3: “t = 2.34 is bigger than t = 1.98, so it’s more significant”
Misleading! t-values depend on sample size and variability. Compare p-values and effect sizes instead.


10.4 Error 4: Confusing paired and independent tests
Check: Are the same people in both conditions? If yes → paired. If no → independent.

2 Before the Lab

2.2 What to Know
Make sure you’re comfortable with these concepts:

Operationalisation: Turning abstract concepts into measurable variables
Hypotheses: H₀ (no effect) vs H₁ (effect exists); one-tailed vs two-tailed
Designs: Between-subjects (different people) vs within-subjects (same people)
The test link: Between → independent t-test; Within → paired t-test

title: Chapter 6: Research Plan Workshop
text:
3 The Three Topics
Your Research Plan will address ONE of these questions:

3.1 Topic 1: Font Difficulty → Memory
Question: Does reading text in a harder-to-read font improve memory retention?
Background: Diemand-Yauman et al. (2011) proposed that “desirable difficulties” can enhance learning. Harder-to-read fonts require more cognitive effort, which might deepen processing and improve retention.
Key operationalisation decisions:

What specific fonts will you use?
How will you ensure only readability differs?
How will you measure memory?



3.2 Topic 2: Hydration → Cognitive Performance
Question: Does drinking water improve cognitive task performance?
Background: Edmonds & Burford (2009) found that children who drank water performed better on cognitive tests. Dehydration may impair attention and processing speed.
Key operationalisation decisions:

How much water? When?
What’s your control condition?
What cognitive task will you use?



3.3 Topic 3: Eye Contact → Perceived Trustworthiness
Question: Does eye contact duration affect how trustworthy a person is perceived to be?
Background: Research on gaze and social perception shows that direct eye contact influences impressions of confidence, competence, and trustworthiness.
Key operationalisation decisions:

Photos or videos?
How will you manipulate gaze direction?
How will you measure trustworthiness?

title: Chapter 6: Research Plan Workshop
text:
4 Templates for the Workshop

4.1 IV Operationalisation Template

“The independent variable is _____________ with two levels:
Condition 1: [Specific details including exact parameters]
Condition 2: [Specific details including exact parameters]”

Good example (caffeine study):

“The independent variable is caffeine consumption with two levels:
Condition 1 (Caffeine): 200mg caffeine capsule (equivalent to ~2 cups of coffee)
Condition 2 (Placebo): Identical-looking capsule containing no caffeine”

Notice the specificity: exact dosage, matched appearance between conditions.


4.2 DV Operationalisation Template

“The dependent variable is _____________ measured by:
Task: [What participants do]
Scoring: [How performance is quantified]
Range: [Possible values]”

Good example (caffeine study):

“The dependent variable is alertness measured by:
Task: Psychomotor Vigilance Test — respond to visual stimuli as quickly as possible
Scoring: Mean reaction time across 30 trials (milliseconds)
Range: Continuous, typically 200-500ms”



4.3 Hypothesis Template
Null hypothesis:

H₀: There is no difference in [DV] between [Condition 1] and [Condition 2].

Alternative hypothesis (two-tailed):

H₁: [DV] will differ between [Condition 1] and [Condition 2].

Alternative hypothesis (one-tailed):

H₁: [DV] will be [higher/lower] in [Condition X] than [Condition Y].



4.4 Justification Template

“I have chosen a [one-tailed / two-tailed] hypothesis because:
Prior research [summary of relevant findings with citations].
Therefore, [I predict/do not predict] a specific direction.”



4.5 Design & Test Justification Template

“This study employs a [between-subjects / within-subjects] design because [specific advantages for your study and how disadvantages are addressed].
Given this design, the data will consist of [two independent groups / paired scores from the same participants].
Therefore, an [independent samples / paired samples] t-test is appropriate because [explain how data structure matches test requirements].”

title: Chapter 6: Research Plan Workshop
text:
7 Common Mistakes to Avoid

7.1 In Operationalisation

Too vague: “We showed participants different fonts” — which fonts exactly?
Confounded conditions: Changing multiple things between conditions
Missing control details: Only describing the experimental condition



7.2 In Hypotheses

No justification: Choosing one-tailed without explaining why
Wrong direction: Citing evidence for one direction but predicting the other
After-the-fact: Planning to decide direction after seeing data (this invalidates one-tailed tests)



7.3 In Design Justification

Stating without explaining: “I will use an independent t-test” with no justification
Mismatched design-test: Claiming within-subjects but selecting independent t-test
Missing the logic: Not explaining how design determines data structure



7.4 In Method Section

Not replicable: Missing crucial details about timing, materials, or procedure
Too brief: Participants, materials, and procedure each need substantive description
Missing counterbalancing: For within-subjects designs, failing to address order effects

2 Part 1: Describing the Centre
When we collect data, the first question is usually: What’s typical?

2.1 The Mean: The Balancing Point
The mean is the arithmetic average. If we measured 5 people’s memory scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean is 7. This is the “balancing point” — if you put these scores on a seesaw, 7 is where it would balance.


2.2 The Median: The Middle Value
The median is the middle value when data are sorted. Half the values are above it, half below.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
With 5 values, the median is the 3rd value (when sorted). Here, both mean and median are 7.


2.3 When Mean and Median Differ
Sometimes they tell different stories. Consider these scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean shoots up to 10, but the median stays at 7. The median is resistant to extreme values (outliers). The mean is pulled by them.
When to use which?

Mean: When data are roughly symmetric, no extreme outliers
Median: When data are skewed or have outliers (like income data)

title: Chapter 4: Descriptive Statistics in Action
text:
3 Part 2: Describing the Spread
The centre isn’t the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look completely different:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both means are 7, but the groups are very different. We need measures of spread.

3.1 The Range: Simplest Spread
The range is just the distance from lowest to highest:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A spans 2 points (6 to 8). Group B spans 10 points (2 to 12). The range immediately shows Group B is more variable.
Limitation: The range only uses two values, so it’s sensitive to outliers.


3.2 The Standard Deviation: The Gold Standard
The standard deviation (SD) measures how far scores typically fall from the mean.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A’s SD is about 0.7 — scores cluster tightly around 7. Group B’s SD is about 4.2 — scores are much more spread out.
Rule of thumb: In roughly normal data, about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean.
If the mean is 7 and SD is 1:

~68% of scores fall between 6 and 8



3.3 The summary() Function: Everything at Once
R’s summary() function gives you a quick overview:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This shows:

Min and Max (the range endpoints)
1st and 3rd Quartile (the middle 50%)
Median (the middle value)
Mean

The SD only makes sense relative to the mean and the scale.

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
2 Reflecting on Data Collection
DataLab was probably your first experience collecting psychological data. You may have noticed things didn’t always go smoothly:

Instructions weren’t always clear
Timing was tricky
Partners did things differently
The environment was distracting
Recording data while running a task was harder than expected

This is normal. In fact, these challenges are exactly why research methods matter. Understanding what can go wrong helps you:

Appreciate why standardised procedures exist
Interpret your own data more thoughtfully
Design better studies in the future

As you read about each task below, think about what happened during your data collection. What might have affected your measurements?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
3 What You Measured
DataLab included a group memory test plus five tasks measuring different aspects of human cognition and behaviour. For each task, we’ll cover the psychological background and then consider methodological issues.

3.1 Task 1: Reaction Time (Reflex Test)

Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus and your response to it. In the ruler-drop task, we measured simple reaction time — how quickly you could respond to a single, expected stimulus.
The physics is elegant: when you catch a falling ruler, the distance it fell before you caught it tells us how long your reaction took. Using the equation for free-falling objects (d = ½gt²), we can convert centimetres into milliseconds.






NoteWhy It Matters



Reaction time is one of the most reliable measures in psychology. Your data will show how consistent (or variable) human performance is, even on simple tasks. We can also look for practice effects — did you get faster across trials?








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Was the ruler held at exactly the same height each time?
Did the participant’s fingers start in exactly the same position?
Was it always clear where to read the catch point?

Potential biases:

Anticipation: Did you start to predict when the drop would happen?
Practice effects: Did you genuinely get faster, or just better at anticipating?
Hand dominance: We only tested one hand — would results differ for the other?

Procedural issues:

How consistent was your partner’s dropping technique?
Were there distractions (noise, movement) that affected some trials?
Did everyone follow the same instructions?





3.2 Memory Test: Mind Palace

The memory task measured working memory — how many items you can hold in mind while performing another task.
Miller (1956) famously proposed that we can hold about 7 ± 2 items in short-term memory — the “magical number seven.” But the distraction task (maths problems) interferes with rehearsal, so performance typically drops.
We’ll also examine the serial position effect: people tend to remember words from the beginning of a list (primacy) and end of a list (recency) better than the middle. Your position-by-position recall data will let us test this pattern.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were the words presented at the same speed for everyone?
Could everyone hear clearly from where they were sitting?
Was the recall period the same length for all participants?

Potential biases:

Prior exposure: Had you seen any of the words recently?
Language background: Were the words equally familiar to everyone?
Strategy use: Some people use chunking or visualisation — should we control for this?

Procedural issues:

Was the distraction task equally difficult for everyone?
Did the timing between presentation and recall vary?
How was recall scored? (exact spelling? close enough?)





3.3 Task 2: Time and Magnitude Perception (Time Warp)

How accurately do we perceive time? Research shows that our internal clocks are surprisingly inaccurate and can be influenced by many factors.
This station measured three types of estimation:

Time estimation — How accurately could you judge 60 seconds?
Visual magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge line lengths by looking?
Tactile magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge lengths by touch alone?







TipCross-Modal Comparison



By comparing visual and tactile estimation, we can explore whether some senses are more accurate than others for judging physical properties.








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

When exactly did the stopwatch start? When you said “start” or when your partner pressed it?
How precisely were line lengths measured?
Was string tension consistent across tactile trials?

Potential biases:

Counting: Did you count seconds in your head? (This is a strategy, not pure time perception)
Anchoring: Did early estimates influence later ones?
Expectation: Did you adjust estimates based on feedback?

Procedural issues:

Could you see any clocks or time displays?
Were there environmental cues (regular sounds, movements)?
Was it quiet enough to concentrate?





3.4 Task 3: Psychic Staring (Sixth Sense)

Can humans detect when they’re being watched? This is a testable empirical question!
The staring detection task uses signal detection theory:

Hits: Correctly detecting when someone IS staring
False alarms: Saying “staring” when they’re NOT
Misses: Saying “not staring” when they ARE
Correct rejections: Correctly detecting when they’re NOT staring

If people cannot actually detect staring, we’d expect performance to be at chance level (about 50% correct, or 3 out of 6 trials).






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Could you detect your partner through peripheral vision?
Were there sounds or movements that gave it away?
Was “staring” defined consistently? (How long? How intense?)

Potential biases:

Response bias: Did you tend to say “yes” or “no” more often?
Pattern-seeking: Did you assume alternating patterns?
Confirmation bias: Did you interpret ambiguous feelings as evidence for your guess?

Procedural issues:

How reliably did your partner randomise staring/not-staring?
Was the duration of each trial consistent?
Could other people in the room affect the “being watched” feeling?





3.5 Task 4: Randomness (Lady Luck)

Humans are notoriously bad at generating random sequences. When asked to produce “random” numbers, people:

Avoid repeating the same number twice in a row (even though true randomness includes repetitions)
Avoid patterns (even though random sequences often contain streaks)
Favour certain numbers (often 7!)

This station also included dice rolling and coin flipping, which let us compare true random outcomes (from dice/coins) with human-generated random sequences.






NoteThe Gambler’s Fallacy



Many people believe that after a streak of heads, tails is “due.” This is false — each flip is independent. Your data will likely show longer runs than most people expect!








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were all 20 numbers recorded correctly?
Were dice rolls and coin flips recorded accurately?
How were “runs” counted? Was this consistent?

Potential biases:

Number preferences: Did cultural factors affect which numbers felt “random”?
Avoidance of repetition: This is a known bias — but did you try to overcome it?
Anchoring: Did your previous number influence your next choice?

Procedural issues:

Was there time pressure that affected your choices?
Did you understand what “random” meant in this context?
Were the dice fair? Were coins flipped properly?





3.6 Task 5: Metacognition (Frontal Lob)

Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking — including how well you know your own abilities.
The throwing task measured calibration: the match between your self-assessed ability and your actual performance.

Overconfidence: Rating yourself higher than your performance
Underconfidence: Rating yourself lower than your performance
Well-calibrated: Your rating matches your performance

Research consistently shows that people are poorly calibrated — often overconfident about easy tasks and underconfident about hard ones.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

How were successful throws defined? What about balls that bounced in?
Who counted the successes — participant or tester?
Was counting accurate across 10 throws?

Potential biases:

Self-serving bias: Did you rate yourself higher because you wanted to be good?
Social desirability: Did having a partner watching affect your self-rating?
Anchoring: Did the 1-10 scale influence what felt like a “reasonable” rating?

Procedural issues:

Was the throwing distance the same for everyone?
Was the target positioned consistently?
Did throwing technique vary (overarm, underarm)?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
4 The Pre-Post Design
DataLab used a within-subjects design to measure mood change. You rated your mood, energy, and stress both before and after the stations.
This design is powerful because each person serves as their own control. By comparing your “before” to your “after,” we eliminate individual differences — we’re measuring change within you, not differences between people.






ImportantTeaching Application



When we learn about paired t-tests, we’ll analyse whether DataLab systematically affected mood, energy, or stress. Did participation make people feel better? Worse? More or less stressed?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
5 Why This Matters
You’ve just experienced something important: collecting data is hard.
The methodological issues above aren’t criticisms — they’re reality. Even professional researchers face these challenges. The difference is that professionals:

Use standardised procedures — detailed protocols that specify exactly how to do each step
Define variables operationally — clear definitions of what counts as a “catch” or a “success”
Train testers — so everyone administers tasks the same way
Control the environment — quiet rooms, consistent setups, minimal distractions
Check inter-rater reliability — do two testers recording the same event get the same result?

When we analyse your DataLab data, we’ll need to keep these limitations in mind. Some variability in the data reflects genuine individual differences. Some reflects measurement error and procedural inconsistencies.
Learning to tell the difference is what research methods is all about.

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
section: 6 Why We Generated Our Own Data
text:
6 Why We Generated Our Own Data

6.1 Learning with Real Data
When we analyse data you’ve generated:

You understand what the numbers represent
You can connect statistics to real experiences
The results are genuinely unknown (not textbook examples)



6.2 Experiencing Both Roles
Acting as both participant and tester taught you:

The importance of standardised procedures
How instructions affect behaviour
Why research protocols exist



6.3 Understanding Limitations
Having collected data yourself, you now understand:

Why researchers obsess over procedures
How small variations can affect results
That “messy data” is normal — interpretation requires care

Your group will work together for the rest of the term — choosing a topic, designing a study, collecting data, and sharing results. Each person then writes their own individual Research Report (2,000 words, due mid–late April).

Part 2: Choose Your Topic

What Makes a Good Topic?
Your project needs to be:

Testable with a t-test — either a between-groups comparison (independent samples) or a within-subjects comparison (repeated measures) across two conditions
Feasible in scale — your group of 3–4 should be able to run ~15–20 participants in a couple of hours. Think short tasks: memorise 20 words, 2-minute distractor, 2-minute recall — that sort of size
Ethically straightforward — no deception that could cause distress, no sensitive topics, nothing requiring specialist equipment

Part 3: Find a Key Paper

Why You Need One
Every project needs a foundation — a paper that gives you:

A concept or theory to base your hypothesis on
An operationalisation you can adapt (how did they measure the DV? What stimuli did they use?)
A procedure you can build from or simplify

A single well-chosen paper is more valuable than three vaguely related ones.


Where to Look
Starting-point papers are available on Learn for each of the 9 example topics:

Project papers folder on Learn — a couple of papers per topic. They’re not all perfect, but they offer a starting point for operationalisation, background, or methodology.

These may not be the ideal paper for your specific angle — a quick literature search may turn up something better:






TipQuick Search Tips




PsycINFO (via Goldsmiths Library) — psychology-specific, peer-reviewed
Google Scholar (scholar.google.com) — broader coverage, citation tracking
Start with your key variables as search terms
Use quotation marks for exact phrases (e.g., "background music" AND recall)



If your group has chosen its own topic (not from the list), finding a source paper is essential — it’s what your methodology and hypothesis will be built on.
1. When you first find a paper, you should read:
The entire paper carefullyThe abstract first, to check relevanceOnly the resultsThe reference list
2. The Method section of a relevant paper helps you because:
You can copy their procedureIt shows how similar studies have been designed and measured the DVIt tells you what results to expectIt’s not useful for your project

TipWhat This Chapter Covers



This reading accompanies the Week 16 lecture on APA report writing. It explains the structure of an APA-style lab report, how to write a Method section (using your Research Plan as a worked example), and the writing conventions you’ll need for academic psychology writing.

The sections of an APA lab report and what goes in each
How to write a Method section (the same structure as your Research Plan)
APA writing conventions (tense, person, statistical notation)
Common mistakes and how to avoid them
This chapter is your reference guide for writing in psychology. You’ll come back to it repeatedly over the coming weeks as you write your Research Report.

title: Week 16 Lecture Reading
text:
The APA Lab Report
Psychology uses a standardised format for reporting research — the APA (American Psychological Association) style. Every lab report follows the same structure, which means readers always know where to find the information they need.
Your Research Report (due mid-late April, 2,500 words) will follow this format exactly.

The Seven Sections








Section
Purpose
Approximate proportion




Title Page
Identifies the study, author, and institution
—


Abstract
~150-word summary of the entire study
~5%


Introduction
Background literature, rationale, and hypothesis
~25-30%


Method
What you did — design, participants, materials, procedure
~25-30%


Results
What you found — descriptive and inferential statistics
~15-20%


Discussion
What it means — interpretation, limitations, future directions
~20-25%


References
Full APA-formatted reference list
—





The Hourglass Shape
APA reports follow an hourglass shape:

Introduction moves from broad to narrow — starting with the general topic, reviewing specific research, and ending with your hypothesis
Method and Results are the narrow middle — precise, detailed, specific
Discussion moves from narrow to broad — starting with your findings, interpreting them, and ending with wider implications

This shape means you tell a story: here’s what we know, here’s what we did, here’s what we found, and here’s what it means.

title: Week 16 Lecture Reading
text:
Section by Section

Title Page
Your title should be concise and informative. It should include your key variables.

Good title: “The Effect of Word Concreteness on Free Recall Performance”


Poor title: “My Psychology Experiment” or “Memory Study”

Include your name, student number, and the module code (PS50008A).


Abstract
The abstract is a brief summary of the entire study, typically around 150 words. It should cover:

One or two sentences of background and rationale
One sentence on method (design, participants, key task)
One or two sentences on key results (with statistics)
One sentence on conclusion and implications







TipWhen to Write the Abstract



Write the abstract last — after every other section is complete. It’s a summary, not a preview. You can’t summarise something you haven’t written yet.




Introduction
The Introduction builds a logical argument from existing literature to your specific research question. Think of it as a funnel:

General topic area — What is the broad field? (e.g., memory research)
Key research findings — What have other researchers found? (cite specific studies)
Gap or question — What hasn’t been addressed or needs further investigation?
Your study — What are you investigating and why?
Hypothesis — Your specific, testable prediction


Common mistakes in Introductions:

Starting with a dictionary definition (“The Oxford Dictionary defines memory as…”)
Listing studies without connecting them (“Smith found X. Jones found Y. Brown found Z.”)
Including your results
Making claims without citing evidence




Method
The Method section describes what you did in enough detail that another researcher could replicate your study. It has four standard subsections.






ImportantYour Research Plan Practises Method Writing



The Research Plan you’re submitting this week is a standalone assessment on its own topic. But it’s structured exactly like a Method section — the same four subsections you’ll use when you write the Method for your Research Report (which is on a different topic, based on your group project).



Design
State your experimental design and justify it. Include:

Type of design (between-subjects or within-subjects)
Independent variable and its levels
Dependent variable and how it’s measured


Weak: “We used a between-subjects design.”


Strong: “A between-subjects design was used. The independent variable was word type with two levels: concrete words and abstract words. The dependent variable was the number of words correctly recalled out of 15. A between-subjects design was chosen to avoid practice and fatigue effects that could confound recall performance.”

Notice the strong version includes justification — it explains why this design was chosen, not just what it is.


Participants
Describe who took part and how they were recruited:

Total number of participants (and per condition if between-subjects)
Recruitment method (e.g., opportunity sampling)
Key demographics (age range, mean age, gender breakdown)
Any inclusion or exclusion criteria


Good example: “Twenty participants (15 female, 5 male; Mage = 21.3, SD = 2.1) were recruited via opportunity sampling from the student population at Goldsmiths, University of London. All were native English speakers aged 18 or over. Ten participants were randomly allocated to each condition.”



Materials
Describe everything you used to run the study:

Stimuli (word lists, images, questionnaires — with examples)
How materials were created or sourced
Key properties (e.g., word frequency, number of items)
Equipment (if relevant)


Good example: “Two word lists were constructed, each containing 15 words. The concrete list contained words referring to physical objects (e.g., hammer, bicycle, elephant). The abstract list contained words referring to concepts or qualities (e.g., freedom, honesty, courage). Lists were matched for word frequency and syllable count using the MRC Psycholinguistic Database.”



Procedure
Describe what happened, step by step, in chronological order:

What participants experienced from start to finish
Timing of each phase
Standardised instructions (summarised, not verbatim)
Ethical safeguards — informed consent and debriefing


Good example: “Participants were tested individually in a quiet room. After providing written informed consent, they were presented with their assigned word list displayed on a computer screen and given two minutes to study the words. The list was then removed and participants counted backwards from 100 for one minute as a distractor task. They were then given two minutes to write down as many words as they could recall, in any order. Finally, participants were fully debriefed about the purpose of the study and thanked for their participation.”


Common mistakes in Method sections:

Too vague — “Participants did a memory test” (What kind? How long? How scored?)
Including results — Method describes what you did, not what you found
Missing justification — State your design AND explain why
Wrong tense — Method uses past tense
Forgetting ethics — Always mention consent and debriefing





Results
The Results section reports what you found using both descriptive and inferential statistics. A standard results paragraph for a t-test includes:

Descriptive statistics — means and standard deviations for each condition
Inferential test — the t-test result with full APA notation
Effect size — Cohen’s d with 95% confidence interval
Brief interpretation — what the numbers mean in words


Complete results paragraph: “Participants in the concrete word condition recalled significantly more words (M = 11.2, SD = 2.4) than those in the abstract word condition (M = 8.7, SD = 2.1). An independent-samples t-test confirmed this difference was statistically significant, t(18) = 2.48, p = .023, d = 1.11, 95% CI [0.17, 2.03]. This represents a large effect, suggesting that word concreteness has a substantial influence on free recall performance.”

We’ll cover Results reporting in full detail in Week 19.


Discussion
The Discussion interprets your findings and places them in context:

Restate key findings (in words, not statistics)
Interpret — what do the results mean? Were your hypotheses supported?
Relate to literature — do your findings support or contradict previous research?
Limitations — what could have affected the results? What would you do differently?
Future directions — what should researchers investigate next?
Conclusion — a brief take-home message

We’ll cover Discussion writing in Week 20.


References
Every source you cite in-text must appear in the reference list, and vice versa. Use APA 7th edition format.

Journal article format:
Walker, I., & Hulme, C. (1999). Concrete words are easier to recall than abstract words: Evidence for a semantic contribution to short-term serial recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 25(5), 1256–1271. https://doi.org/10.1037/0278-7393.25.5.1256







TipUse a Reference Manager



Zotero (free) or Mendeley (free) will format your references automatically and save you hours of manual formatting. Install one now if you haven’t already.

title: Week 16 Lecture Reading
text:
APA Writing Conventions

Tense








Section
Tense
Example




Introduction (established findings)
Present
“Research suggests that…”


Introduction (specific past studies)
Past
“Walker and Hulme (1999) found that…”


Method
Past
“Participants were randomly allocated…”


Results
Past
“The difference was statistically significant…”


Discussion (your findings)
Past
“The results showed that…”


Discussion (implications)
Present
“These findings suggest that…”





Person and Voice

Third person is preferred throughout

“Participants were asked to…” (not “I asked participants to…”)
“The study aimed to…” (not “We aimed to…”)

Passive voice is acceptable in Method and Results

“Words were presented for two minutes”

Active voice for describing others’ research

“Walker and Hulme (1999) demonstrated that…”




Statistical Notation
Key rules:

Italicise all statistical symbols: t, F, r, p, M, SD, d, n, N
No leading zero for statistics bounded by ±1: p = .023, r = .72
Leading zero for statistics that can exceed ±1: M = 0.45
Exact p-values to three decimal places: p = .023 (not p < .05)
Exception: when p < .001, report as p < .001 (never p = .000)


APA t-test format: t(18) = 2.48, p = .023, d = 1.11, 95% CI [0.17, 2.03]

title: Week 16 Lecture Reading
text:
Key Terms

APA format — The standardised style for writing and formatting psychology research reports, set by the American Psychological Association.
Replication — The ability of another researcher to repeat a study using the same method. A good Method section enables replication.
Operationalisation — Defining a variable in terms of how it is measured. For example, “memory” operationalised as “number of words correctly recalled out of 15.”
Effect size — A standardised measure of the magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size. Cohen’s d is used for comparing two means.

title: Week 16 Lecture Reading
text:
Summary

APA lab reports follow a standard seven-section structure: Title, Abstract, Introduction, Method, Results, Discussion, References
The report has an hourglass shape — broad to narrow to broad
Your Research Plan practises Method writing — the same structure you’ll use for your Research Report
Use past tense for Method and Results, present tense for established findings
Italicise statistical symbols; no leading zero for p and r
Justify every decision — don’t just say what, explain why
The Research Report builds week by week from now

title: Week 15: Correlation
text:
Key Concepts

Scatterplots

Scatterplot: A graph showing the relationship between two continuous variables
Direction: Positive (upward trend) or negative (downward trend)
Strength: How closely points cluster around the line of best fit
Linearity: Whether the relationship follows a straight line



Correlation Coefficients

Pearson’s r: Measures linear relationship between two continuous variables
Spearman’s rho: Measures monotonic relationship; uses ranked data
Range: Both range from -1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive)
Zero: No linear relationship (but could still be non-linear!)



Interpreting Correlation Strength



r value
Interpretation




.10 - .29
Weak


.30 - .49
Moderate


.50 - 1.0
Strong



Note: These are guidelines; context matters for interpretation.


Correlation vs Causation

Third variable problem: An unmeasured variable may cause both
Directionality problem: A correlates with B, but does A cause B or B cause A?
Temporal precedence: Cause must precede effect in time



APA Reporting

Report as: r(df) = .xx, p = .xxx or rho(df) = .xx, p = .xxx
Example: “There was a significant positive correlation between confidence and accuracy, r(48) = .42, p = .003.”

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
What Is Correlation?
Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables.

Strength: How tightly the data points cluster around a line (from weak to strong)
Direction: Whether variables increase together (positive) or one increases as the other decreases (negative)


The Correlation Coefficient (r)
The correlation coefficient r ranges from -1 to +1:



Value
Interpretation




r = +1
Perfect positive relationship


r = +0.7
Strong positive relationship


r = +0.3
Weak positive relationship


r = 0
No linear relationship


r = -0.3
Weak negative relationship


r = -0.7
Strong negative relationship


r = -1
Perfect negative relationship









ImportantDirection vs Strength



The sign tells you direction; the absolute value tells you strength. r = -0.8 is a stronger relationship than r = +0.3.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
Reading Scatterplots

Why Visualise?
Before looking at numbers, always examine a scatterplot. It reveals:

The direction of the relationship (positive, negative, or none)
The strength of the relationship (tight cluster vs spread out)
The shape (linear vs curved)
Any unusual patterns or outliers



What to Look For
Each point represents one participant:

X-axis: One variable
Y-axis: The other variable

Pattern Guide:



Pattern

Interpreting Correlation Output
When you run a correlation test, you’ll see output like this:

     0.15  0.63

What Each Part Means

The test statistic

Is it significant? → Yes, p = 0.003 < 0.05
What’s the CI? → [0.15, 0.63] - the true r is likely in this range

TipInterpreting the Confidence Interval



A 95% CI of [0.15, 0.63] means we’re fairly confident the true population correlation is somewhere in this range. Since it doesn’t include 0, the correlation is statistically significant.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
Pearson vs Spearman

Pearson’s r (Most Common)
Use when:

Both variables are continuous
Relationship is approximately linear
Data are roughly normally distributed



Spearman’s rho (ρ)
Use when:

Data are ordinal (ranked)
Relationship is monotonic but not linear
Data have outliers or are skewed

Both are interpreted the same way — they range from -1 to +1 with the same strength guidelines.

title: Chapter 10: Understanding Correlation Output
text:
Correlation Does NOT Mean Causation






WarningCritical Point



A correlation between X and Y does NOT mean X causes Y. This is possibly the most important lesson in research methods.



Why Not?
Three possible explanations for any correlation:

X causes Y: More sleep → better performance
Y causes X: Better performance → more sleep (less stress)
Z causes both: Good health → more sleep AND better performance

Without experimental manipulation, we cannot determine which explanation is correct.


Classic Example
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated.
Does ice cream cause drowning? No! A third variable (hot weather) causes both:

Hot weather → more ice cream sales
Hot weather → more swimming → more drowning



DataLab Example
Self-rating and throwing performance might be correlated.
Does thinking you’re good make you perform better? Possible alternatives:

Past experience → higher self-rating AND better performance
Natural ability → higher self-rating AND better performance

We can’t determine causation from correlation alone.

title: Week 15 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 1: Reading Paired T-Test Output

Exercise 1: Basic Paired T-Test (EDS-Style)
A mental rotation study measured response times for 10 participants at two rotation angles. Here’s the R output:
> # Descriptive statistics
> data %>%
+   group_by(condition) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(RT), SD = sd(RT), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  condition      Mean    SD     n
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 30_degree      285.  42.3    10
2 150_degree     312.  51.1    10

> # Paired t-test
> t.test(data$RT_30, data$RT_150, paired = TRUE)

    Paired t-test

data:  data$RT_30 and data$RT_150
t = -2.847, df = 9, p-value = 0.0192
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -49.82 -5.38
sample estimates:
mean of the differences
                  -27.6
a) Why is paired = TRUE appropriate for this study?






TipShow Answer





paired = TRUE is appropriate because: - The same 10 participants completed both conditions - Each participant provided data for BOTH 30° and 150° rotations - This is a within-subjects (repeated measures) design - Each score in the 30° condition has a matched score in the 150° condition



b) What are the key statistics from this output?






TipShow Answer






t-statistic: t = -2.847
Degrees of freedom: df = 9 (number of pairs - 1 = 10 - 1)
p-value: p = 0.0192
95% CI for the difference: [-49.82, -5.38]
Mean difference: -27.6ms (30° was faster than 150° by ~28ms)




c) Is this result statistically significant?






TipShow Answer





Yes, because p = .0192 < .05. We reject the null hypothesis that there is no difference between conditions.



d) Write a complete APA results paragraph.






TipShow Answer






A paired-samples t-test revealed that participants responded significantly faster to 30° rotations (M = 285ms, SD = 42.3ms) than to 150° rotations (M = 312ms, SD = 51.1ms), t(9) = -2.85, p = .019, 95% CI [-49.82, -5.38]. This supports the hypothesis that mental rotation time increases with greater rotation angles.







Exercise 2: Interpreting the Mean Difference
From Exercise 1:
sample estimates:
mean of the differences
                  -27.6
a) What does -27.6 mean?






TipShow Answer





On average, the 30° condition was 27.6ms faster than the 150° condition. The negative sign indicates the first condition (30°) had lower values than the second (150°).



b) How does the sign relate to the direction of the effect?






TipShow Answer






Negative difference = First variable is LOWER than second
Here: RT_30 - RT_150 = -27.6, so RT_30 < RT_150
30° rotations are faster (lower RT) than 150° rotations







Exercise 3: The Confidence Interval
From Exercise 1:
95 percent confidence interval:
 -49.82 -5.38
a) What does this interval tell us?






TipShow Answer





We are 95% confident that the true population difference between the 30° and 150° conditions is between -49.82ms and -5.38ms.
In other words: In the population, 30° rotations are between 5.38ms and 49.82ms faster than 150° rotations.



b) Why is it significant that the entire interval is negative?






TipShow Answer






The interval doesn’t include zero
This means the difference is unlikely to be zero in the population
We can be confident there IS a real difference
The interval being entirely negative tells us the direction: 30° is consistently faster

title: Week 15 Self-Assessment
section: Part 2: Independent vs Paired - Key Differences
text:
Part 2: Independent vs Paired - Key Differences

Exercise 4: Comparing Output
Independent t-test output:
    Welch Two Sample t-test
t = 2.36, df = 37.2, p-value = 0.0236
Paired t-test output:
    Paired t-test
t = -2.847, df = 9, p-value = 0.0192
a) How do the degrees of freedom differ?






TipShow Answer






Independent: df is based on total sample size (~n₁ + n₂ - 2, or Welch’s adjusted df)
Paired: df = number of pairs - 1 (e.g., 10 pairs → df = 9)

The paired test has fewer df because it’s based on the number of matched pairs, not individual data points.



b) Why might a paired test be more powerful?






TipShow Answer





Paired tests control for individual differences: - Each person serves as their own control - Reduces variability due to person-to-person differences - This “removes” the variance between participants - Results in a more sensitive test (more likely to detect a real effect)






Exercise 5: Choosing the Right Test
For each scenario, state whether you would use a paired or independent t-test, and why:
a) Comparing anxiety before and after a therapy session.






TipShow Answer





Paired t-test - Same participants measured at two time points (before and after).



b) Comparing test scores between a treatment group and control group.






TipShow Answer





Independent t-test - Different participants in each group (treatment vs control).



c) Measuring response time to faces vs houses (same participants see both).






TipShow Answer





Paired t-test - Same participants in both conditions (within-subjects design).



d) Comparing memory performance between young adults and older adults.






TipShow Answer





Independent t-test - Different participants (you can’t be both young and old).



e) Participants rate two brands of coffee for taste.






TipShow Answer





Paired t-test - Same participants rating both brands.

title: Week 15 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 3: EDS Practice Questions

Exercise 6: Mental Rotation Scenario
This mirrors the EDS Assignment format:
Scenario: Researcher investigated mental rotation. 10 participants viewed pairs of 3D shapes rotated by either 30° or 150° and judged if they were the same or different. Response time (ms) was recorded.
> # Descriptive statistics
> data %>%
+   group_by(rotation) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(RT), SD = sd(RT), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  rotation    Mean    SD     n
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 30_degree   289.  38.7    10
2 150_degree  318.  45.2    10

> # Statistical test
> t.test(data$RT_30, data$RT_150, paired = TRUE)

    Paired t-test

data:  data$RT_30 and data$RT_150
t = -3.12, df = 9, p-value = 0.0124
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -50.13 -7.87
sample estimates:
mean of the differences
                    -29
Question 1 (5 marks): State the researcher’s hypothesis.






TipShow Answer





The researcher hypothesized that response times would be longer for 150° rotations compared to 30° rotations. More specifically, greater rotation angles require more mental rotation, leading to longer processing times.



Question 2 (16-20 marks): Identify the design components.






TipShow Answer






Design type: Within-subjects / repeated measures
Independent variable: Rotation angle (30° vs 150°)
Dependent variable: Response time (in milliseconds)
Data type: Ratio data (continuous, has a true zero)




Question 3 (10 marks): Report the descriptive statistics in APA format and interpret the pattern.






TipShow Answer





APA format: > Participants responded faster in the 30° condition (M = 289ms, SD = 38.7ms) than in the 150° condition (M = 318ms, SD = 45.2ms).
Interpretation: > The descriptives show that response times were approximately 29ms slower when shapes were rotated 150° compared to 30°. This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that greater rotation angles require more mental processing.



Question 4 (15 marks): Interpret the t-test output.






TipShow Answer





a) Why paired = TRUE? (3 marks) The paired test is appropriate because the same 10 participants completed both conditions (within-subjects design).
b) State t, df, p (3 marks) t(9) = -3.12, p = .012
c) Is this significant? (4 marks) Yes, the result is statistically significant because p = .012 < .05. We reject the null hypothesis of no difference.
d) Interpret the CI (5 marks) The 95% CI [-50.13, -7.87] indicates we are 95% confident the true difference lies between -50.13ms and -7.87ms. Since this interval doesn’t include zero, we can be confident there is a genuine difference. The entirely negative interval confirms that 30° rotations are faster than 150° rotations.



Question 5 (5 marks): Write a complete APA results paragraph.






TipShow Answer






A paired-samples t-test was conducted to examine the effect of rotation angle on response time. Participants responded significantly faster to shapes rotated 30° (M = 289ms, SD = 38.7ms) than shapes rotated 150° (M = 318ms, SD = 45.2ms), t(9) = -3.12, p = .012, 95% CI [-50.13, -7.87]. These findings support the hypothesis that mental rotation time increases with greater rotation angles.

title: Week 15 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 4: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Exercise 7: Error Identification
What’s wrong with each statement?
a) “The paired t-test showed t = 2.5, df = 19, so there were 19 participants.”






TipShow Answer





Error: In a paired t-test, df = n - 1. So df = 19 means there were 20 participants (or 20 pairs), not 19.



b) “The confidence interval was [-8.2, 4.5], so the result was significant.”






TipShow Answer





Error: This CI includes zero, so the result is NOT significant. When CI includes zero, we cannot rule out no difference.



c) “We used an independent t-test because each participant was tested twice.”






TipShow Answer





Error: If each participant was tested twice, you need a paired t-test, not independent. Independent tests are for different participants in each condition.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
TipBefore You Begin



This chapter introduces correlation — a fundamental tool for understanding relationships between variables. Unlike t-tests, which compare groups, correlation asks whether two continuous variables tend to move together.


This chapter covers:

Relationships between variables
Scatterplots and visual patterns
Pearson’s r (for linear relationships)
Spearman’s rho (for ranked data)
Interpreting correlation strength
Why correlation does not imply causation

All concepts are illustrated using DataLab examples from your class.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
TipBefore You Begin



This chapter introduces correlation — a fundamental tool for understanding relationships between variables. Unlike t-tests, which compare groups, correlation asks whether two continuous variables tend to move together.


This chapter covers:

Relationships between variables
Scatterplots and visual patterns
Pearson’s r (for linear relationships)
Spearman’s rho (for ranked data)
Interpreting correlation strength
Why correlation does not imply causation

All concepts are illustrated using DataLab examples from your class.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
Part 1: Thinking About Relationships

A New Question
So far, we’ve focused on comparing groups:

Do concrete words lead to better memory than abstract words?
Does mood improve after the DataLab session?

But many research questions ask about relationships:

Do people who sleep more perform better on cognitive tasks?
Is self-confidence related to actual performance?
Do extraverts report higher mood?

These questions aren’t about group differences. They’re about whether two variables co-vary — when one goes up, does the other tend to go up (or down)?


What Is a Correlation?

Correlation: A statistical measure of the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables.

Correlation answers: When one variable changes, does the other variable tend to change in a predictable way?


Positive vs Negative Relationships
Positive correlation: As one variable increases, the other tends to increase.

Sleep hours ↑ → Performance ↑
Study time ↑ → Exam scores ↑
Age ↑ → Vocabulary ↑

Negative correlation: As one variable increases, the other tends to decrease.

Stress ↑ → Sleep quality ↓
TV time ↑ → Exercise ↓
Anxiety ↑ → Performance ↓

No correlation: No predictable relationship between variables.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
Part 2: Scatterplots — Seeing Relationships

Why Visualise First?
Before calculating any numbers, you should always plot your data. A scatterplot reveals:

The direction of the relationship (positive, negative, or none)
The strength of the relationship (tight cluster vs spread out)
The shape (linear vs curved)
Any unusual patterns or outliers



Anatomy of a Scatterplot
Each point represents one participant:

X-axis: One variable (often the predictor or independent variable)
Y-axis: The other variable (often the outcome or dependent variable)
