title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
Part 3: Pearson’s r

The Correlation Coefficient
Pearson’s r is the most common measure of correlation. It quantifies what you see in a scatterplot as a single number.

Pearson’s r: A measure of the linear relationship between two continuous variables, ranging from -1 to +1.



Interpreting r



Value of r
Meaning




r = +1
Perfect positive correlation


r = 0
No linear correlation


r = -1
Perfect negative correlation



The sign tells you the direction; the magnitude tells you the strength.


Strength Guidelines
Cohen (1988) suggested these benchmarks:




r




.10
Small


.30
Medium


.50
Large









WarningContext Matters



These are rough guidelines. In some fields (e.g., personality psychology), r = .30 is typical. In others (e.g., physics), r = .90 might be expected.




What r Actually Measures
Pearson’s r measures how well the data points cluster around a straight line.

r = 1: All points fall exactly on an upward-sloping line
r = 0: Points are scattered with no linear pattern
r = -1: All points fall exactly on a downward-sloping line

In practice, you’ll rarely see r = 1 or r = -1 in psychology. Real data is messy!


The Formula (For Reference)
\[r = \frac{\sum{(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}}{\sqrt{\sum{(x_i - \bar{x})^2} \sum{(y_i - \bar{y})^2}}}\]
You won’t need to calculate this by hand — software does it instantly. But the key idea is:

The numerator measures how much x and y co-vary (move together)
The denominator standardises this to fall between -1 and +1

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
section: Part 4: Worked Example — Self-Rating vs Performance
text:
Part 4: Worked Example — Self-Rating vs Performance

DataLab Context
In the Frontal Lob task, participants rated how good they thought they’d be at throwing (1-10 scale), then we measured their actual accuracy.
Research question: Do people who rate themselves higher actually perform better?


The Data
Suppose we have these results from 20 participants:

Mean self-rating: 5.8
Mean accuracy: 52%
Pearson’s r = 0.42



Interpretation
r = 0.42 suggests a medium positive correlation between self-rating and actual performance.
In words: People who rated themselves as better throwers tended to be somewhat better — but the relationship isn’t perfect. There’s substantial individual variation.


Visualising r = 0.42
Accuracy (%)
    |
70  |        •     •
    |      •   •  •
60  |    •  •   •
    |   • •    •
50  |  •  •
    | •
40  |•
    +------------------
       4    6    8    10
         Self-rating
The upward trend is visible, but points don’t fall tightly on a line.


Statistical Significance of r
We can test whether r is significantly different from zero (i.e., whether there’s evidence of a relationship in the population).
With n = 20 and r = 0.42:

t-statistic: 1.95
df = 18
p = .067

Since p > .05, we would say: “The correlation was not statistically significant, r(18) = .42, p = .067.”






NoteSample Size Matters



With larger samples, the same r would be significant. Small samples lack the power to detect moderate correlations.




Reporting Correlations (APA Format)

There was a positive correlation between self-rated ability and actual throwing accuracy, although this did not reach statistical significance, r(18) = .42, p = .067.

Or, if significant:

Self-rated ability was significantly positively correlated with actual throwing accuracy, r(58) = .42, p = .001.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
Part 5: Spearman’s Rho (ρ)

When to Use Spearman
Pearson’s r assumes:

Both variables are continuous
The relationship is linear

When these assumptions are violated, use Spearman’s rho (ρ or rs).

Spearman’s rho: A correlation based on ranked data. It measures monotonic relationships (consistently increasing or decreasing, not necessarily linear).



Ranked Data
Spearman works by:

Converting each variable to ranks (1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.)
Calculating the correlation between the ranks

This makes it robust to outliers and non-linear patterns.


When to Choose Which







Situation
Use




Both variables are continuous and normally distributed
Pearson’s r


One or both variables are ordinal (e.g., Likert scales)
Spearman’s ρ


Relationship appears non-linear but monotonic
Spearman’s ρ


Data has outliers
Spearman’s ρ





DataLab Example
Rating scales (1-10) are technically ordinal — we can’t be sure the difference between 3 and 4 equals the difference between 7 and 8. For the mood ratings in DataLab, Spearman’s rho might be more appropriate than Pearson’s r.


Interpretation Is the Same
Spearman’s ρ is interpreted identically to Pearson’s r:

Ranges from -1 to +1
Same strength guidelines (.10 small, .30 medium, .50 large)
Same APA reporting format

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
section: Part 6: Understanding What Correlation Tells You
text:
Part 6: Understanding What Correlation Tells You

What r Squared Tells You
A useful way to understand correlation strength is r² (r squared).

r² (coefficient of determination): The proportion of variance in one variable that is “explained by” or “shared with” the other variable.




r
r²
Interpretation




.10
.01
1% shared variance


.30
.09
9% shared variance


.50
.25
25% shared variance


.70
.49
49% shared variance



Even a “medium” correlation of r = .30 means the two variables share only 9% of their variance. That leaves 91% unexplained!


The importance of R-squared






ImportantReality Check



A correlation of r = .42 sounds reasonable. But r² = .18 means self-rating explains only 18% of the variance in performance. The other 82% is due to other factors — practice, natural ability, luck, measurement error, etc.


This is why psychology is hard. Human behaviour is influenced by many factors, and any single variable rarely explains more than a small portion.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
section: Part 7: Correlation Does NOT Mean Causation
text:
Part 7: Correlation Does NOT Mean Causation

The Most Important Lesson

CRITICAL POINT: A correlation between X and Y does NOT mean X causes Y. This is possibly the most important thing you’ll learn in research methods.



Why Not?
Three possible explanations for any correlation:

X causes Y: More sleep → better performance
Y causes X: Better performance → more sleep (less stress)
Z causes both: Good health → more sleep AND better performance

Without experimental manipulation, we cannot determine which explanation is correct.


Classic Examples
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated.
Does ice cream cause drowning? No! A third variable (hot weather) causes both:

Hot weather → more ice cream sales
Hot weather → more swimming → more drowning

Countries with more Nobel Prize winners consume more chocolate.
Does chocolate make you smarter? More likely: - Wealthier countries → more chocolate consumption - Wealthier countries → better education → more Nobel Prizes


The DataLab Example
Self-rating and throwing performance are correlated (r = .42).
Does thinking you’re good make you perform better? Maybe — but there are alternatives:

Past experience → higher self-rating AND better performance
Natural ability → higher self-rating AND better performance
Overconfidence → high self-rating but NOT better performance

We can’t determine causation from correlation alone.


When Can We Infer Causation?
Only with experimental manipulation:

Randomly assign participants to conditions
Manipulate one variable
Measure the effect on another variable

Because random assignment controls for confounding variables, differences between groups can be attributed to the manipulation.






NoteThe Memory Experiment



The memory study (abstract vs concrete words) WAS an experiment. Random assignment to conditions allows causal inference: word type caused the difference in recall.
The self-rating vs performance study was correlational — no causal inference possible.

title: Chapter 9: Correlation
text:
Part 8: Common Mistakes with Correlation

Mistake 1: Assuming Linearity
Pearson’s r only measures linear relationships. Data can have a perfect curvilinear relationship with r = 0.
    Y |      •
      |    •   •
      |  •       •
      | •         •
      |•           •
      +-------------
              X
This U-shaped pattern has no linear correlation, but there’s clearly a relationship!
Solution: Always plot your data first.


Mistake 2: Restricted Range
If you only measure people who are similar on one variable, correlations appear weaker than they really are.
Example: If you only study university students (high ability), you might find no correlation between IQ and grades — but in the general population, there is one.


Mistake 3: Outliers
A single extreme point can dramatically inflate or deflate r.
Without outlier: r = .20      With outlier: r = .75

    •   •                         •   •           •
  •   •                         •   •
    • •                           • •
  •   •                         •   •
Solution: Check for outliers; consider Spearman’s ρ.


Mistake 4: Confusing Significance with Strength
With large samples, even tiny correlations become “significant”:

n = 1000, r = .08 → p < .05 (significant!)
But r² = .006 → explains 0.6% of variance (meaningless!)

Always report and interpret the effect size (r), not just p.

title: Week 14: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Key Concepts

Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST)

Null hypothesis (H₀): There is no effect or no difference
Alternative hypothesis (H₁): There is an effect or difference
p-value: Probability of obtaining results this extreme if H₀ were true
Alpha level: Threshold for significance (typically .05)



Making Decisions

p < .05: Reject H₀, result is statistically significant
p ≥ .05: Fail to reject H₀, result is not statistically significant
Type I error: Rejecting H₀ when it’s true (false positive)
Type II error: Failing to reject H₀ when it’s false (false negative)



t-tests



Design
t-test Type
R Function




Between-subjects
Independent samples
t.test(x, y)


Within-subjects
Paired samples
t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)





Confidence Intervals

What they show: Range of plausible values for the population parameter
95% CI interpretation: If we repeated the study many times, 95% of CIs would contain the true value
CI and significance: If the CI for a difference doesn’t include zero, the result is significant at p < .05
Width: Narrower CI = more precision



Effect Sizes (Cohen’s d)

What it measures: Difference between means in standard deviation units
Benchmarks: Small (0.2), Medium (0.5), Large (0.8)
Why important: Statistical significance ≠ practical importance
Report both: Always include effect size alongside p-value



APA Reporting

Format: t(df) = x.xx, p = .xxx, d = x.xx, 95% CI [x.xx, x.xx]
Example: t(48) = 2.34, p = .023, d = 0.67, 95% CI [0.12, 1.22]
Include: Test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, effect size, CI

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
When to Use a t-test
The t-test answers the question: Is the difference between two means larger than we’d expect by chance?
Use a t-test when you have:

A continuous outcome variable (e.g., reaction time, mood score)
Two groups to compare OR two measurements from the same people
Reasonably normally distributed data (or a large enough sample)


Types of t-tests








Type
When to Use
Example




Independent samples
Different people in each group
Room A vs Room B


Paired samples
Same people measured twice
Pre vs Post mood


One sample
Compare to a known value
Sample mean vs 50%

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
Independent Samples t-test
Use this when comparing different people in two groups.

Example: Comparing Rooms
Did Room A and Room B differ in reaction time?


Understanding the Output
    Welch Two Sample t-test

    data:  reaction_time by room
    t = -2.34, df = 45.2, p-value = 0.024
    alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
    95 percent confidence interval:
     -42.5  -3.2
    sample estimates:
    mean in group A   mean in group B
              265.3             288.1


What Each Part Means







Output
Meaning




t = -2.34
The t-statistic: how many standard errors the difference is from 0


df = 45.2
Degrees of freedom


p-value = 0.024
Probability of this difference (or larger) if null hypothesis is true


95 percent confidence interval
Range of plausible values for the true difference


sample estimates
The actual group means





Key Questions to Answer

What are the means? → Room A: 265.3 ms, Room B: 288.1 ms
What is t? → -2.34
Is it significant? → Yes, p = 0.024 < 0.05
What’s the CI? → [-42.5, -3.2] - the true difference is likely in this range
What does it mean? → Room A was faster than Room B







ImportantInterpreting the p-value



A p-value of 0.024 means: if there were truly no difference between rooms, we’d see a difference this large (or larger) about 2.4% of the time. Since this is less than 0.05, we conclude the difference is statistically significant.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
Paired Samples t-test
Use this when comparing the same people measured at two time points.

Example: Pre-Post Mood
Did mood change after DataLab?


Understanding the Output
    Paired t-test

    data:  mood_pre and mood_post
    t = -3.45, df = 29, p-value = 0.002
    alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
    95 percent confidence interval:
     -1.82  -0.45
    sample estimates:
    mean difference
              -1.13


Key Questions to Answer

What is the mean difference? → -1.13 (mood increased by 1.13 points)
Is it significant? → Yes, p = 0.002 < 0.05
What’s the CI? → [-1.82, -0.45] - the true change is likely in this range
What does it mean? → Mood significantly improved after DataLab



Why Paired Tests Are More Powerful
Paired tests account for individual differences. Consider:

Person A: Pre = 5, Post = 7 (change = +2)
Person B: Pre = 8, Post = 10 (change = +2)

Both people increased by 2 points, even though their baseline scores differ. The paired test focuses on the change within each person, not the raw scores.






TipRule of Thumb



If the same individuals provide both measurements, use a paired test. It’s more sensitive because it removes between-person variability.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
One Sample t-test
Use this to compare your sample mean to a specific value.

Example: Comparing to Chance
Is staring detection accuracy different from 50% (chance)?


Understanding the Output
    One Sample t-test

    data:  staring_accuracy
    t = 1.87, df = 29, p-value = 0.072
    alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0.5
    95 percent confidence interval:
     0.48  0.61
    sample estimates:
    mean of x
        0.545


Key Questions to Answer

What is the sample mean? → 54.5%
Is it significantly different from 50%? → No, p = 0.072 > 0.05
What does it mean? → Performance is not significantly better than chance

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
Effect Size: Cohen’s d
The p-value tells you whether a difference is statistically significant, but not whether it’s practically meaningful. For that, we use effect sizes.
Cohen’s d expresses the difference in standard deviation units:



d value
Interpretation




0.2
Small effect


0.5
Medium effect


0.8
Large effect




Example Output
    Cohen's d

    d estimate: 0.62
    95% CI: [0.15, 1.09]

    Interpretation: medium






ImportantWhy Effect Size Matters



A study with n = 1000 might find p < .001 for a tiny effect (d = 0.1). The effect is “real” but practically meaningless. Always report and interpret effect sizes alongside p-values.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
Assumptions of the t-test

1. Independence
Observations should be independent (one person’s score doesn’t influence another’s). This is about study design.


2. Normality
The data should be approximately normally distributed, especially for small samples.






TipRobustness



The t-test is quite robust to violations of normality, especially with larger samples (n > 30 per group). Don’t worry too much unless your data are severely skewed.




3. Homogeneity of Variance (for independent samples)
Groups should have similar variability. The Welch’s t-test (default in most software) handles unequal variances automatically.

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
Reporting t-tests (APA Style)

Template

[Group 1] (M = XX.X, SD = X.X) [were/was] [significantly/not significantly] [higher/lower/different] than [Group 2] (M = XX.X, SD = X.X), t(df) = X.XX, p = .XXX, d = X.XX.



Independent Samples Example

Participants in Room A (M = 265.3 ms, SD = 45.2) had significantly faster reaction times than those in Room B (M = 288.1 ms, SD = 52.1), t(45.2) = -2.34, p = .024, d = 0.47.



Paired Samples Example

Mood significantly increased from pre-session (M = 5.2, SD = 1.8) to post-session (M = 6.3, SD = 1.6), t(29) = 3.45, p = .002, d = 0.62.



Elements to Include

Group means and SDs
The t-value and df
The p-value
Effect size (Cohen’s d)
Direction of the difference

title: Chapter 8: Understanding t-test Output
text:
Common Interpretation Errors

Error 1: “p > .05 means no difference”
Wrong! A non-significant result means we can’t rule out chance — not that there’s definitely no effect. The study might lack power.


Error 2: “p < .001 means a huge effect”
Wrong! Statistical significance depends on sample size. Large samples can detect tiny effects. Always check effect size.


Error 3: “t = 2.34 is bigger than t = 1.98, so it’s more significant”
Misleading! t-values depend on sample size and variability. Compare p-values and effect sizes instead.


Error 4: Confusing paired and independent tests
Check: Are the same people in both conditions? If yes → paired. If no → independent.

title: Week 14 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 1: Reading Independent T-Test Output

Exercise 1: Basic Independent T-Test
A researcher compared anxiety scores between students who exercise regularly (n = 20) and those who don’t (n = 20). Here’s the R output:
> # Descriptive statistics
> data %>%
+   group_by(exercise) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(anxiety), SD = sd(anxiety), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  exercise       Mean    SD     n
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 no_exercise    48.2  12.4    20
2 regular        39.5  10.8    20

> # Independent t-test
> t.test(anxiety ~ exercise, data = data, paired = FALSE)

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  anxiety by exercise
t = 2.36, df = 37.2, p-value = 0.0236
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1.21 16.19
sample estimates:
mean in group no_exercise   mean in group regular
                     48.2                    39.5
a) What type of t-test is this?






TipShow Answer





This is a Welch Two Sample t-test (independent samples t-test). It compares two different groups of participants.



b) What are the key statistics from this output?






TipShow Answer






t-statistic: t = 2.36
Degrees of freedom: df = 37.2 (Welch’s adjustment)
p-value: p = 0.0236
95% CI for the difference: [1.21, 16.19]
Mean difference: 48.2 - 39.5 = 8.7 points




c) Is this result statistically significant at α = .05?






TipShow Answer





Yes, because p = .0236 < .05. We reject the null hypothesis.



d) Report this result in APA format.






TipShow Answer






An independent samples t-test revealed that students who did not exercise regularly reported significantly higher anxiety (M = 48.2, SD = 12.4) than those who exercised regularly (M = 39.5, SD = 10.8), t(37.2) = 2.36, p = .024, 95% CI [1.21, 16.19].







Exercise 2: Why Independent?
a) In Exercise 1, why was an independent t-test appropriate?






TipShow Answer





An independent t-test was appropriate because: - Two different groups of participants - Each person is in only one condition (exercise OR no exercise) - The groups are independent - scores in one group don’t affect scores in the other - This is a between-subjects design



b) What would make a paired t-test appropriate instead?






TipShow Answer





A paired t-test would be appropriate if: - The same participants were measured twice - For example: measuring anxiety BEFORE and AFTER an exercise program - Each data point in condition 1 is linked to a data point in condition 2 - This is a within-subjects design






Exercise 3: Interpreting the Confidence Interval
From Exercise 1:
95 percent confidence interval:
 1.21 16.19
a) What does this confidence interval represent?






TipShow Answer





We are 95% confident that the true population difference in anxiety scores between non-exercisers and regular exercisers is between 1.21 and 16.19 points.



b) Why does it matter that the interval doesn’t include zero?






TipShow Answer





If the interval included zero, the true difference might be zero (no real difference). Since it doesn’t include zero: - We can be confident there IS a real difference - This is consistent with the significant p-value - The groups genuinely differ in the population

title: Week 14 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 2: Design Recognition

Exercise 4: Independent or Paired?
For each study, identify whether an independent or paired t-test would be appropriate:
a) Comparing memory test scores between males and females.






TipShow Answer





Independent t-test - Different participants in each group (you can’t be both male and female in this study).



b) Measuring reaction time before and after drinking coffee.






TipShow Answer





Paired t-test - Same participants measured twice (before and after).



c) Comparing exam scores between students taught with Method A vs Method B.






TipShow Answer





Independent t-test - Different students in each teaching method (assuming random assignment to methods).



d) Rating the same 30 products for attractiveness and then for quality.






TipShow Answer





Paired t-test - Same products rated twice (on two different dimensions).






Exercise 5: Design Components
A study compares problem-solving ability between people who slept 8 hours vs 4 hours.
a) What is the independent variable?






TipShow Answer





Sleep duration (8 hours vs 4 hours) - the grouping variable.



b) What is the dependent variable?






TipShow Answer





Problem-solving ability (score on the problem-solving task).



c) What type of experimental design is this?






TipShow Answer





Between-subjects (independent groups) design - different people in each sleep condition.



d) What type of data is the DV?






TipShow Answer





Likely interval or ratio data (numerical scores on a problem-solving test).

title: Week 14 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 3: Reading and Reporting Practice

Exercise 6: Full Interpretation
A researcher investigated whether background music affects concentration. Participants completed a concentration task in silence (n = 25) or with background music (n = 25).
> data %>%
+   group_by(condition) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(score), SD = sd(score), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  condition  Mean    SD     n
  <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 music      72.4  11.2    25
2 silence    78.8   9.6    25

> t.test(score ~ condition, data = data)

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  score by condition
t = -2.17, df = 46.8, p-value = 0.0352
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -12.33  -0.47
sample estimates:
mean in group music mean in group silence
               72.4                  78.8
a) State the hypothesis that this study was testing.






TipShow Answer





The researcher hypothesized that background music would affect concentration task performance. (More specifically, they may have predicted that music would either help or hinder concentration.)



b) What do the results show?






TipShow Answer





Participants who worked in silence scored higher (M = 78.8) than those with background music (M = 72.4). The difference of 6.4 points was statistically significant (p = .035).



c) Write a complete APA results paragraph.






TipShow Answer






An independent samples t-test was conducted to examine the effect of background music on concentration. Participants who completed the task in silence (M = 78.8, SD = 9.6) scored significantly higher than those who listened to background music (M = 72.4, SD = 11.2), t(46.8) = -2.17, p = .035, 95% CI [-12.33, -0.47]. These results suggest that background music may impair concentration on cognitive tasks.







Exercise 7: Non-Significant Results
A researcher compared creativity scores between morning people (n = 30) and evening people (n = 30).
> t.test(creativity ~ chronotype, data = data)

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  creativity by chronotype
t = 0.84, df = 57.1, p-value = 0.405
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.81  6.89
sample estimates:
mean in group evening mean in group morning
                 52.3                  50.2
a) Is this result statistically significant?






TipShow Answer





No, the result is not significant because p = .405 > .05. We fail to reject the null hypothesis.



b) What does the confidence interval tell us?






TipShow Answer





The 95% CI [-2.81, 6.89] includes zero, which is consistent with a non-significant result. The true difference could be negative, zero, or positive - we can’t be confident about the direction of any difference.



c) How would you report this result?






TipShow Answer






An independent samples t-test revealed no significant difference in creativity scores between evening people (M = 52.3) and morning people (M = 50.2), t(57.1) = 0.84, p = .405, 95% CI [-2.81, 6.89].

title: Week 14 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 4: Conceptual Questions

Exercise 8: True or False
a) An independent t-test requires the same participants to be in both conditions.






TipShow Answer





False. An independent t-test compares different participants in each condition. If the same participants are in both conditions, you use a paired t-test.



b) If p > .05, we can conclude there is no difference between groups.






TipShow Answer





False. A non-significant result means we failed to find evidence of a difference. It doesn’t prove there is no difference - we may have lacked statistical power (e.g., small sample size).



c) The degrees of freedom in a Welch t-test can be a decimal number.






TipShow Answer





True. Welch’s correction adjusts the degrees of freedom based on the variances in each group, often resulting in non-integer df values.



d) A confidence interval that doesn’t include zero indicates a significant result.






TipShow Answer





True (at the corresponding alpha level). If the 95% CI doesn’t include zero, the p-value will be < .05.

TipBefore You Begin



This chapter brings together everything you need to analyse and interpret your results: hypothesis testing to determine IF there’s an effect, confidence intervals to show HOW CERTAIN you are, and effect sizes to show HOW BIG it is. This is one of the most important (and most misunderstood) topics in research methods.


This chapter covers:

Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST)
What p-values mean (and don’t mean)
Confidence intervals and what they tell us
Effect sizes (Cohen’s d) and practical importance
Independent samples t-test (between-subjects)
Paired samples t-test (within-subjects)
Complete APA reporting with all components

All concepts are illustrated using DataLab examples from your class.

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
section: Part 1: The Logic of Hypothesis Testing
text:
Part 1: The Logic of Hypothesis Testing

The Fundamental Question
In research, we often want to know whether an effect is “real” — whether our observed difference reflects something true about the world, or whether it could have occurred by chance.
Consider your DataLab memory data:

Lab A (abstract words): M = 5.4
Lab B (concrete words): M = 6.8

There’s clearly a difference of 1.4 words. But is this difference meaningful, or could it have happened by chance? Maybe if you tested different students, the results would be reversed.


The Three Questions
When analysing results, you need to answer three questions:


Is the effect real? — Hypothesis testing and p-values
How certain are we? — Confidence intervals
How big is it? — Effect sizes (Cohen’s d)


A complete analysis addresses all three. Let’s examine each in turn.


The Null Hypothesis
To test whether our effect is real, we start with an assumption:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): The assumption that there is no effect or no difference in the population.

For the memory experiment:

H₀: Word type has no effect on memory. Any observed difference is due to chance.
In formal terms: μ_abstract = μ_concrete (the population means are equal)



The Alternative Hypothesis
The alternative (or research) hypothesis represents what we’re actually interested in:

Alternative Hypothesis (H₁ or Ha): The prediction that there is an effect or difference.

For the memory experiment:

H₁ (two-tailed): Word type affects memory (μ_abstract ≠ μ_concrete)
H₁ (one-tailed): Concrete words are remembered better than abstract words (μ_concrete > μ_abstract)



The Logic of NHST
Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) follows this logic:

Assume H₀ is true (assume there’s no real effect)
Ask: How likely is our observed data if H₀ were true?
If the data is very unlikely under H₀, reject H₀ and conclude there probably is an effect







ImportantKey Insight



We never “prove” anything. We either reject H₀ (suggesting there’s an effect) or fail to reject H₀ (the data doesn’t provide enough evidence for an effect).

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Part 2: Understanding p-values

What Is a p-value?

p-value: The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the observed results, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

Let’s unpack this:

We calculate how extreme our data is
We ask: “If there were truly no effect, how often would we see data this extreme just by chance?”
The p-value answers this question



A Concrete Example
Imagine the memory experiment has a p-value of 0.03.
This means: If word type truly had no effect on memory, we would observe a difference as large as (or larger than) 1.4 words in only 3% of experiments, just by chance.
Because 3% is quite rare, we conclude that the null hypothesis is probably wrong — word type probably does affect memory.


The Significance Threshold (α)
We need a cutoff for deciding when p is “small enough” to reject H₀. This is called alpha (α).

Alpha (α): The significance level — the threshold below which we reject the null hypothesis. Conventionally set at 0.05 (5%).


If p < α (typically p < .05): Reject H₀ — result is “statistically significant”
If p ≥ α (typically p ≥ .05): Fail to reject H₀ — result is “not statistically significant”



What p-values Do NOT Mean






WarningCritical Misconceptions



The p-value is NOT:

The probability that H₀ is true
The probability that H₁ is false
The probability that the results occurred by chance
A measure of effect size or importance

A p-value only tells you how surprising your data would be IF H₀ were true. It says nothing about how likely H₀ actually is.




The Correct Interpretation

Wrong: “There’s a 3% chance this finding is due to chance.”
Correct: “If the null hypothesis were true, we’d see results this extreme only 3% of the time.”

This distinction matters! The p-value is calculated under the assumption that H₀ is true. It doesn’t tell you whether H₀ is actually true.

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
section: Part 3: Type I and Type II Errors
text:
Part 3: Type I and Type II Errors

Two Ways to Be Wrong
When we make decisions based on p-values, we can make two types of errors:









H₀ is actually TRUE (no effect)
H₀ is actually FALSE (real effect)




Reject H₀
Type I Error (False Positive)
Correct Decision


Fail to reject H₀
Correct Decision
Type II Error (False Negative)





Type I Error (False Positive)

Type I Error: Rejecting H₀ when it’s actually true — claiming an effect exists when it doesn’t.


The probability of a Type I error equals α (typically 5%)
If you use α = .05, you’ll falsely detect “effects” 5% of the time when there’s actually nothing there

DataLab Example: You conclude that concrete words are better remembered than abstract words, but actually the difference you observed was just due to random variation in who happened to be in each lab.


Type II Error (False Negative)

Type II Error: Failing to reject H₀ when it’s actually false — missing a real effect.


The probability of a Type II error is denoted β (beta)
Power = 1 - β = the probability of correctly detecting a real effect

DataLab Example: Concrete words really are easier to remember, but your study had too few participants to detect this reliably. You conclude “no significant difference” and miss the real effect.


The Trade-off
You can’t minimise both errors simultaneously:

Setting a stricter α (e.g., .01 instead of .05) reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
Using larger samples reduces Type II errors without increasing Type I errors (this is why sample size matters!)

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
section: Part 4: Confidence Intervals — How Certain Are We?
text:
Part 4: Confidence Intervals — How Certain Are We?

Beyond Point Estimates
A mean like 6.8 is a point estimate — our best single guess at the population value. But how confident are we in this estimate?

Confidence Interval (CI): A range of values that is likely to contain the true population parameter. A 95% CI represents the range within which we’re reasonably confident the true value lies.

Instead of reporting: “Lab B mean = 6.8”
Report: “Lab B mean = 6.8, 95% CI [6.07, 7.53]”
This tells readers not just our estimate but how precise that estimate is.


Interpreting 95% Confidence Intervals






WarningCommon Misconception



A 95% CI does NOT mean “there’s a 95% probability the true value is in this interval.”


The correct interpretation:

If we repeated this study many times and calculated a 95% CI each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true population value.

Once calculated, any specific CI either contains the true value or it doesn’t — we just don’t know which.


What CIs Tell Us

The range of plausible values: The true population mean is probably somewhere in this range
Precision: Narrower CI = more precise estimate (usually from larger samples)
Uncertainty: Wider CI = more uncertainty about the true value



CIs and Statistical Significance

Key rule: If the 95% CI for a difference does not include zero, the difference is statistically significant at p < .05.

For our memory study:

Difference between labs = 1.4 words
95% CI for the difference = [0.42, 2.38]
The CI does NOT include zero
Therefore: p < .05 (significant difference)

If the CI had been [-0.20, 3.00], it would include zero, suggesting the difference might not be real.


Why Report CIs?

They provide more information than p-values alone
They show the range of plausible effects
Readers can judge whether the effect is practically meaningful
They’re becoming required in many journals

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
section: Part 5: Effect Sizes — How Big Is It?
text:
Part 5: Effect Sizes — How Big Is It?

Statistical Significance ≠ Practical Importance






WarningCritical Distinction



A statistically significant result can be trivially small. With a large enough sample, even a 0.1-point difference could be “significant” — but is that meaningful?


This is why we need effect sizes.


Cohen’s d

Cohen’s d: A standardised measure of the difference between two means, expressed in standard deviation units.
\[d = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{s_{pooled}}\]

Effect sizes are independent of sample size. A d = 0.50 means the same thing whether you have 20 or 2,000 participants.


Interpreting Cohen’s d
Cohen (1988) provided benchmarks:



d value
Interpretation
What it looks like




0.2
Small
Means overlap 85%


0.5
Medium
Means overlap 67%


0.8
Large
Means overlap 53%









NoteContext Matters



These benchmarks are rough guidelines. In some fields (e.g., clinical interventions), d = 0.3 is impressive. In others (e.g., perceptual differences), d = 0.3 might be trivial.




Calculating Cohen’s d: Example
DataLab Memory Data:

Lab A: M = 5.4, SD = 1.8
Lab B: M = 6.8, SD = 2.0

First, calculate pooled SD:
\[s_{pooled} = \sqrt{\frac{(SD_1)^2 + (SD_2)^2}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.8^2 + 2.0^2}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3.24 + 4.0}{2}} = \sqrt{3.62} = 1.90\]
Then calculate d:
\[d = \frac{6.8 - 5.4}{1.90} = \frac{1.4}{1.90} = 0.74\]
This is a medium-to-large effect — the lab manipulation had a meaningful impact on memory.


Why Effect Sizes Matter

Practical importance: Tells you if the effect is big enough to care about
Comparability: Allows comparison across different studies and measures
Meta-analysis: Effect sizes are combined across studies to estimate true effects
Complete picture: p-values tell you IF there’s an effect; d tells you HOW BIG

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Part 6: The Independent Samples t-test

When to Use It
The independent samples t-test compares means from two different groups of participants.
Use it when:

You have two separate groups
Each participant is in only one group (between-subjects design)
You want to compare the groups on a continuous outcome

DataLab Example: Comparing memory scores between Lab A (abstract words) and Lab B (concrete words) — different students in each lab.


The t-statistic
The t-test produces a t-statistic that captures the ratio of signal to noise:

\[t = \frac{\text{Difference between means}}{\text{Standard error of the difference}}\]
In words: signal ÷ noise


Larger t = bigger difference relative to variability = more evidence against H₀
Smaller t = difference is small relative to variability = weaker evidence



Worked Example: Independent t-test
DataLab Data:

Lab A (abstract): M = 5.4, SD = 1.8, n = 30
Lab B (concrete): M = 6.8, SD = 2.0, n = 30

Step 1: Calculate the pooled standard error
\[SE_{diff} = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.8^2}{30} + \frac{2.0^2}{30}} = \sqrt{0.108 + 0.133} = 0.49\]
Step 2: Calculate t
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_2 - \bar{x}_1}{SE_{diff}} = \frac{6.8 - 5.4}{0.49} = \frac{1.4}{0.49} = 2.86\]
Step 3: Degrees of freedom
df = n₁ + n₂ - 2 = 30 + 30 - 2 = 58
Step 4: Look up p-value
With df = 58, t = 2.86 gives p = .006
Step 5: Calculate effect size
d = (6.8 - 5.4) / 1.90 = 0.74
Step 6: Make a decision
Since p = .006 < .05, we reject H₀. The difference is statistically significant, with a medium-to-large effect.

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Part 7: The Paired Samples t-test

When to Use It
The paired samples t-test compares two measurements from the same participants.
Use it when:

The same people provide both scores (within-subjects design)
You want to compare before vs after, or condition 1 vs condition 2 within the same person

DataLab Examples:

Pre-session mood vs post-session mood
Dominant hand accuracy vs non-dominant hand accuracy



Why “Paired”?
Each person has a pair of scores. We’re interested in within-person change — did individuals improve, decline, or stay the same?


The Key Difference from Independent t-test
Instead of comparing two separate groups, we:

Calculate the difference score for each person
Test whether the mean difference is significantly different from zero


Paired t-test logic: If there’s no effect, the average difference should be zero. We test whether our observed mean difference is far enough from zero to be statistically significant.



Worked Example: Paired t-test
DataLab Data (Mood pre-post):
For 30 participants:

Mean pre-mood: 5.3
Mean post-mood: 6.5
Mean difference: M_diff = 1.2
SD of differences: SD_diff = 1.8

Step 1: Calculate standard error of the mean difference
\[SE_{diff} = \frac{SD_{diff}}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.8}{\sqrt{30}} = \frac{1.8}{5.48} = 0.33\]
Step 2: Calculate t
\[t = \frac{\bar{d}}{SE_{diff}} = \frac{1.2}{0.33} = 3.64\]
Step 3: Degrees of freedom
df = n - 1 = 30 - 1 = 29
Step 4: Look up p-value
With df = 29, t = 3.64 gives p = .001
Step 5: Calculate effect size
\[d = \frac{\bar{d}}{SD_{diff}} = \frac{1.2}{1.8} = 0.67\]
Step 6: Make a decision
Since p = .001 < .05, we reject H₀. Mood significantly improved after the session.


Why Paired Tests Are More Powerful
Paired tests control for individual differences. Some people are naturally happier; some have better memories. By comparing each person to themselves, we remove this “noise,” making it easier to detect true effects.

title: Chapter 7: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Part 8: Complete APA Reporting

The Formula

APA format for t-tests:
t(df) = X.XX, p = .XXX, d = X.XX, 95% CI [X.XX, X.XX]

All five components:

t = test statistic
df = degrees of freedom (in parentheses)
p = exact p-value (or p < .001 if very small)
d = Cohen’s d effect size
95% CI = confidence interval for the difference



Complete Example: Independent t-test

An independent samples t-test revealed that participants who studied concrete words (M = 6.8, SD = 2.0) recalled significantly more words than those who studied abstract words (M = 5.4, SD = 1.8), t(58) = 2.86, p = .006, d = 0.74, 95% CI [0.42, 2.38].

Notice this includes:

Descriptive statistics for both groups
The t-statistic with degrees of freedom
The exact p-value
The effect size (Cohen’s d)
The 95% confidence interval for the difference



Complete Example: Paired t-test

A paired samples t-test showed that participants’ mood ratings were significantly higher after the DataLab session (M = 6.5, SD = 1.4) compared to before (M = 5.3, SD = 1.6), t(29) = 3.64, p = .001, d = 0.67, 95% CI [0.54, 1.86].

Key Concepts

Operationalisation

Definition: Turning abstract concepts into concrete, measurable variables
IV operationalisation: How exactly will you manipulate the independent variable?
DV operationalisation: How exactly will you measure the dependent variable?
Key question: Would another researcher be able to replicate your study from your description?



Hypotheses

Null hypothesis (H₀): There is no effect — the default assumption
Alternative hypothesis (H₁): There IS an effect — what you’re testing
One-tailed: Predicts direction (“A > B”) — use when theory/evidence strongly supports a direction
Two-tailed: Predicts difference without direction (“A ≠ B”) — use when direction is uncertain



Design Trade-offs








Design
Advantage
Disadvantage




Between-subjects
No order effects, no practice effects
Individual differences add noise, needs more participants


Within-subjects
Controls individual differences, more statistical power
Order effects possible, demand characteristics





The Design → Test Link



Your Design
Your Statistical Test




Between-subjects (different people)
Independent samples t-test


Within-subjects (same people)
Paired samples t-test

What specific fonts will you use?

How will you measure memory?



Topic 2: Hydration → Cognitive Performance

How much water? When?
What’s your control condition?
What cognitive task will you use?



Topic 3: Eye Contact → Perceived Trustworthiness
Question: Does eye contact duration affect how trustworthy a person is perceived to be?
Background: Research on gaze and social perception shows that direct eye contact influences impressions of confidence, competence, and trustworthiness.
Key operationalisation decisions:

Photos or videos?
How will you manipulate gaze direction?
How will you measure trustworthiness?

title: Chapter 6: Research Plan Workshop
text:
Templates for the Workshop

IV Operationalisation Template

“The independent variable is _____________ with two levels:
Condition 1: [Specific details including exact parameters]
Condition 2: [Specific details including exact parameters]”

Good example (caffeine study):

“The independent variable is caffeine consumption with two levels:
Condition 1 (Caffeine): 200mg caffeine capsule (equivalent to ~2 cups of coffee)
Condition 2 (Placebo): Identical-looking capsule containing no caffeine”

Notice the specificity: exact dosage, matched appearance between conditions.


DV Operationalisation Template

“The dependent variable is _____________ measured by:
Task: [What participants do]
Scoring: [How performance is quantified]
Range: [Possible values]”

Good example (caffeine study):

“The dependent variable is alertness measured by:
Task: Psychomotor Vigilance Test — respond to visual stimuli as quickly as possible
Scoring: Mean reaction time across 30 trials (milliseconds)
Range: Continuous, typically 200-500ms”



Hypothesis Template
Null hypothesis:

H₀: There is no difference in [DV] between [Condition 1] and [Condition 2].

Alternative hypothesis (two-tailed):

H₁: [DV] will differ between [Condition 1] and [Condition 2].

Alternative hypothesis (one-tailed):

H₁: [DV] will be [higher/lower] in [Condition X] than [Condition Y].



Justification Template

“I have chosen a [one-tailed / two-tailed] hypothesis because:
Prior research [summary of relevant findings with citations].
Therefore, [I predict/do not predict] a specific direction.”



Design & Test Justification Template

“This study employs a [between-subjects / within-subjects] design because [specific advantages for your study and how disadvantages are addressed].
Given this design, the data will consist of [two independent groups / paired scores from the same participants].
Therefore, an [independent samples / paired samples] t-test is appropriate because [explain how data structure matches test requirements].”

title: Chapter 6: Research Plan Workshop
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid

In Operationalisation

Too vague: “We showed participants different fonts” — which fonts exactly?
Confounded conditions: Changing multiple things between conditions
Missing control details: Only describing the experimental condition



In Hypotheses

No justification: Choosing one-tailed without explaining why
Wrong direction: Citing evidence for one direction but predicting the other
After-the-fact: Planning to decide direction after seeing data (this invalidates one-tailed tests)



In Design Justification

Stating without explaining: “I will use an independent t-test” with no justification
Mismatched design-test: Claiming within-subjects but selecting independent t-test
Missing the logic: Not explaining how design determines data structure



In Method Section

Not replicable: Missing crucial details about timing, materials, or procedure
Too brief: Participants, materials, and procedure each need substantive description
Missing counterbalancing: For within-subjects designs, failing to address order effects

title: Week 13 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 1: Reading Correlation Output

Exercise 1: Basic Correlation Output
A researcher examined the relationship between study hours and exam scores. Here’s the R output:
> cor.test(data$study_hours, data$exam_score)

    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  data$study_hours and data$exam_score
t = 4.23, df = 28, p-value = 0.0002
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.36 0.79
sample estimates:
      cor
0.624
a) What is the correlation coefficient?






TipShow Answer





r = 0.624 (shown in the “sample estimates” section as “cor”).



b) Is this correlation statistically significant at α = .05?






TipShow Answer





Yes, it is statistically significant because p = 0.0002, which is less than .05.



c) How would you describe the strength and direction of this relationship?






TipShow Answer





This is a moderate to strong positive correlation. As study hours increase, exam scores tend to increase.

Direction: Positive (both variables move in the same direction)
Strength: Moderate-strong (r = 0.624 is between 0.5 and 0.7)




d) Report this correlation in APA format.






TipShow Answer






There was a significant positive correlation between study hours and exam scores, r(28) = .62, p < .001, 95% CI [.36, .79].

Or:

Study hours were significantly positively correlated with exam scores, r = .62, p < .001.







Exercise 2: Interpreting the Confidence Interval
Using the output from Exercise 1:
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.36 0.79
a) What does this confidence interval tell us?






TipShow Answer





We are 95% confident that the true population correlation falls between 0.36 and 0.79. The interval is entirely positive, confirming the positive relationship.



b) Why is it important that this interval doesn’t include zero?






TipShow Answer





If the interval included zero, we couldn’t rule out the possibility of no relationship. Since it doesn’t include zero, we have evidence of a genuine correlation in the population.






Exercise 3: Different Correlation Strengths
Match each correlation coefficient to its description:



Coefficient
Options




r = -0.89
A. Weak positive


r = 0.23
B. Strong negative


r = 0.52
C. Moderate positive


r = -0.15
D. Weak negative









TipShow Answer






r = -0.89 → B. Strong negative
r = 0.23 → A. Weak positive
r = 0.52 → C. Moderate positive
r = -0.15 → D. Weak negative

section: Part 2: Descriptive Statistics for Correlational Studies
text:
Part 2: Descriptive Statistics for Correlational Studies

Exercise 4: Reading Paired Descriptives
A study measured anxiety and sleep quality in 50 participants:
> data %>%
+   summarise(
+     mean_anxiety = mean(anxiety),
+     sd_anxiety = sd(anxiety),
+     mean_sleep = mean(sleep_quality),
+     sd_sleep = sd(sleep_quality)
+   )

# A tibble: 1 x 4
  mean_anxiety sd_anxiety mean_sleep sd_sleep
         <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1         42.3       12.1       5.8      1.9
a) Report the descriptive statistics for anxiety in APA format.






TipShow Answer






Anxiety scores ranged from… (M = 42.3, SD = 12.1)

Or simply: Mean anxiety was 42.3 (SD = 12.1).



b) What additional information would you need to fully interpret these descriptives?






TipShow Answer





You would benefit from knowing: - The range of the anxiety scale (e.g., 0-100) - What higher/lower scores mean (is high anxiety bad?) - The range of the sleep quality scale - Sample size (n)






Exercise 5: Correlation with Full Descriptives
Here’s complete output for a study on age and memory performance:
> # Descriptive statistics
> data %>%
+   summarise(
+     n = n(),
+     mean_age = mean(age),
+     sd_age = sd(age),
+     mean_memory = mean(memory_score),
+     sd_memory = sd(memory_score)
+   )

# A tibble: 1 x 5
      n mean_age sd_age mean_memory sd_memory
  <int>    <dbl>  <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1    45     52.4   15.3        68.2      18.7

> # Correlation test
> cor.test(data$age, data$memory_score)

    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  data$age and data$memory_score
t = -3.87, df = 43, p-value = 0.0004
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.68 -0.24
sample estimates:
       cor
-0.508
a) Write a complete results paragraph in APA format.






TipShow Answer






A total of 45 participants (mean age = 52.4 years, SD = 15.3) completed a memory task (M = 68.2, SD = 18.7). There was a significant negative correlation between age and memory performance, r(43) = -.51, p < .001, 95% CI [-.68, -.24], indicating that older participants tended to show lower memory scores.




b) What is the coefficient of determination (r²) and what does it tell us?






TipShow Answer





r² = (-0.508)² = 0.258 = 25.8%
This tells us that approximately 26% of the variance in memory scores can be explained by (or is shared with) age. The remaining 74% is due to other factors.

title: Week 13 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 3: Correlation vs Causation

Exercise 6: Critical Thinking
A researcher finds a significant correlation (r = .65) between ice cream sales and drowning deaths.
a) Can we conclude that ice cream causes drowning? Why or why not?






TipShow Answer





No, correlation does not imply causation. Both variables are likely influenced by a third variable (confound): hot weather. Hot weather increases both ice cream sales AND swimming (which increases drowning risk).



b) What type of variable is “hot weather” in this example?






TipShow Answer





Hot weather is a confounding variable (or third variable). It affects both the IV and DV, creating a spurious correlation.





Exercise 7: Identifying Confounds
For each correlation, identify a potential confounding variable:
a) Shoe size correlates with reading ability in children.






TipShow Answer





Age is the confound. Older children have bigger feet AND better reading ability.



b) Number of firefighters at a scene correlates with property damage.






TipShow Answer





Fire size/severity is the confound. Larger fires require more firefighters AND cause more damage.

title: Week 13 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 4: Design Recognition

Exercise 8: Study Design
A researcher wants to know if there’s a relationship between hours of sleep and exam performance among university students. They survey 100 students, asking about their typical sleep duration and collecting their most recent exam grade.
a) What type of design is this?






TipShow Answer





This is a correlational design (also called observational or non-experimental). The researcher is not manipulating any variables, just measuring the natural relationship between two variables.



b) What are two variables being measured?






TipShow Answer






Hours of sleep (typical/habitual)
Exam performance/grade




c) Why can’t we conclude that sleep causes better exam performance?






TipShow Answer






Variables are not manipulated (no random assignment)
Cannot rule out confounding variables (e.g., conscientiousness affects both sleep habits and studying)
Direction of causality unclear (maybe good grades reduce stress → better sleep)
Would need an experiment to establish causation

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
text:
Part 1: What is Operationalisation?

The Gap Between Ideas and Measurement
Research starts with ideas: Does stress affect memory? Does eye contact build trust? Does hydration improve thinking?
These are interesting questions, but they’re not yet testable. To test them, we need to answer:

What exactly do we mean by “stress” or “memory” or “trust”?
How will we create different levels of our independent variable?
How will we measure the dependent variable?

This is where operationalisation comes in.

Operationalisation: The process of turning an abstract concept into a concrete, measurable variable with a specific procedure for manipulation or measurement.



Why Operationalisation Matters
Good operationalisation enables:

Replication: Other researchers can repeat your study exactly
Communication: Readers understand precisely what you did
Validity: Your measure actually captures what you claim to measure
Control: You know exactly what differs between conditions

Poor operationalisation leads to:

Ambiguity: “We measured mood” — how? With what?
Confounds: Multiple things differ between conditions
Irreplicability: No one can reproduce your findings
Invalid conclusions: You measured something, but not what you think



Operationalising the Independent Variable
The IV is what you manipulate. You need to specify exactly how the conditions differ.
Vague: “Participants were either stressed or not stressed”
Operationalised: “Participants in the stress condition completed a timed mental arithmetic task (counting backwards from 2,043 by 17s) while being observed by an experimenter who maintained a neutral expression. Participants in the control condition sat quietly for the same duration (3 minutes) without any task.”
Notice how the operationalised version tells you:

What the stressor was (timed arithmetic)
Specific parameters (starting number, subtraction amount)
The social element (observed, neutral expression)
The control condition (matched for time, no task)
Duration (3 minutes)



Operationalising the Dependent Variable
The DV is what you measure. You need to specify the exact measurement procedure.
Vague: “We measured their memory”
Operationalised: “Memory was assessed using a free recall task. Participants were shown 20 words (10 concrete nouns, 10 abstract nouns) for 3 seconds each. After a 30-second filled delay (counting backwards from 50), participants wrote down as many words as they could remember in 2 minutes. The dependent variable was the total number of correctly recalled words (maximum = 20).”
This version specifies:

The type of memory test (free recall)
The stimuli (20 words, types specified)
Presentation timing (3 seconds each)
The retention interval (30 seconds, filled)
The recall procedure (written, 2 minutes)
The scoring method (total correct, max = 20)

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
section: Part 2: The Three Research Plan Topics
text:
Part 2: The Three Research Plan Topics
Your Research Plan assessment requires you to design an experiment on one of three topics. Let’s work through the operationalisation challenges for each.

Topic 1: Font Difficulty → Memory
The Research Question: Does reading text in a harder-to-read font improve memory retention?
Background: Diemand-Yauman et al. (2011) proposed that “desirable difficulties” — challenges that require more cognitive effort during learning — can enhance long-term retention. Reading disfluent fonts requires more effort, which might deepen processing.

Operationalising “Font Difficulty”
You need two conditions that differ ONLY in font readability:



Condition
Font Specification




Fluent (Easy)
Arial, 16-point, black on white


Disfluent (Hard)
Comic Sans MS, 12-point, 75% grey on white



The key principle: Keep everything else constant (same words, same screen, same instructions) so that font is the only thing that differs.
Alternative operationalisations:

Fluent vs Italic versions of the same font
Standard vs reduced contrast
Clear vs slightly blurred text







WarningPotential Confound



If your fonts differ in more than just readability (e.g., one is much smaller, or associated with different contexts), you can’t be sure which difference caused any effect.




Operationalising “Memory”
Common options:









Measure
Description
Pros
Cons




Free recall
Write down everything remembered
Sensitive to deeper processing
Floor/ceiling effects possible


Recognition
Multiple choice: “Was this word shown?”
Easy to score
May not detect subtle effects


Cued recall
Given category, recall specific items
Balanced difficulty
Requires careful stimulus design



Your choice should be justified based on prior research or theoretical considerations.



Topic 2: Hydration → Cognitive Performance
The Research Question: Does drinking water improve cognitive task performance?
Background: Edmonds & Burford (2009) found that children who drank water before cognitive tests performed better. Dehydration may impair attention and processing speed.

Operationalising “Hydration”
Options for your IV manipulation:









Approach
Water Condition
Control Condition
Considerations




Simple manipulation
Drink 300ml water
No drink
Confound: act of drinking vs water


Placebo control
Drink 300ml water
Sip water (no swallowing)
Controls for drinking action


Standardised
Drink 250ml after 2-hour abstention
2-hour abstention, no drink
Controls prior hydration state









NoteDesign Consideration



Consider whether participants knowing they’re in a “hydration” study might create expectation effects. If people believe water helps cognition, their performance might improve regardless of actual hydration.




Operationalising “Cognitive Performance”
Options include:

Attention tasks: Simple/choice reaction time, sustained attention (continuous performance task)
Working memory: Digit span, n-back task
Processing speed: Symbol-digit substitution, pattern comparison
Executive function: Stroop task, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test

Your choice should match the theoretical mechanism. If hydration affects attention, use an attention task.



Topic 3: Eye Contact → Perceived Trustworthiness
The Research Question: Does eye contact duration affect how trustworthy a person is perceived to be?
Background: Argyle & Dean (1965) established that eye contact is a fundamental component of social interaction. Subsequent research has linked direct gaze to perceptions of competence, confidence, and trustworthiness.

Operationalising “Eye Contact”
Options for manipulation:









Approach
High Eye Contact
Low Eye Contact
Considerations




Photographs
Eyes looking at camera
Eyes looking slightly away
Maximum control, less realistic


Videos
80% direct gaze
20% direct gaze
More realistic, harder to control


Duration
5 seconds of direct gaze
1 second of direct gaze
Tests duration specifically



Using photos or videos allows tight control — you can be sure the only difference is eye contact. Live interactions are more ecologically valid but introduce many confounds (voice, body language, natural variation).


Operationalising “Trustworthiness”
Options:









Measure
Example
Pros
Cons




Single rating scale
“How trustworthy is this person?” (1-7)
Simple, direct
May not capture full concept


Multiple-item scale
Trust subscale from established measure
More reliable
Longer, may be redundant


Behavioural measure
“Would you lend this person £10?”
Face valid
Binary data less sensitive


Economic game
How much would you invest with them?
Behavioural, continuous
Complex to administer



Multi-item scales are generally more reliable than single items. Consider using an established trustworthiness measure if one exists.

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
text:
Part 3: Writing Hypotheses

Review: Null and Alternative Hypotheses
Every statistical test compares your data against a null hypothesis.

Null Hypothesis (H₀): There is no effect — any observed difference is due to chance.
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): There IS an effect — the observed difference is not due to chance.

For the font study:

H₀: Font type has no effect on memory (μ_fluent = μ_disfluent)
H₁: Font type does affect memory (μ_fluent ≠ μ_disfluent)



One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed Hypotheses
The alternative hypothesis can be:
Two-tailed (non-directional): Predicts there IS a difference, without specifying which direction.

H₁: Memory scores will differ between fluent and disfluent font conditions.

One-tailed (directional): Predicts the specific direction of the difference.

H₁: Memory scores will be higher in the disfluent font condition than the fluent font condition.



When to Use Each







Use Two-Tailed When…
Use One-Tailed When…




Effect could reasonably go either way
Strong theoretical basis for direction


Prior literature is mixed
Consistent prior findings support one direction


You’re exploring a new question
Replicating established effect


You want to detect unexpected effects
You’re focused on confirming a specific prediction





Justifying Your Choice
For your Research Plan, you must justify why you chose one-tailed or two-tailed:
Example two-tailed justification:

“A two-tailed hypothesis was used because prior research on disfluency effects has produced mixed results. While Diemand-Yauman et al. (2011) found memory benefits, subsequent replications have been inconsistent (Rummer et al., 2016). Given this uncertainty, we test for any difference rather than predicting a specific direction.”

Example one-tailed justification:

“A one-tailed hypothesis was used because the desirable difficulties framework (Bjork & Bjork, 2011) and the original disfluency research (Diemand-Yauman et al., 2011) both predict that harder-to-read fonts should enhance memory. We therefore predict that recall will be higher in the disfluent condition.”







ImportantAssessment Requirement



Your Research Plan MUST include justification for your hypothesis direction choice. This demonstrates critical thinking about the research literature and your theoretical position.




Writing Complete Hypotheses
A complete hypothesis statement includes:

The IV and its levels
The DV and how it’s measured
The predicted relationship

Complete two-tailed:

“Participants who read a word list in a disfluent font (Comic Sans MS, 12pt, 75% grey) will show different free recall scores compared to participants who read the same word list in a fluent font (Arial, 16pt, black).”

Complete one-tailed:

“Participants who read a word list in a disfluent font (Comic Sans MS, 12pt, 75% grey) will recall significantly more words than participants who read the same word list in a fluent font (Arial, 16pt, black).”

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
section: Part 4: Design Decisions — Between vs Within
text:
Part 4: Design Decisions — Between vs Within

The Fundamental Trade-off
You’ve chosen your topic, operationalised your variables, and written your hypotheses. Now you must decide how to assign participants to conditions.

Between-Subjects Design: Different participants in each condition. Each person experiences only ONE level of the IV.
Within-Subjects Design: Same participants in all conditions. Each person experiences EVERY level of the IV.



Between-Subjects Design
How it works:

Randomly assign 30 participants to Condition A
Randomly assign 30 different participants to Condition B
Compare the mean scores of each group

Advantages:

No order effects: Participants can’t be influenced by having done another condition first
No practice effects: Performance doesn’t improve/decline across conditions
No demand characteristics from comparison: Participants don’t try to be “consistent” or “different”
Simpler procedure: Each participant does one thing

Disadvantages:

Individual differences add noise: Smart people in one group inflate that mean
Needs more participants: Twice as many people for two conditions
Pre-existing group differences: Even with randomisation, groups might differ



Within-Subjects Design
How it works:

All 30 participants complete Condition A
Same 30 participants complete Condition B
Compare each person’s scores across conditions

Advantages:

Controls individual differences: Each person is their own control
More statistical power: Less “noise” makes real effects easier to detect
Fewer participants needed: Same people generate data for all conditions
Can detect small effects: Removing individual differences unmasks subtle differences

Disadvantages:

Order effects: First condition might affect second
Practice effects: Performance changes with repeated testing
Fatigue effects: Performance declines with longer sessions
Demand characteristics: Participants might guess what you expect



Design Decisions for Each Topic

Font Difficulty → Memory








Design
Implementation
Key Concern




Between
Group A reads fluent, Group B reads disfluent
Individual differences in memory ability


Within
Everyone reads BOTH font versions
Memory for first list affects second



Typical choice: Between-subjects
Reasoning: If participants read the same words in both fonts, memory from the first reading will contaminate the second. If we use different word lists, we can’t be sure the lists are equivalent in difficulty.


Hydration → Cognitive Performance








Design
Implementation
Key Concern




Between
Group A drinks water, Group B doesn’t
Individual differences in cognitive ability


Within
Same person tested hydrated and not hydrated
Requires two sessions or dehydration manipulation



Typical choice: Between-subjects (simpler) or within-subjects with two sessions (more powerful but logistically harder)


Eye Contact → Trustworthiness








Design
Implementation
Key Concern




Between
Different participants see different gaze conditions
Individual differences in trust tendencies


Within
Same participants rate BOTH gaze conditions
Demand to rate them differently



Typical choice: Within-subjects with counterbalancing
Reasoning: If each participant rates multiple faces, we can have them see some faces with direct gaze and some with averted gaze. This controls for individual differences in how trusting people generally are.



Counterbalancing in Within-Subjects Designs
If you use a within-subjects design, you must address order effects through counterbalancing:

Counterbalancing: Varying the order of conditions across participants so that order effects cancel out.

Half of participants: Condition A first, then Condition B
Other half: Condition B first, then Condition A

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
section: Part 5: Connecting Design to Statistical Test
text:
Part 5: Connecting Design to Statistical Test

The Critical Link
This section is essential for your Research Plan. You must demonstrate understanding of WHY your design choice leads to your test choice.






ImportantKey Principle



The structure of your data (determined by your design) dictates which statistical test is appropriate.




Between-Subjects → Independent Samples t-test
The logic:

You have two groups of participants
Each participant provides one score
The scores from Group A are independent of scores from Group B
We compare the two group means

Why “independent”?: The scores in one group tell us nothing about the scores in the other group. Participant 1 in Group A has no connection to Participant 1 in Group B.
Example:

“This study uses a between-subjects design with different participants randomly assigned to each font condition. The data therefore consist of two independent groups of recall scores. An independent samples t-test is the appropriate analysis because it compares the means of two unrelated groups.”



Within-Subjects → Paired Samples t-test
The logic:

You have one group of participants
Each participant provides two scores (one per condition)
The scores are paired — each person’s Condition A score is linked to their Condition B score
We compare the mean difference within each person

Why “paired”?: Participant 1’s score in Condition A is meaningfully connected to Participant 1’s score in Condition B — they come from the same person.
Example:

“This study uses a within-subjects design with each participant rating faces in both gaze conditions. Because each participant provides paired scores (one trustworthiness rating for direct gaze, one for averted gaze), a paired samples t-test is appropriate. This test analyses whether the mean difference in ratings within individuals is significantly different from zero.”



The Consequences of Using the Wrong Test
What happens if you use the wrong test?







Error
Consequence




Independent t-test on paired data
Loses statistical power (harder to detect real effects)


Paired t-test on independent data
Violates assumptions, produces invalid results



Both errors lead to incorrect conclusions about your research question.


Complete Justification Template
For your Research Plan, structure your justification like this:

“This study employs a [between-subjects / within-subjects] design because [reason for design choice — reference advantages and how disadvantages are managed].
Given this design, the data will consist of [description of data structure — independent groups OR paired scores].
Therefore, [an independent samples / a paired samples] t-test is the appropriate statistical analysis. This test will compare [what is being compared] to determine whether [the research question].”

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
text:
Part 6: Method Section Structure
Your Research Plan requires a brief Method section. Here’s what belongs in each subsection.

Design
State the design type and define your variables:

“This study employed a between-subjects experimental design. The independent variable was font type with two levels: fluent (Arial, 16pt, black) and disfluent (Comic Sans MS, 12pt, 75% grey). The dependent variable was free recall score (number of words correctly recalled from a 20-word list, range 0-20).”

Must include:

Design type (between-subjects, within-subjects)
IV with levels fully operationalised
DV with measurement details



Participants
Describe who participated and how they were assigned:

“Sixty undergraduate psychology students will be recruited through the department participant pool. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the fluent font condition (n = 30) or the disfluent font condition (n = 30).”

Must include:

Target sample size
Recruitment method
Assignment method (random, counterbalanced)

For within-subjects designs, specify counterbalancing:

“Order of conditions will be counterbalanced, with half of participants seeing direct gaze faces first and half seeing averted gaze faces first.”



Materials
Describe everything participants will see or use:

“Stimuli consisted of 20 common concrete nouns selected from the MRC Psycholinguistic Database, matched for word frequency and imageability. In the fluent condition, words were displayed in 16-point Arial (black text on white background). In the disfluent condition, the same words were displayed in 12-point Comic Sans MS (75% grey on white background). Presentation was controlled using PsychoPy. Participants recorded responses on a blank A4 sheet.”

Must include:

Stimulus details (what, how selected)
Condition-specific differences
Measurement tools/materials



Procedure
Describe what happens, step by step:

“Participants will be tested individually in a quiet laboratory room. After providing informed consent, they will be seated at a computer and given standardised instructions to memorise the upcoming word list. Twenty words will be presented sequentially for 3 seconds each. After the final word, participants will count backwards from 50 for 30 seconds (filled delay), then write down as many words as they can remember for 2 minutes. The session will last approximately 10 minutes.”

Must include:

Setting
Sequence of events
Timing for each phase
Key instructions given
Total duration

title: Chapter 5: Building Your Research
text:
Summary







Concept
Key Point




Operationalisation
Turning abstract concepts into concrete, measurable variables


IV operationalisation
Exactly how you create different conditions


DV operationalisation
Exactly how you measure the outcome


Two-tailed hypothesis
Predicts difference without direction — use when uncertain


One-tailed hypothesis
Predicts specific direction — use when theory supports it


Between-subjects
Different people in each condition — no order effects but individual differences


Within-subjects
Same people in all conditions — controls individual differences but order effects


Independent t-test
Compares means from different groups (between-subjects)


Paired t-test
Compares means from same people (within-subjects)


Design-test link
Your design structure determines which test is appropriate

title: Chapter 4: Descriptive Statistics in Action
text:
Part 1: Describing the Centre
When we collect data, the first question is usually: What’s typical?

The Mean: The Balancing Point
The mean is the arithmetic average. If we measured 5 people’s memory scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean is 7. This is the “balancing point” — if you put these scores on a seesaw, 7 is where it would balance.


The Median: The Middle Value
The median is the middle value when data are sorted. Half the values are above it, half below.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
With 5 values, the median is the 3rd value (when sorted). Here, both mean and median are 7.


When Mean and Median Differ
Sometimes they tell different stories. Consider these scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean shoots up to 10, but the median stays at 7. The median is resistant to extreme values (outliers). The mean is pulled by them.
When to use which?

Mean: When data are roughly symmetric, no extreme outliers
Median: When data are skewed or have outliers (like income data)

title: Chapter 4: Descriptive Statistics in Action
text:
Part 2: Describing the Spread
The centre isn’t the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look completely different:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both means are 7, but the groups are very different. We need measures of spread.

The Range: Simplest Spread
The range is just the distance from lowest to highest:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A spans 2 points (6 to 8). Group B spans 10 points (2 to 12). The range immediately shows Group B is more variable.
Limitation: The range only uses two values, so it’s sensitive to outliers.


The Standard Deviation: The Gold Standard
The standard deviation (SD) measures how far scores typically fall from the mean.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A’s SD is about 0.7 — scores cluster tightly around 7. Group B’s SD is about 4.2 — scores are much more spread out.
Rule of thumb: In roughly normal data, about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean.
If the mean is 7 and SD is 1:

~68% of scores fall between 6 and 8



The summary() Function: Everything at Once
R’s summary() function gives you a quick overview:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This shows:

Min and Max (the range endpoints)
1st and 3rd Quartile (the middle 50%)
Median (the middle value)
Mean

text:
Part 3: Seeing Descriptives in Psychology Data
Let’s look at what descriptive statistics tell us with realistic psychology examples.

Example 1: Reaction Times
Imagine we measured 10 participants’ reaction times (in milliseconds):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Interpretation:

Mean reaction time is about 285ms
The median (284ms) is similar, suggesting roughly symmetric data
SD of about 28ms tells us most people fall within ±28ms of the mean
Range of 245 to 334ms shows the fastest and slowest participants



Example 2: Memory Scores by Condition
Now let’s compare two groups. Lab A saw abstract words, Lab B saw concrete words:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Interpretation:

Lab A mean: ~5.3 words recalled
Lab B mean: ~7.3 words recalled
The difference is 2 words — but is that meaningful?
Both SDs are around 1, so 2 words is about 2 standard deviations — a substantial difference



Example 3: Pre-Post Mood Ratings
Same people rated their mood before and after the session:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Interpretation:

Mean mood increased by 1.1 points on average
The SD of change (0.7) tells us most people improved by 0.4 to 1.8 points
This is a within-subjects comparison — same people before and after

Standard Deviation in Context
The SD only makes sense relative to the mean and the scale.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Memory: Mean = 6, SD = 0.77. An SD of 0.77 on a 10-point scale is fairly consistent.
RT: Mean = 277ms, SD = 23ms. Is that a lot of variability? It’s about 8% of the mean — fairly typical for reaction times.



When Means Can Mislead
Consider these two possible DataLab results:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both means are 6, but Scenario B’s huge SD (3.7) signals that something interesting is happening — perhaps there are two distinct groups.
