title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 1: Reading R Descriptive Output
For the EDS Assignment, you’ll receive R output and need to interpret it. Let’s practice!

Exercise 1: Basic Descriptive Output
A researcher measured the number of words recalled by 8 participants. Here’s the R output:
> summary_stats <- data %>%
+   summarise(
+     Mean = mean(words_recalled),
+     SD = sd(words_recalled),
+     Median = median(words_recalled),
+     n = n()
+   )
> summary_stats

# A tibble: 1 x 4
   Mean    SD Median     n
  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <int>
1   6.5  1.41      6     8
a) What is the mean number of words recalled?






TipShow Answer





The mean is 6.5 words (shown in the Mean column).



b) What is the standard deviation?






TipShow Answer





The standard deviation is 1.41 words (shown in the SD column).



c) What does the comparison of mean (6.5) and median (6) suggest about the distribution?






TipShow Answer





The mean (6.5) is slightly higher than the median (6), suggesting a very slight positive skew. However, they’re close enough that the distribution is approximately symmetric.






Exercise 2: Group Comparison Output
A study compared reaction times between two conditions. Here’s the R output:
> data %>%
+   group_by(condition) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(RT), SD = sd(RT), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  condition  Mean    SD     n
  <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 caffeine   285.  42.3    15
2 placebo    312.  51.1    15
a) How many participants were in each condition?






TipShow Answer





15 participants in each condition (shown in the n column).



b) Which condition had faster reaction times?






TipShow Answer





The caffeine condition had faster reaction times (lower mean: 285ms vs 312ms).



c) Write a sentence describing these results in APA format.






TipShow Answer






Participants in the caffeine condition responded faster (M = 285ms, SD = 42.3ms) than those in the placebo condition (M = 312ms, SD = 51.1ms).

title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 2: Interpreting Distributions

Exercise 3: Distribution Shapes
For each scenario, predict the distribution shape:
a) Exam scores on an easy test (most students score 80-100%)






TipShow Answer





Negatively skewed (ceiling effect). Most scores cluster near the top, with a tail toward lower scores.



b) Reaction times to a visual stimulus






TipShow Answer





Positively skewed. There’s a lower bound (can’t be negative or below ~150ms), but no upper bound. Occasional slow responses create a right tail.



c) Heights of adult women






TipShow Answer





Approximately normal (symmetric, bell-shaped). Heights tend to cluster around the average with fewer very short or very tall individuals.





Exercise 4: Mean vs Median in R Output
A researcher reports this R output:
> salary_stats
# A tibble: 1 x 2
     Mean Median
    <dbl>  <dbl>
1  52000  38000
a) What does this tell you about the distribution?






TipShow Answer





The mean (£52,000) is much higher than the median (£38,000), indicating positive skew. A few very high salaries pull the mean up.



b) Which measure (mean or median) better represents the “typical” salary? Why?






TipShow Answer





The median (£38,000) better represents the typical salary because it’s not affected by the extreme high values. More than half of workers earn less than the mean.

section: Part 3: APA Reporting from R Output
text:
Part 3: APA Reporting from R Output

Exercise 5: Complete the Report
Use this R output to answer the questions:
> memory_stats
# A tibble: 1 x 3
   Mean    SD Median
  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   6.8   1.4      7
Fill in the blanks:

Participants recalled an average of _____ words (M = _____, SD = _____). The median was _____, suggesting the distribution was approximately _____.







TipShow Answer






Participants recalled an average of 6.8 words (M = 6.8, SD = 1.4). The median was 7, suggesting the distribution was approximately symmetric (since mean ≈ median).






Exercise 6: Write Full APA Description
Use this R output:
> data %>%
+   group_by(time_of_day) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(accuracy), SD = sd(accuracy), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  time_of_day  Mean    SD     n
  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 morning      78.2  12.4    20
2 evening      71.5  14.1    20
Write a complete sentence reporting these descriptives in APA format.






TipShow Answer






Participants showed higher accuracy in the morning (M = 78.2%, SD = 12.4%) compared to the evening (M = 71.5%, SD = 14.1%).

Or:

Mean accuracy was higher in the morning condition (M = 78.2, SD = 12.4) than in the evening condition (M = 71.5, SD = 14.1).

title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 4: Conceptual Questions

Exercise 7: True or False
Mark each statement True or False:
a) The mean is always the best measure of central tendency.






TipShow Answer





False. The median is better for skewed data or when outliers are present.



b) Standard deviation tells you about the shape of the distribution.






TipShow Answer





False. SD tells you about spread/variability, not shape. You need to compare mean and median (or look at a histogram) to assess shape.



c) If the mean is greater than the median, the distribution is positively skewed.






TipShow Answer





True. In a positively skewed distribution, extreme high values pull the mean above the median.



d) In R output, n typically refers to the sample size.






TipShow Answer





True. The n column shows the number of observations (participants/data points) in each group.





Exercise 8: The 68-95-99.7 Rule
Reaction times are normally distributed with Mean = 300ms and SD = 40ms.
a) What range contains approximately 68% of reaction times?






TipShow Answer





Mean ± 1 SD = 300 ± 40 = 260ms to 340ms



b) What range contains approximately 95% of reaction times?






TipShow Answer





Mean ± 2 SD = 300 ± 80 = 220ms to 380ms



c) A participant has a reaction time of 200ms. Is this unusual? Why?






TipShow Answer





Yes, this is unusual. 200ms is (300-200)/40 = 2.5 SDs below the mean. Only about 0.6% of values fall this far from the mean in a normal distribution.

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 1: The Building Blocks — Variables

What Is a Variable?
A variable is anything that can vary — any characteristic, number, or quantity that can take different values.
In the DataLab:

Memory scores varied (some people remembered 4 words, others 8)
Mood ratings varied (some felt 3/10, others 8/10)
Reaction times varied (some caught the ruler quickly, others slowly)



Independent and Dependent Variables
In experimental research, we distinguish between two types of variables:

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or controls — the presumed cause.
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures — the outcome that may be affected.

The DV depends on the IV. We’re asking: Does the outcome depend on the condition?


DataLab Example: Memory Task
In the memory experiment:

IV: Word type (abstract vs concrete)
DV: Number of words recalled (0-10)

Lab A saw abstract words (justice, freedom, wisdom). Lab B saw concrete words (chair, river, mountain). The researcher manipulated which words you saw — that’s the IV.
What we measured — how many words you recalled — is the DV. We wanted to know if recall depended on the word type.


When There Is No IV
Not all research involves manipulation. Sometimes we simply measure two things and look at their relationship.
In the Frontal Lob task, you rated how good you thought you’d be at throwing (1-10), and then we measured your actual accuracy. Neither was manipulated — we just measured both.






ImportantKey Insight



When there’s no manipulation, there’s no IV. This is called a correlational design, and we’ll cover it shortly.




Data Types
The DV can be measured in different ways:








Data Type
Description
Example




Continuous
Can take any value (including decimals)
Reaction time (245.3ms)


Discrete
Whole numbers only (counts)
Words recalled (7)


Categorical
Categories with no numerical order
Lab group (A or B)


Ordinal
Categories with an order
Rating (1-10 scale)



In the DataLab:

Memory score is discrete (you can’t recall 6.5 words)
Reaction time is continuous (could be 245.3ms or 245.4ms)
Mood rating is ordinal (1-10 scale with order, but intervals may not be equal)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 2: Design Types
The design refers to how participants are assigned to conditions.

Between-Subjects Design

Between-subjects design: Different participants in each condition.

In the memory experiment, you were in either Lab A (abstract words) or Lab B (concrete words) — never both. Different people were in each condition.
Why “between”? We’re comparing between groups — Lab A people versus Lab B people.
Advantage: No order effects (practice, fatigue, boredom)
Disadvantage: Individual differences may affect results (maybe Lab B just happened to have better memorisers)


Within-Subjects Design

Within-subjects design: The same participants measured in all conditions.

In the pre-post mood survey, you rated your mood before and after the session. The same person provided both data points.
Why “within”? We’re comparing within the same person — your pre-mood versus your post-mood.
Advantage: Each person is their own control! Individual differences are controlled because we’re comparing you to yourself.
Disadvantage: Order effects possible (practice, fatigue)


Within-Subjects Examples from DataLab



Task
Same Person Compared




Pre/Post mood
Before vs after session


Pre/Post energy
Before vs after session


Pre/Post stress
Before vs after session


Frontal Lob
Dominant vs non-dominant hand





Matched Pairs Design

Matched pairs design: Participants are paired on a key characteristic, then one from each pair goes to each condition.

This is a hybrid — different people in each condition (like between-subjects), but they’re matched to be similar (reducing individual difference problems).
Example: Match students by the amount of sleep they reported the night before. Let’s say two participants reported five hours and two participants reported 10 hours. One from each pair gets abstract words, the other gets concrete words. This would allow me to control for sleep quantity (five or ten hours), as I would have each level represented in each group. It means I would have to ask about sleep before allocating to condition, and so is a little bit more complicated in everyday life.


Correlational Design

Correlational design: Measuring the relationship between two variables — no manipulation.

When we measured self-rating and actual throwing performance, we didn’t manipulate either. We simply measured both and asked: Are they related? This could be the same for hours of sleep and memory performance, or any of the personality traits we measured and any other outcome variable.






WarningCritical Point



In correlational designs, there is NO IV. Neither variable is the “cause” — we’re just measuring a relationship.




Summary: Design Types








Design
Key Feature
Example




Between-subjects
Different people in each condition
Lab A vs Lab B


Within-subjects
Same people in all conditions
Pre vs Post mood


Matched pairs
Participants paired, one per condition
Matched by ability


Correlational
Relationship measured, no manipulation
Self-rating vs performance

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 3: Writing Hypotheses
A hypothesis is a prediction about what you expect to find.

Experimental vs Null Hypothesis

Experimental hypothesis (H₁ or Ha): Predicts an effect or difference will exist.
Null hypothesis (H₀): Predicts no effect or no difference.

For the memory experiment:

H₁: Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words.
H₀: There will be no difference in recall between word types.

Statistical testing works by assuming H₀ is true, then checking if the data is surprising enough to reject that assumption.


One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed hypothesis: Predicts the direction of the effect.
Two-tailed hypothesis: Predicts a difference but not which direction.

One-tailed examples:

“Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words” (predicts concrete > abstract)
“Mood will improve after the session” (predicts post > pre)
“Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant hand” (predicts dominant > non-dominant)

Two-tailed examples:

“Word type will affect memory” (could be better or worse)
“Mood will change after the session” (could go up or down)
“There will be a difference in accuracy between hands” (no direction predicted)



When to Use Which?
Use one-tailed when:

Previous research strongly suggests a direction
Your theory predicts a specific direction
You only care about effects in one direction

Use two-tailed when:

You’re uncertain about the direction
Effects in either direction would be interesting
You’re being conservative (harder to reach significance)



Hypotheses for Each DataLab Task



Task
One-tailed Hypothesis




Memory
Concrete words will be recalled better than abstract words


Pre-Post Mood
Mood will improve after the session


Frontal Lob
Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant


Sixth Sense
Detection accuracy will be greater than chance (50%)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 4: Descriptive Statistics
Before running statistical tests, we need to describe our data. Descriptive statistics summarise the key features.

The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average — the most common measure of central tendency.
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]
Calculating by hand:

Add up all values (Σx)
Divide by the number of values (n)

Example: Memory scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9

Sum: 5 + 7 + 6 + 8 + 9 = 35
Count: 5
Mean: 35 ÷ 5 = 7



The Standard Deviation
The mean alone doesn’t tell the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look very different:

Group A: 6, 6, 7, 7, 8 (Mean = 6.8)
Group B: 2, 5, 7, 9, 11 (Mean = 6.8)

Group B is much more spread out. We need to measure this variability.

Standard Deviation (SD) measures how spread out the data is from the mean.

Low SD = scores clustered together (consistent)
High SD = scores spread out (variable)




Calculating SD by Hand
Formula:
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}\]
Steps:

Calculate the mean
Subtract the mean from each value (deviation)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by (n-1)
Take the square root

Example: Scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9 (Mean = 7)



Score
Deviation (x - mean)
Squared




5
5 - 7 = -2
4


7
7 - 7 = 0
0


6
6 - 7 = -1
1


8
8 - 7 = +1
1


9
9 - 7 = +2
4


Sum

10




Variance = 10 ÷ (5-1) = 2.5
SD = √2.5 = 1.58



Why n-1?
We divide by (n-1), not n, because we’re estimating the population SD from a sample. This “degrees of freedom” correction makes our estimate unbiased.


Interpreting SD
For normally distributed data:

~68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean
~95% fall within 2 SDs
~99.7% fall within 3 SDs

If the mean memory score is 7 with SD = 1.58:

About 68% of people scored between 5.4 and 8.6
About 95% scored between 3.8 and 10.2



The Key Insight






ImportantSignal vs Noise



A difference between means only matters if it’s big relative to the spread.

Signal = difference between group means
Noise = variability within groups (SD)
The key question: Is the signal bigger than the noise?

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 5: Reporting Descriptive Statistics
When writing up research, report descriptives clearly using APA format.

Basic Format
Report both mean AND standard deviation:

(M = value, SD = value)

Example:

Participants’ memory scores were moderate (M = 6.8, SD = 1.58).



Comparing Groups
When comparing conditions, report descriptives for each:

Lab A participants (M = 5.8, SD = 1.4) recalled fewer words than Lab B participants (M = 6.5, SD = 1.3).



APA Conventions

Use italics for statistical symbols: M, SD, t, p, r, d
Report two decimal places
No leading zero for values that cannot exceed 1 (e.g., p = .023, not p = 0.023)

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
Reflecting on Data Collection
DataLab was probably your first experience collecting psychological data. You may have noticed things didn’t always go smoothly:

Instructions weren’t always clear
Timing was tricky
Partners did things differently
The environment was distracting
Recording data while running a task was harder than expected

This is normal. In fact, these challenges are exactly why research methods matter. Understanding what can go wrong helps you:

Appreciate why standardised procedures exist
Interpret your own data more thoughtfully
Design better studies in the future

As you read about each task below, think about what happened during your data collection. What might have affected your measurements?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
What You Measured
DataLab included a group memory test plus five tasks measuring different aspects of human cognition and behaviour. For each task, we’ll cover the psychological background and then consider methodological issues.

Task 1: Reaction Time (Reflex Test)

Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus and your response to it. In the ruler-drop task, we measured simple reaction time — how quickly you could respond to a single, expected stimulus.
The physics is elegant: when you catch a falling ruler, the distance it fell before you caught it tells us how long your reaction took. Using the equation for free-falling objects (d = ½gt²), we can convert centimetres into milliseconds.






NoteWhy It Matters



Reaction time is one of the most reliable measures in psychology. Your data will show how consistent (or variable) human performance is, even on simple tasks. We can also look for practice effects — did you get faster across trials?








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Was the ruler held at exactly the same height each time?
Did the participant’s fingers start in exactly the same position?
Was it always clear where to read the catch point?

Potential biases:

Anticipation: Did you start to predict when the drop would happen?
Practice effects: Did you genuinely get faster, or just better at anticipating?
Hand dominance: We only tested one hand — would results differ for the other?

Procedural issues:

How consistent was your partner’s dropping technique?
Were there distractions (noise, movement) that affected some trials?
Did everyone follow the same instructions?





Memory Test: Mind Palace

The memory task measured working memory — how many items you can hold in mind while performing another task.
Miller (1956) famously proposed that we can hold about 7 ± 2 items in short-term memory — the “magical number seven.” But the distraction task (maths problems) interferes with rehearsal, so performance typically drops.
We’ll also examine the serial position effect: people tend to remember words from the beginning of a list (primacy) and end of a list (recency) better than the middle. Your position-by-position recall data will let us test this pattern.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were the words presented at the same speed for everyone?
Could everyone hear clearly from where they were sitting?
Was the recall period the same length for all participants?

Potential biases:

Prior exposure: Had you seen any of the words recently?
Language background: Were the words equally familiar to everyone?
Strategy use: Some people use chunking or visualisation — should we control for this?

Procedural issues:

Was the distraction task equally difficult for everyone?
Did the timing between presentation and recall vary?
How was recall scored? (exact spelling? close enough?)





Task 2: Time and Magnitude Perception (Time Warp)

How accurately do we perceive time? Research shows that our internal clocks are surprisingly inaccurate and can be influenced by many factors.
This station measured three types of estimation:

Time estimation — How accurately could you judge 60 seconds?
Visual magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge line lengths by looking?
Tactile magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge lengths by touch alone?







TipCross-Modal Comparison



By comparing visual and tactile estimation, we can explore whether some senses are more accurate than others for judging physical properties.








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

When exactly did the stopwatch start? When you said “start” or when your partner pressed it?
How precisely were line lengths measured?
Was string tension consistent across tactile trials?

Potential biases:

Counting: Did you count seconds in your head? (This is a strategy, not pure time perception)
Anchoring: Did early estimates influence later ones?
Expectation: Did you adjust estimates based on feedback?

Procedural issues:

Could you see any clocks or time displays?
Were there environmental cues (regular sounds, movements)?
Was it quiet enough to concentrate?





Task 3: Psychic Staring (Sixth Sense)

Can humans detect when they’re being watched? This is a testable empirical question!
The staring detection task uses signal detection theory:

Hits: Correctly detecting when someone IS staring
False alarms: Saying “staring” when they’re NOT
Misses: Saying “not staring” when they ARE
Correct rejections: Correctly detecting when they’re NOT staring

If people cannot actually detect staring, we’d expect performance to be at chance level (about 50% correct, or 3 out of 6 trials).






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Could you detect your partner through peripheral vision?
Were there sounds or movements that gave it away?
Was “staring” defined consistently? (How long? How intense?)

Potential biases:

Response bias: Did you tend to say “yes” or “no” more often?
Pattern-seeking: Did you assume alternating patterns?
Confirmation bias: Did you interpret ambiguous feelings as evidence for your guess?

Procedural issues:

How reliably did your partner randomise staring/not-staring?
Was the duration of each trial consistent?
Could other people in the room affect the “being watched” feeling?





Task 4: Randomness (Lady Luck)

Humans are notoriously bad at generating random sequences. When asked to produce “random” numbers, people:

Avoid repeating the same number twice in a row (even though true randomness includes repetitions)
Avoid patterns (even though random sequences often contain streaks)
Favour certain numbers (often 7!)

This station also included dice rolling and coin flipping, which let us compare true random outcomes (from dice/coins) with human-generated random sequences.






NoteThe Gambler’s Fallacy



Many people believe that after a streak of heads, tails is “due.” This is false — each flip is independent. Your data will likely show longer runs than most people expect!








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were all 20 numbers recorded correctly?
Were dice rolls and coin flips recorded accurately?
How were “runs” counted? Was this consistent?

Potential biases:

Number preferences: Did cultural factors affect which numbers felt “random”?
Avoidance of repetition: This is a known bias — but did you try to overcome it?
Anchoring: Did your previous number influence your next choice?

Procedural issues:

Was there time pressure that affected your choices?
Did you understand what “random” meant in this context?
Were the dice fair? Were coins flipped properly?





Task 5: Metacognition (Frontal Lob)

Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking — including how well you know your own abilities.
The throwing task measured calibration: the match between your self-assessed ability and your actual performance.

Overconfidence: Rating yourself higher than your performance
Underconfidence: Rating yourself lower than your performance
Well-calibrated: Your rating matches your performance

Research consistently shows that people are poorly calibrated — often overconfident about easy tasks and underconfident about hard ones.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

How were successful throws defined? What about balls that bounced in?
Who counted the successes — participant or tester?
Was counting accurate across 10 throws?

Potential biases:

Self-serving bias: Did you rate yourself higher because you wanted to be good?
Social desirability: Did having a partner watching affect your self-rating?
Anchoring: Did the 1-10 scale influence what felt like a “reasonable” rating?

Procedural issues:

Was the throwing distance the same for everyone?
Was the target positioned consistently?
Did throwing technique vary (overarm, underarm)?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
The Pre-Post Design
DataLab used a within-subjects design to measure mood change. You rated your mood, energy, and stress both before and after the stations.
This design is powerful because each person serves as their own control. By comparing your “before” to your “after,” we eliminate individual differences — we’re measuring change within you, not differences between people.






ImportantTeaching Application



When we learn about paired t-tests, we’ll analyse whether DataLab systematically affected mood, energy, or stress. Did participation make people feel better? Worse? More or less stressed?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
Why This Matters
You’ve just experienced something important: collecting data is hard.
The methodological issues above aren’t criticisms — they’re reality. Even professional researchers face these challenges. The difference is that professionals:

Use standardised procedures — detailed protocols that specify exactly how to do each step
Define variables operationally — clear definitions of what counts as a “catch” or a “success”
Train testers — so everyone administers tasks the same way
Control the environment — quiet rooms, consistent setups, minimal distractions
Check inter-rater reliability — do two testers recording the same event get the same result?

When we analyse your DataLab data, we’ll need to keep these limitations in mind. Some variability in the data reflects genuine individual differences. Some reflects measurement error and procedural inconsistencies.
Learning to tell the difference is what research methods is all about.

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
section: Why We Generated Our Own Data
text:
Why We Generated Our Own Data

Learning with Real Data
When we analyse data you’ve generated:

You understand what the numbers represent
You can connect statistics to real experiences
The results are genuinely unknown (not textbook examples)



Experiencing Both Roles
Acting as both participant and tester taught you:

The importance of standardised procedures
How instructions affect behaviour
Why research protocols exist



Understanding Limitations
Having collected data yourself, you now understand:

Why researchers obsess over procedures
How small variations can affect results
That “messy data” is normal — interpretation requires care

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
How You Worked in Pairs
At each task, you worked with a partner:

One person was the participant (completed the task)
One person was the tester (administered the task, recorded data)
Then you swapped roles

This meant everyone experienced both perspectives.
You received a sequence card telling you which tasks to complete in which order.

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
What Is This Module?
Research Methods & Experimental Design
How psychologists:

Ask questions about the mind and behaviour
Design studies to answer those questions
Collect and analyse data
Draw valid conclusions


Emphasise this is a practical, skills-based module. Not just theory — they will DO research.

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
The Problem with Common Sense

“Opposites attract”
“Birds of a feather flock together”
Both can’t be true… can they?



Common sense often gives contradictory answers. Science provides a systematic way to find out what’s actually true.

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Everyday Thinking vs Scientific Thinking


Everyday Thinking

Based on personal experience
Influenced by biases
Accepts anecdotes as evidence
Confirmation bias

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Step 1: The Research Question
Where do research questions come from?

Curiosity about behaviour
Gaps in existing research
Real-world problems
Theory testing
Unexpected observations


Example: Do people lie more when texting than face-to-face?

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Step 2: The Hypothesis

A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about what you expect to find.

Good hypothesis:

“Participants will tell more lies per conversation when communicating via text message compared to face-to-face.”

Not a hypothesis:

“I wonder if texting affects lying.”

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Step 3: Design the Study
Key decisions:

Who will you study? (participants)
What will you measure? (variables)
How will you measure it? (methods)
What comparisons will you make? (design)


We’ll spend most of this module on this step.

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Step 4: Collect Data

Follow your plan precisely
Treat participants ethically
Record everything carefully
Minimise errors and bias

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Step 5: Analyse Data

Statistics are tools for finding patterns in data and determining whether those patterns are meaningful.

This is where R comes in — and what you’ll learn in the labs.

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Step 6: Interpret Results

What do the findings mean?
Do they support the hypothesis?
What are the limitations?
What questions remain?


Then the cycle continues…

Variables

A variable is anything that can vary — any characteristic that can take different values across observations.

Examples:

Age
Reaction time
Mood rating
Experimental condition

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Types of Variables


Categorical

Distinct categories
No inherent order (nominal)
Or ordered (ordinal)

Examples: gender, condition, education level

Continuous

Numerical values
Can take any value in a range
Interval or ratio scales

Examples: age, reaction time, score

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design
text:
Independent vs Dependent Variables

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or selects
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures as the outcome


Example: Testing whether caffeine affects reaction time

IV: Caffeine (yes/no)
DV: Reaction time (milliseconds)

Research methods provide systematic ways to answer questions about behaviour
Scientific thinking differs from everyday reasoning

Variables are the building blocks of research

title: Group Project Options 2025–26
text:
🐒 LittleMonkeyLab



Group Project Options 2025–26


PS50008A — Gordon’s ideas of fun studies



Research Methods & Experimental Design · Goldsmiths, University of London

made with Quarto + R




How to use this guide: Each project below has a between-subjects and within-subjects variant. All use a two-condition design testable with an independent or paired t-test. All are designed to be completable in one lab session (~20 participants, ~5–10 min per participant) with minimal/free materials. These study plans show the shape and size of a good group project! You do not need to get any more complex than this, and marks are NOT related to complexity — usually, the other way around!
📚 Suggested readings for all projects are available in the Project Articles folder on Learn.gold.


Projects


A


The Effect of Smiling on Perceived Approachability


Social Effect: Medium–Large


▶


Background: Facial expressions are powerful social signals. Research consistently shows that smiling faces are rated as more approachable, trustworthy, and warm than neutral faces (Hess et al., 2000). This is a robust social perception effect with clear theoretical grounding in evolutionary psychology and social cognition.

IV: Facial expression (neutral vs smiling) DV: Approachability rating (1–7 Likert scale, averaged across faces)


Between-subjects variant

Group 1 rates 8 photos of people with neutral expressions on approachability (1 = not at all, 7 = very approachable)
Group 2 rates the same 8 people with smiling expressions on approachability
Photos matched for age, gender balance (4 male, 4 female), and attractiveness
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants rate 16 photos: 8 with neutral expressions and 8 with smiling expressions (different people in each set, matched for age/gender)
Photos presented in randomised order
DV is mean approachability rating for neutral vs smiling faces (within-participant comparison)

Materials: 16 printed photos (or PowerPoint slides), rating sheets, pens. Photos sourced from open-access face databases (e.g., Chicago Face Database, Radboud Faces Database).
Expected effect: Medium-to-large (d ≈ 0.6–1.0). Smiling-approachability effect is very robust across cultures.

Indicative readings:
Hess, U., Adams, R. B., & Kleck, R. E. (2000). Facial appearance, gender, and emotion expression. Emotion, 5(1), 119–124.
Willis, J., & Todorov, A. (2006). First impressions: Making up your mind after a 100-ms exposure to a face. Psychological Science, 17(7), 592–598.






B


The Effect of Background Music on Concentration


Cognitive Effect: Medium


▶


Background: The irrelevant sound effect (Salamé & Baddeley, 1989) demonstrates that background sound impairs serial recall. Music with lyrics is particularly disruptive due to phonological interference. Well-established effect with reasonable effect sizes.

IV: Sound condition (silence vs music with lyrics) DV: Number of items correctly recalled in serial order (out of 10–15)


Between-subjects variant

Group 1 studies a list of 15 words in silence
Group 2 studies the same list while pop music with lyrics plays from a speaker
2-minute study period → 1-minute distractor → 2-minute written recall
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants study two different word lists (counterbalanced order), one in silence, one with music
Lists matched for word frequency and concreteness
Same timing structure
Each participant provides two recall scores

Materials: 2 word lists (printed), portable speaker, music track (pre-selected), recall sheets, pens
Expected effect: Medium (d ≈ 0.5–0.7). Irrelevant sound effect is well-replicated.

Indicative readings:
Salamé, P., & Baddeley, A. (1989). Effects of background music on phonological short-term memory. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 41A, 107–122.
Perham, N., & Vizard, J. (2011). Can preference for background music mediate the irrelevant sound effect? Applied Cognitive Psychology, 25(4), 625–631.






C


The Effect of Colour on Memory for Words


Cognitive Effect: Small–Medium


▶


Background: The Von Restorff isolation effect and colour-attention research suggest that words presented in colour (especially red) are better remembered than words in black. Practical, visual manipulation that’s easy to set up.

IV: Word colour (black text vs red text) DV: Number of words correctly recalled (out of 15–20)


Between-subjects variant

Group 1 studies a list of 20 words printed in black ink
Group 2 studies the same list printed in red ink
2-minute study → 1-minute distractor → 2-minute free recall
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants study one list of 20 words: 10 in black, 10 in red (randomly intermixed)
DV is number of red words recalled vs number of black words recalled (within-participant comparison)
Same timing structure

Materials: Printed word lists (colour printer needed for red version), recall sheets, pens
Expected effect: Small-to-medium (d ≈ 0.3–0.5). Colour effects are often found but magnitude varies.

Indicative readings:
Dzulkifli, M. A., & Mustafar, M. F. (2013). The influence of colour on memory performance: A review. Malaysian Journal of Medical Sciences, 20(2), 3–9.
Kuhbandner, C., & Pekrun, R. (2013). Joint effects of emotion and color on memory. Emotion, 13(3), 375–379.






D


The Effect of Imagery on Word Recall


Cognitive Effect: Medium–Large


▶


Background: Paivio’s dual coding theory (1971) predicts that forming mental images of words leads to better recall than rote repetition, because information is encoded in both verbal and visual systems. One of the most robust effects in memory research.

IV: Learning instruction (rote repetition vs mental imagery) DV: Number of words correctly recalled (out of 15–20)


Between-subjects variant

Group 1 told to repeat each word silently as they study the list
Group 2 told to form a vivid mental image of each word as they study
Same word list (concrete nouns), 2-minute study → 1-minute distractor → 2-minute recall
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants study two different word lists (counterbalanced)
List A: instructed to use rote repetition
List B: instructed to use mental imagery
Same timing structure
Each participant provides two recall scores

Materials: 2 word lists of concrete nouns (printed), instruction sheets, recall sheets, pens
Expected effect: Medium-to-large (d ≈ 0.6–1.0). Dual coding is one of the most reliable effects in cognitive psychology.

Indicative readings:
Paivio, A. (1971). Imagery and verbal processes. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.
Bower, G. H. (1970). Imagery as a relational organizer in associative learning. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 9(5), 529–533.






E


The Effect of Phone Presence on Attention


Social Cognitive Effect: Small–Medium


▶


Background: The “brain drain” hypothesis (Ward et al., 2017) suggests that the mere visible presence of a smartphone — even switched off — reduces available cognitive capacity because people must actively resist attending to it. A highly contemporary topic with strong student engagement.

IV: Phone presence (phone visible on desk vs phone out of sight) DV: Score on a short attention/concentration task (e.g., digit span or proofreading accuracy)


Between-subjects variant

Group 1 completes a concentration task with their phone placed face-down on the desk in front of them
Group 2 completes the same task with their phone in their bag/pocket (out of sight)
Task: proofread a short passage and circle errors (10 deliberate errors), or complete a digit span task
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants complete two equivalent tasks (counterbalanced): one with phone on desk, one with phone in bag
Tasks matched for difficulty (e.g., two different passages with same number of errors)
Each participant provides two accuracy scores

Materials: Printed proofreading passages (or digit span sheets), answer sheets, pens. Participants use their own phones.
Expected effect: Small-to-medium (d ≈ 0.3–0.5). Effect is debated but consistently found in some paradigms — good for discussion either way.

Indicative readings:
Ward, A. F., Duke, K., Gneezy, A., & Bos, M. W. (2017). Brain drain: The mere presence of one’s own smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 2(2), 140–154.
Thornton, B., Faires, A., Robbins, M., & Rollins, E. (2014). The mere presence of a cell phone may be distracting. Social Psychology, 45(6), 479–488.






F


The Effect of Testing on Learning (Retrieval Practice)


Cognitive Effect: Medium–Large


▶


Background: The testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) shows that actively retrieving information from memory improves long-term retention more than re-studying. Extremely robust finding with practical implications for student learning.

IV: Study method (re-study vs retrieval practice) DV: Number of facts correctly recalled on final test (out of 10–15)


Between-subjects variant

Both groups read a short factual passage (2 minutes)
Group 1: re-reads the passage for another 2 minutes
Group 2: spends 2 minutes answering recall questions about the passage (no feedback)
2-minute delay → final recall test (same questions for both groups)



Within-subjects variant

All participants read two short passages (counterbalanced)
Passage A: followed by re-study
Passage B: followed by retrieval practice (recall questions)
Final test on both passages after delay
Each participant provides two recall scores

Materials: 2 factual passages, practice recall questions, final test sheets, pens
Expected effect: Medium-to-large (d ≈ 0.5–0.8). Testing effect is very robust even at short delays.

Indicative readings:
Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463.






G


The Effect of Social Presence on Task Performance


Social Effect: Small–Medium


▶


Background: Zajonc’s (1965) drive theory of social facilitation predicts that the presence of others enhances performance on simple/well-learned tasks but impairs performance on complex/novel tasks. One of the oldest findings in social psychology, with a clear theoretical framework and straightforward manipulation.

IV: Social condition (alone vs observed) DV: Number of items completed correctly on a simple task (e.g., easy anagrams or basic arithmetic)


Between-subjects variant

Group 1 completes 20 easy anagrams (5-letter words) alone in a room
Group 2 completes the same anagrams while being watched by two confederates (seated nearby, observing silently)
3-minute time limit
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants complete two sets of 20 anagrams (counterbalanced): one alone, one while observed
Sets matched for difficulty
Each participant provides two accuracy/speed scores

Materials: Printed anagram sheets, answer sheets, pens, timer. 2 confederates needed for “observed” condition.
Expected effect: Small-to-medium (d ≈ 0.3–0.6). Effect is reliable for simple tasks; may reverse for complex tasks — excellent for discussion.

Indicative readings:
Zajonc, R. B. (1965). Social facilitation. Science, 149(3681), 269–274.
Bond, C. F., & Titus, L. J. (1983). Social facilitation: A meta-analysis of 241 studies. Psychological Bulletin, 94(2), 265–292.






H


The Effect of Anchoring on Numerical Estimates


Social Cognitive Effect: Large


▶


Background: Tversky and Kahneman’s (1974) anchoring and adjustment heuristic shows that exposure to an arbitrary number biases subsequent numerical estimates, even when the anchor is clearly irrelevant. One of the most robust findings in judgment and decision-making, with strong real-world implications (pricing, negotiations, sentencing).

IV: Anchor value (high vs low) DV: Mean numerical estimate across a set of questions


Between-subjects variant

Both groups answer 8 general knowledge estimation questions (e.g., “How many countries are in Africa?”)
Group 1 first sees a high anchor for each question (e.g., “More or fewer than 120?”)
Group 2 first sees a low anchor for each question (e.g., “More or fewer than 15?”)
Participants decide more/fewer, then give their own estimate
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants answer 16 questions: 8 with high anchors, 8 with low anchors (randomised order)
Questions matched for difficulty across the two sets
DV is mean estimate for high-anchor questions vs mean estimate for low-anchor questions

Materials: Printed questionnaire sheets, pens. No technology required.
Expected effect: Large (d ≈ 0.8–1.2). Anchoring is one of the most robust effects in cognitive psychology — almost always significant.

Indicative readings:
Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131.
Furnham, A., & Boo, H. C. (2011). A literature review of the anchoring effect. Journal of Socio-Economics, 40(1), 35–42.






I


The Effect of Name Type on Competence Ratings


Social Effect: Small–Medium


▶


Background: Research on name-based stereotyping shows that identical CVs or descriptions receive different evaluations depending on the name attached. This taps into implicit social cognition and stereotyping — a topic students find compelling and which generates strong discussions about bias, fairness, and ecological validity.

IV: Name type (stereotypically “traditional/formal” vs “modern/informal” first names) DV: Mean competence rating (1–7 Likert scale, averaged across rated dimensions)


Between-subjects variant

Both groups read 4 identical short professional profiles (e.g., job applicant descriptions)
Group 1 profiles have traditional names (e.g., Elizabeth, James, Margaret, William)
Group 2 profiles have modern/informal names (e.g., Jayden, Destiny, Kai, Skye)
Participants rate each profile on competence, professionalism, and likely success (1–7)
Different participants in each condition



Within-subjects variant

All participants rate 8 profiles: 4 with traditional names, 4 with modern names (randomised order)
Profiles are different people but matched for qualifications and experience
DV is mean competence rating for traditional vs modern names (within-participant comparison)

Materials: Printed profiles and rating sheets, pens. Profiles need careful construction to be realistic and matched.
Expected effect: Small-to-medium (d ≈ 0.3–0.6). Effects are typically found but can be moderated by participant demographics — good for discussion.

Indicative readings:
Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. American Economic Review, 94(4), 991–1013.
Erwin, P. G. (2006). Children’s evaluative stereotypes of masculine, feminine, and androgynous first names. The Psychological Record, 56(4), 513–519.

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
Station Overview
The Reflex Test measures how quickly your nervous system can respond to a visual stimulus. Using a simple ruler-drop task, participants catch a falling ruler and convert the distance caught to reaction time in milliseconds. This station demonstrates the practice effect — reaction times typically improve across repeated trials.

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
What Participants Do

Partner A holds the ruler at the 30cm mark, letting it hang vertically
Partner B positions thumb and finger at the 0cm mark — without touching!
Partner A drops the ruler without warning (within 5 seconds)
Partner B catches it as fast as possible
Read the distance in cm at the top of your thumb
Complete 5 trials, then swap roles

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
Research Questions

Do reaction times improve with practice across 5 trials?


Is there a difference between dominant and non-dominant hand reaction times?


Do individual differences (sleep, caffeine) predict reaction time?

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
Experimental Design



Element
Description




Design
Within-groups (repeated measures across 5 trials)


IV
Trial number (1–5)


DV
Reaction time (milliseconds)


Controls
Fixed ruler position, same partner dropping

NoteThe Physics



Reaction time is calculated using the physics of free fall:
\[RT_{ms} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times distance_{cm}/100}{9.81}} \times 1000\]
A catch at 15cm ≈ 175ms reaction time

text:
Suggested Analyses
Primary analysis:

Paired t-test comparing Trial 1 vs Trial 5

Descriptive statistics:

Mean and SD across all trials
Calculate improvement score (Trial 1 − Trial 5)

Exploratory analyses:

Correlate sleep hours with mean RT
Compare dominant vs non-dominant hand (if both recorded)

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Convert cm to ms using physics formula
cm_to_ms <- function(cm) {
  sqrt(2 * (cm / 100) / 9.81) * 1000
}

# Calculate RT in milliseconds
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(
    rt_trial1_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial1_cm),
    rt_trial2_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial2_cm),
    rt_trial3_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial3_cm),
    rt_trial4_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial4_cm),
    rt_trial5_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial5_cm)
  )

# Mean RT across trials
datalab <- datalab |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(rt_mean_ms = mean(c(rt_trial1_ms, rt_trial2_ms, rt_trial3_ms,
                             rt_trial4_ms, rt_trial5_ms), na.rm = TRUE))

# Paired t-test: Trial 1 vs Trial 5
t.test(datalab$rt_trial1_ms, datalab$rt_trial5_ms, paired = TRUE)

# Visualise practice effect
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

datalab |>
  select(participant_id, rt_trial1_ms:rt_trial5_ms) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -participant_id,
               names_to = "trial",
               values_to = "rt_ms") |>
  mutate(trial = parse_number(trial)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trial, y = rt_ms, group = participant_id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#275882") +
  labs(x = "Trial", y = "Reaction Time (ms)",
       title = "Practice Effect in Reflex Test")

text:

This station demonstrates:

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
Tips for Facilitators

Ensure the ruler is held at exactly 30cm and hangs straight
Partner A should drop without warning but within 5 seconds
Read the cm mark at the top of the thumb, not where fingers touch
Record any missed catches — these are still informative data
If equipment issues arise, note them in the comments field

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
Station Overview
The Lady Luck station investigates how well humans can generate and perceive randomness. Participants generate “random” numbers, roll dice, and flip coins. The key finding: humans are bad at being random — we systematically avoid repetitions and produce sequences that are “too varied” to be truly random.

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
What Participants Do

Part A: Random Number Generation

Say 20 “random” numbers between 1 and 10 aloud
Partner records each number
Try to be as random as possible!



Part B: Dice Rolling

Predict: Will you roll more 6s than expected by chance?
Roll the die 10 times
Record each outcome (1–6)



Part C: Coin Flipping

Flip a coin 10 times
Record each outcome (Heads or Tails)
Note the longest run of the same outcome

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
Research Questions

Do human-generated “random” numbers differ from true random?


Do people roll more or fewer 6s than expected (1.67 out of 10)?


Do people expect fewer runs in random sequences than actually occur?

NoteThe Psychology of Randomness



Humans typically:

Avoid repetitions — we think 3, 7, 2, 9, 4 is “more random” than 3, 3, 7, 7, 2
Underestimate runs — in 10 coin flips, a run of 3+ is actually common!
Use the gambler’s fallacy — thinking tails is “due” after several heads

These biases make human-generated “random” sequences systematically different from true random.

~2


Digit frequencies
Too uniform
More variable


Coin runs
Surprise at long runs
Common

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
Suggested Analyses
Primary analyses:

One-sample t-test: Is mean of generated numbers different from 5.5?
Count repetitions and compare to expected (~2 in 20 numbers)

Dice and coin analyses:

Compare dice 6s to expected (binomial test)
Count coin heads vs expected 5

Exploratory analyses:

Frequency distribution of each digit (1–10)
Longest run length vs expectations

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate mean of random numbers (wide to long)
library(tidyr)
datalab_rand <- datalab |>
  select(participant_id, rand_num1:rand_num20) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("rand_num"),
    names_to = "position",
    values_to = "number"
  )

# Mean per participant
rand_means <- datalab_rand |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(rand_mean = mean(number, na.rm = TRUE))

# One-sample t-test: Is mean different from 5.5?
t.test(rand_means$rand_mean, mu = 5.5)

# Count repetitions (adjacent same numbers)
count_reps <- function(nums) {
  sum(nums[-1] == nums[-length(nums)], na.rm = TRUE)
}

datalab <- datalab |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(rand_repeats = count_reps(c_across(rand_num1:rand_num20)))

# Compare repetitions to expected (~2)
t.test(datalab$rand_repeats, mu = 2)

# Visualise digit frequencies
ggplot(datalab_rand, aes(x = factor(number))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#275882") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(datalab_rand) / 10,
             colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Number Generated",
    y = "Frequency",
    title = "Human 'Random' Number Distribution",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = expected if truly random"
  )

title: Pre-Post Survey
text: The Pre-Post Survey measures participants’ mood, energy, and stress levels before and after completing the DataLab stations. This creates a classic within-subjects pre-post design, allowing us to test whether the DataLab experience affected how participants feel.

# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate change scores

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Station Overview
The Time Warp station investigates how accurately we perceive time and physical dimensions. Participants estimate a 60-second interval, visually estimate line lengths, tactilely estimate string lengths (with eyes closed), and guess the room temperature. This station generates error scores that reveal systematic biases in human perception.

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
What Participants Do

Part A: 60-Second Estimation

Close your eyes
When your partner says “Start”, sense time passing
Say “Stop” when you think 60 seconds have passed
Partner records the actual time elapsed



Part B: Visual Estimation (Lines)

Look at Line Card A — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with Line Card B



Part C: Tactile Estimation (Strings)

Feel String 1 with eyes closed — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with String 2



Part D: Temperature Estimation

Guess the current room temperature in °C

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Research Questions

Do people systematically over- or under-estimate 60 seconds?


Is visual estimation more accurate than tactile estimation?


Does counting during time estimation improve accuracy?

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Experimental Design



Element
Description




Design

IV

DV

Controls
Consistent environment, no visible clocks

text:

Measure

TipWhy Do We Underestimate Time?



When waiting without distraction, people often feel time passing more slowly than it actually is, leading them to say “stop” before 60 seconds have elapsed. This is called temporal underestimation.

Paired comparison: Visual vs tactile estimation accuracy

Exploratory analyses:

Compare music vs silence conditions on time perception

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate time error
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(time_error = time_estimate_sec - 60)

# One-sample t-test: Is mean error different from 0?
t.test(datalab$time_error, mu = 0)

# Descriptive statistics
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_error = sd(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_under = mean(time_error < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Compare counters vs non-counters
datalab |>
  group_by(time_counting) |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_error = sd(time_error, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Visualise time estimation
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = time_estimate_sec)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#275882", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Time Estimate (seconds)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "60-Second Estimation Distribution",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = actual 60 seconds"
  )

title: Correlation
text: Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. It tells us how much one variable tends to change when the other changes.

title: Correlation
text: Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. It tells us how much one variable tends to change when the other changes.

title: Correlation

The Correlation Coefficient
Denoted as r (sample) or ρ (rho, population), the correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to +1.

Interpretation

r = 0

r = -1

title: Correlation

Correlation ≠ Causation
Critical concept: Correlation does not imply causation.
A and B are correlated:

Possible explanations:
1. A causes B        A → B
2. B causes A        B → A
3. C causes both     C → A, C → B
4. Coincidence       No causal link

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric test that compares two related samples, matched samples, or repeated measurements on a single sample. It tests whether the distribution of differences is symmetric about zero.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric test that compares two related samples, matched samples, or repeated measurements on a single sample. It tests whether the distribution of differences is symmetric about zero.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
When to Use
Use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test when:

Comparing two related/paired conditions
Data are ordinal, or continuous but non-normal
Difference scores are skewed
Outliers are present in the differences
Assumptions of the paired t-test are violated

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
How It Works

Calculate the difference for each pair
Rank the absolute values of differences
Assign signs (+ or -) based on difference direction
Sum positive and negative ranks separately
Compare to expected distribution

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
The Test Statistic
\[W = \min(W^+, W^-)\]
Where:

\(W^+\) = sum of positive ranks
\(W^-\) = sum of negative ranks

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
Assumptions



Assumption
Notes




Paired data
Each observation has a matched pair


Ordinal differences
Differences can be ranked


Symmetric distribution
Differences roughly symmetric around median

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
Effect Size
Calculate matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation (\(r\)):
\[r = \frac{W^+ - W^-}{W^+ + W^-}\]



r value
Interpretation




0.1
Small effect


0.3
Medium effect


0.5
Large effect

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
R Code Example
# Wilcoxon signed-rank test
wilcox.test(condition_a, condition_b, paired = TRUE)

# Or with exact p-value
wilcox.test(condition_a, condition_b, paired = TRUE, exact = TRUE)

# Effect size
library(effectsize)
rank_biserial(condition_a, condition_b, paired = TRUE)

text:

A Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed a significant difference between Condition A (Mdn = 450) and Condition B (Mdn = 410), W = 156, p = .008, r = .42.

Note: Report medians rather than means for non-parametric tests.

text: Pearson’s r (also called Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient) measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. It is the parametric correlation test.

title: Pearson’s r
text: Pearson’s r (also called Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient) measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. It is the parametric correlation test.

title: Pearson’s r
text:
When to Use
Use Pearson’s r when:

Both variables are interval or ratio scale
Relationship is linear
Data are approximately normally distributed
No significant outliers
Homoscedasticity (equal variance throughout range)

title: Pearson’s r
text:
The Formula
\[r = \frac{\sum(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \sum(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}\]
Or using z-scores:
\[r = \frac{\sum z_X z_Y}{n-1}\]

Continuous data
Interval or ratio scale

# Just the correlation coefficient

# Correlation matrix for multiple variables

title: Pearson’s r
text:
Reporting (APA Style)

A Pearson correlation revealed a significant positive relationship between study hours and exam scores, r(48) = .65, p < .001, 95% CI [.45, .79].

Where:

r = correlation coefficient

= degrees of freedom (N - 2)

title: Pearson’s r
text:
Coefficient of Determination
r² tells us the proportion of variance explained:
\[r^2 = \text{shared variance}\]
If r = .70, then r² = .49, meaning 49% of variance in Y is explained by X.

title: Pearson’s r

Non-Parametric Alternative
If assumptions are violated, use Spearman’s rho.

The Frontal Lob station data is ideal for Pearson’s r: correlate self-rated throwing ability with actual success rate. Both are continuous variables, and the relationship is expected to be linear. Calculate r² to determine how much variance in performance is “explained” by self-ratings.

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text: The Mann-Whitney U test (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is a non-parametric test that compares the distributions of two independent groups. It tests whether one group tends to have larger values than the other.

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text: The Mann-Whitney U test (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is a non-parametric test that compares the distributions of two independent groups. It tests whether one group tends to have larger values than the other.

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
When to Use
Use a Mann-Whitney U test when:

Comparing two independent groups
Data are ordinal, or continuous but non-normal
Sample sizes are small
Outliers are present
Assumptions of the independent t-test are violated

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
How It Works

Combine all observations from both groups
Rank all values from lowest to highest
Sum the ranks for each group
Compare rank sums to expected values

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
The Test Statistic
\[U = n_1 n_2 + \frac{n_1(n_1 + 1)}{2} - R_1\]
Where:

\(n_1, n_2\) = sample sizes of groups
\(R_1\) = sum of ranks in group 1

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:

Assumption
Notes




Independence
Observations between groups independent


Ordinal data
At minimum, can rank the values


Similar shape
Distributions have similar shape

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
Effect Size
Calculate rank-biserial correlation (\(r\)):
\[r = \frac{2U}{n_1 n_2} - 1\]



r value
Interpretation




0.1
Small effect


0.3
Medium effect


0.5
Large effect

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
R Code Example
# Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum)
wilcox.test(score ~ group, data = mydata)

# With exact p-value for small samples
wilcox.test(score ~ group, data = mydata, exact = TRUE)

# Effect size
library(effectsize)
rank_biserial(score ~ group, data = mydata)

Effect

title: Order Effects
text:
The Problem
In a within-groups design:

If everyone does A then B
And B scores higher than A
Is it because B is genuinely better?
Or because participants improved with practice?

We can’t tell! The effect is confounded with order.

title: Order Effects
text:
Solutions

1. Counterbalancing
Half do A→B, half do B→A
Group 1: A → B
Group 2: B → A

Order effects balance out across groups


2. Randomisation
Randomise condition order for each participant


3. Include Order as a Factor
Analyse whether order interacted with condition:
# Check for order effects
model <- aov(dv ~ condition * order + Error(participant_id/condition))
summary(model)

title: Order Effects
text:
Detecting Order Effects
Signs that order effects may be present:

Significant condition × order interaction
Performance systematically changes across trials
Large difference between first and last conditions

title: Order Effects
text:
Related Concepts

Within-Groups Design - where order effects occur
Counterbalancing - the solution to order effects
Practice Effect - a specific type of order effect

title: Order Effects
text:
DataLab Connection
At the Reflex Test station, reaction times typically improve across trials due to practice. Counterbalancing the order of simple vs. choice conditions helps separate true condition differences from practice effects.

title: Practice Effect
text: A practice effect is the improvement in performance that occurs when participants become more familiar with a task through repetition, independent of the experimental manipulation.

title: Practice Effect

Order

Score

Method A
12/20

title: Practice Effect
text:
Controlling Practice Effects

1. Counterbalancing
Group 1: Method A → Method B
Group 2: Method B → Method A

If Method B still better in both orders → genuine effect


2. Practice Trials
Give participants practice before the real task:
Practice trials (not scored)
    ↓
Condition A (scored)
    ↓
Condition B (scored)


3. Long Delays Between Conditions
Allows any practice benefit to dissipate.


4. Different Stimuli
Use different (but equivalent) materials in each condition.

title: Practice Effect
text:
Distinguishing Practice from True Effects
Check the condition × order interaction:
# If this interaction is significant, order matters
summary(aov(score ~ condition * order + Error(id/condition)))
                    Order
                 A-first    B-first
Condition A        12         14      ← Both improve
Condition B        18         16      ← with practice

If B > A in both orders → genuine condition effect

title: Practice Effect
text:
DataLab Connection
The Reflex Test station directly demonstrates practice effects: participants catch a dropped ruler across 5 trials. Reaction times typically improve from Trial 1 to Trial 5 as participants learn the timing and develop better strategies. A paired t-test comparing Trial 1 vs Trial 5 can quantify the practice effect.

text:
A confounding variable (or confound) is a variable that:

Also affects the dependent variable

This makes it impossible to determine whether changes in the DV are due to the IV or the confound.

        Person D (IQ=120) → Condition 2

title: Standard Deviation
text: The standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the mean. It quantifies the spread or dispersion of values in a dataset.

title: Standard Deviation
text: The standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the mean. It quantifies the spread or dispersion of values in a dataset.

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Formula
Sample standard deviation:
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n-1}}\]
Population standard deviation:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(X_i - \mu)^2}{N}}\]
Note: Sample formula uses n-1 (Bessel’s correction) for unbiased estimation.

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Interpretation



SD value
Interpretation




Small SD
Values clustered near the mean


Large SD
Values spread widely from mean


SD = 0
All values identical

title: Standard Deviation
text:
The 68-95-99.7 Rule
For normally distributed data:
                     ▲
                    ╱│╲
                   ╱ │ ╲
            68%   ╱  │  ╲   
                 ╱   │   ╲
           95%  ╱    │    ╲  
               ╱     │     ╲
          99.7%      │      
──────────┼────┼─────┼─────┼────┼──────►
        -3SD -2SD  -1SD   Mean  +1SD +2SD +3SD

• 68% of values within ±1 SD
• 95% of values within ±2 SD  
• 99.7% of values within ±3 SD

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Calculation Steps

Calculate the mean
Subtract mean from each value (deviations)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by n-1 (variance)
Take the square root

title: Standard Deviation
text:
R Code Example
# Standard deviation
sd(scores)

# With missing values
sd(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Population SD (divide by n, not n-1)
sqrt(mean((scores - mean(scores))^2))

# Variance (SD squared)
var(scores)

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Reporting (APA Style)

Participants had a mean reaction time of 450 ms (SD = 52).

Always report SD alongside the mean to convey both central tendency and spread.

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Comparing Variability
Coefficient of Variation (for comparing SDs across different scales):

title: Type I Error
text: A Type I error occurs when we reject the null hypothesis when it is actually true. We conclude there is an effect when there really isn’t one. This is also called a “false positive.”

title: Type I Error
text: A Type I error occurs when we reject the null hypothesis when it is actually true. We conclude there is an effect when there really isn’t one. This is also called a “false positive.”

title: Type I Error
text:
Understanding the Error



Reality
Decision: Reject H₀
Decision: Don’t Reject H₀




H₀ True (no effect)
Type I Error ❌
Correct ✓


H₀ False (effect exists)
Correct ✓
Type II Error ❌

title: Type I Error
text:
Probability of Type I Error

Denoted by α (alpha)
Conventionally set at .05 (5%)
This is the significance level

\[P(\text{Type I Error}) = \alpha = .05\]
This means: If we run 100 studies where H₀ is true, we’ll incorrectly reject it about 5 times.

title: Type I Error
text:
Real-World Example
Drug trial:

H₀: Drug has no effect
H₁: Drug has an effect

Type I error: Concluding the drug works when it actually doesn’t
Consequence: Ineffective drug gets approved

title: Type I Error
text:
Why .05?
The .05 threshold is a convention, meaning:

We accept a 5% risk of Type I error
We’re 95% confident when rejecting H₀
It’s a balance between too strict and too lenient

title: Type I Error
text:
Reducing Type I Error



Method
Trade-off




Lower α (e.g., .01)
Increases Type II error risk


Bonferroni correction
For multiple comparisons


Pre-registration
Prevents p-hacking


Replication
Confirms findings

title: Type I Error
section: Type I Error and Multiple Testing
text:
Type I Error and Multiple Testing
With 20 tests at α = .05:
\[P(\text{at least one Type I}) = 1 - (1-.05)^{20} = .64\]
64% chance of at least one false positive!
Solution: Adjust α for multiple comparisons.

title: Null Hypothesis
text:
Why Test the Null?
We can’t directly prove H₁ is true, but we can show H₀ is unlikely:
Logic of hypothesis testing:

1. Assume H₀ is true (no effect)
2. Calculate probability of our data under H₀
3. If probability very low (p < .05):
   → Data unlikely under H₀
   → Reject H₀ in favour of H₁

Important: “Fail to reject H₀” ≠ “Accept H₀”
We never prove H₀ is true; we just lack evidence against it.

title: Syllabus
text:
Module Description
This module introduces foundation students to the principles of psychological research. You will learn how to design experiments, collect and analyse data, and report findings in accordance with professional standards.
A distinctive feature of this module is DataLab—in Week 11, you generate the dataset you’ll analyse throughout the term. This means you learn statistics using your own data, not abstract examples.

title: Syllabus
text:
Learning Outcomes
On successful completion of this module, you will be able to:

Conceptual Understanding (C)

Identify experimental designs (between-participants, within-participants, matched pairs, correlational)
Distinguish between IVs and DVs
Formulate appropriate hypotheses (one-tailed, two-tailed)
Understand null hypothesis significance testing
Select appropriate statistical tests
Interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes
Recognise the difference between correlation and causation
Critically evaluate research claims



Practical Skills (P)

Calculate descriptive statistics by hand
Run t-tests and correlations in R
Produce appropriate data visualisations
Check statistical assumptions
Report results in APA format



Research Skills (R)

Develop research questions
Operationalise variables
Design appropriate methodologies
Collect data systematically
Write research reports
Critique methodological approaches
Consider ecological validity

Group Project
Working in groups is a core part of this module. Later in the term, your group (comprising 4-5 students) will design and run your own study, collect real data, and write it up as a research report. The group project is a substantial part of your assessment, and the quality of your collaboration directly affects your experience and your grade.

Forming Your Groups
In Week 11, you will work in small groups (2-4 students). This matters, so we are having a nice gentle start!
Pay attention to who communicates clearly, who seems enthusiastic, who you can rely on. Consider working with people you feel comfortable working with outside class hours. Your group will work together on labs from Week 16 onwards and on the research project which makes up a large part of this module. It doesn’t mean that you can’t start planning your group members and group working strategy now though!






ImportantChoose Wisely



Group formation is your first opportunity to see how groups naturally assemble and how different people work together. Group work is a VERY psychological phenomenon and the thing we are asked to talk about most often when writing references for jobs or further study.

title: MCQ Exam
text:
Exam Structure
The paper contains multiple “Investigations” — each is a short scenario describing a research study. For each Investigation, you answer 6 questions:

Design: Identify the design (between/within/matched/correlational)
IV: Identify the independent variable (or recognise no IV)
DV: Identify the dependent variable
Hypothesis: Identify the appropriate hypothesis type
Test: Select the appropriate statistical test
Interpretation: Interpret the results

There will be a series of other MCQs testing comprehension of other aspects of the course to date.

Correlational
Pearson’s r

The Decision Framework
Design → Variables → Hypothesis → Test → Interpret

Task Structure
You will receive a research scenario with pre-generated R output. Your task is to interpret the output and demonstrate your understanding of the statistical analysis - no coding or hand calculations required.

Section A: Statistical Mechanics (50 marks)

Section B: Methods and Theory (50 marks)

Suggest TWO methodological improvements
Discuss individual differences / extensions
Propose a more ecologically valid alternative (minimum half page)

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text: The experimental hypothesis (H₁ or Hₐ) predicts that the independent variable will have an effect on the dependent variable. It is also called the alternative hypothesis or research hypothesis.

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text: The experimental hypothesis (H₁ or Hₐ) predicts that the independent variable will have an effect on the dependent variable. It is also called the alternative hypothesis or research hypothesis.

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Key Characteristics



Feature
Description




Predicts effect
States IV will influence DV


Testable
Can be supported or refuted by data


Based on theory
Derived from existing knowledge


Symbol
H₁ or Hₐ

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Types of Experimental Hypotheses








Type
Description
Example




Directional
Specifies direction
“Caffeine will increase alertness”


Non-directional
Predicts difference only
“Caffeine will affect alertness”

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Writing Hypotheses
A good hypothesis:

States the IV and DV clearly
Predicts the relationship
Is operationalised
Is testable


Example
Abstract: “Caffeine affects memory”
Operationalised: “Participants who consume 200mg caffeine will recall significantly more words from a 30-word list than participants who consume a placebo.”

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Hypothesis Testing Logic
State hypotheses
      │
      ▼
H₀: No effect (µ₁ = µ₂)
H₁: Effect exists (µ₁ ≠ µ₂)
      │
      ▼
Collect data
      │
      ▼
Calculate p-value
      │
      ├── p < .05 → Reject H₀, support H₁
      │
      └── p ≥ .05 → Fail to reject H₀

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Important Notes

We never “prove” H₁
We either reject or fail to reject H₀
Supporting H₁ means the data are unlikely under H₀
Non-significant results don’t prove H₀ is true

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Related Concepts

Null Hypothesis - the “no effect” prediction
Directional Hypothesis - one-tailed
Non-directional Hypothesis - two-tailed
p-value - probability used to evaluate hypotheses

text:

For each DataLab station, formulate a clear experimental hypothesis. For Reflex Test: “Reaction times will be significantly faster in the simple condition than in the choice condition.”

title: Significance Level
text: The significance level (α, alpha) is the threshold probability used to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis. It represents the maximum acceptable risk of making a Type I error.

title: Significance Level
text: The significance level (α, alpha) is the threshold probability used to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis. It represents the maximum acceptable risk of making a Type I error.

title: Significance Level
text:
Standard Levels



Significance Level
Interpretation
Use




α = .05
5% risk
Standard in psychology


α = .01
1% risk
More conservative


α = .001
0.1% risk
Very conservative

title: Significance Level
text:
How It Works
Decision rule:

If p-value < α → Reject H₀ (significant)
If p-value ≥ α → Fail to reject H₀ (not significant)

With α = .05:
  p = .03 → Significant (p < .05) ✓
  p = .07 → Not significant (p > .05) ✗

title: Significance Level
text:
Why .05?
The .05 level was popularised by Ronald Fisher and has become convention:

1 in 20 chance of false positive
Balance between Type I and Type II errors
Not a natural law—just a social convention

Pre-registration helps ensure this

title: Type II Error
text: A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false. We conclude there is no effect when there really is one. This is also called a “false negative.”

title: Type II Error
text: A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false. We conclude there is no effect when there really is one. This is also called a “false negative.”

title: Type II Error
text:
Probability of Type II Error

Denoted by β (beta)
Typically ranges from .10 to .20
Related to statistical power: Power = 1 - β

\[P(\text{Type II Error}) = \beta\]

title: Type II Error
text:
Real-World Example
Drug trial:

H₀: Drug has no effect
H₁: Drug has an effect

Type II error: Concluding the drug doesn’t work when it actually does
Consequence: Effective treatment never gets approved

title: Type II Error
