DataLab Connection
With small samples at DataLab stations, Type II errors are a real concern. A non-significant result might mean no effect exists, OR that we lacked the power to detect it. Always consider sample size when interpreting null results.

title: Variance
text: Variance measures the average squared deviation of data points from the mean. It quantifies how spread out the values in a dataset are.

title: Variance
text: Variance measures the average squared deviation of data points from the mean. It quantifies how spread out the values in a dataset are.

title: Variance
text:
Formula
Sample variance:
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n-1}\]
Population variance:
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(X_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]
Note: Sample formula uses n-1 (Bessel’s correction) for unbiased estimation.

title: Variance
text:
Calculation Steps

Calculate the mean of the data
Subtract the mean from each value (deviations)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by n-1 (for sample) or N (for population)

title: Variance
text:
Properties



Property
Description




Always positive
Squared values can’t be negative


Units squared
If data in ms, variance in ms²


Sensitive to outliers
Squaring amplifies extreme values


Foundation for SD
Standard deviation = √variance

title: Variance
text:
Why Square the Deviations?

Raw deviations sum to zero (cancel out)
Squaring makes all values positive
Gives more weight to larger deviations
Has useful mathematical properties

title: Variance
text:
Interpretation



Variance
Interpretation




Small
Values cluster near the mean


Large
Values spread widely from mean


Zero
All values identical

title: Variance
text:
R Code Example
# Sample variance
var(scores)

# With missing values
var(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Population variance (divide by n, not n-1)
mean((scores - mean(scores))^2)

# Relationship to SD
var(scores) == sd(scores)^2

title: Variance
text:

Variance
Standard Deviation




Squared units
Original units


Harder to interpret
Easier to interpret


Mathematically convenient
More intuitive


Used in calculations
Used in reporting

title: Variance
text:
Related Concepts

Standard Deviation - square root of variance
Mean - centre point from which deviations are calculated

title: Variance
text:
DataLab Connection
Variance helps compare the consistency of performance across participants. High variance in reaction times at the Reflex Test station indicates large individual differences.

title: Mode
text:
R Code Example
# R doesn't have a built-in mode function
# Create your own
get_mode <- function(x) {
  uniq <- unique(x)
  uniq[which.max(tabulate(match(x, uniq)))]
}

get_mode(responses)

# Or use table to see frequencies
table(responses)
sort(table(responses), decreasing = TRUE)

# For multiple modes
get_modes <- function(x) {
  tab <- table(x)
  names(tab)[tab == max(tab)]
}

title: Range
text: The range is the simplest measure of dispersion, calculated as the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a dataset.

title: Range

text:
Formula
\[\text{Range} = X_{max} - X_{min}\]

title: Range
text:
Example
Dataset: 23, 45, 67, 89, 102
\[\text{Range} = 102 - 23 = 79\]

title: Range
text:
Properties



Property
Description

Easy to calculate

Easy to understand

text:

Advantages
Disadvantages

title: Range

One outlier dramatically changes the range!

title: Range

At Reflex Test, check the range of reaction times. Values outside a plausible range (e.g., < 100 ms or > 2000 ms) may indicate errors or inattention and might need to be excluded.

title: p-value
text: A p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

title: p-value
text: A p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

title: p-value
text:
Common Misconceptions







Wrong interpretation
Correct interpretation




Probability the null is true
Probability of data given null


Probability results are due to chance
Extremity of data under null


Effect size measure
Only indicates statistical significance


Smaller p = larger effect
Smaller p = stronger evidence against null

title: p-value
text:
The Logic of p-values

Assume null hypothesis is true (no effect)
Calculate probability of getting data this extreme or more
If probability very low (p < .05), reject null
Conclude the effect is “statistically significant”

title: p-value
text:

p-value
Interpretation

Not significant

p < .01

Note: The .05 threshold is a convention, not a law of nature.

title: p-value
text:
What p-values Depend On



Factor
Effect on p-value




Effect size
Larger effect → smaller p


Sample size
Larger n → smaller p


Variability

title: p-value
text:
Critical Perspective
Problems with over-reliance on p-values:

Dichotomous thinking (significant/not)
Ignores effect size
Sample size dependent
Publication bias (“p-hacking”)
.049 vs .051 treated very differently

title: p-value

Always report exact p-values unless p < .001.

p-value + effect size




“Significant”

Complete picture

title: p-value
text:
DataLab Connection
The Sixth Sense station tests performance against chance: with 6 trials, we expect 3 correct (50%) by random guessing. The p-value tells us the probability of observing our data if the null hypothesis (no ability to detect gaze) is true. At Lady Luck, test whether human-generated “random” sequences differ significantly from true random (p-value from one-sample t-test against mean = 5.5).

title: Mean

The Lady Luck station tests whether human-generated “random” numbers have the expected mean. If truly random, the mean of 20 numbers (1–10) should be 5.5. title: Between-Groups Design
text: A between-groups design (also called between-subjects or independent-groups design) is an experimental approach where different participants are assigned to different conditions of the independent variable.

title: Between-Groups Design
text: A between-groups design (also called between-subjects or independent-groups design) is an experimental approach where different participants are assigned to different conditions of the independent variable.

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
Key Characteristics



Feature
Description




Participants
Different individuals in each condition


Comparison
Between separate groups


Sample size
Requires more participants overall


Control
Relies on random assignment

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
Advantages

No order effects: Each participant only experiences one condition
No carryover: No contamination between conditions
Shorter sessions: Participants complete only one condition
Fresh perspective: No hypothesis guessing from repeated exposure

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
Disadvantages

Individual differences: Variability between people adds noise
Larger samples needed: More participants required for statistical power
Random assignment critical: Groups must be equivalent at baseline

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
Example
Testing whether caffeine improves memory:

Group A: 30 participants receive caffeine
Group B: 30 different participants receive placebo
Comparison: Memory scores compared between groups

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
Ensuring Group Equivalence
Random assignment is essential:

Generate random numbers for each participant
Assign to conditions based on random order
Check baseline equivalence on key variables

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
Related Concepts

Within-Groups Design
Random Assignment
Independent t-test (the analysis typically used)

title: Between-Groups Design
text:
DataLab Connection
The Mind Palace station uses a between-groups design: Lab 304A sees abstract words with music, while Lab 304B sees concrete words in silence. An independent t-test compares total recall between the two lab conditions.

title: Counterbalancing
text: Counterbalancing is a technique used in within-groups designs to distribute order effects evenly across conditions. Different participants experience conditions in different orders.

Simple approach for two conditions:
First half:   A → B
Second half:  B → A
This controls for linear trends (e.g., steady fatigue).

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Implementation
Sample: N = 40 participants
Conditions: 2 (Visual, Auditory)

Random assignment to order:
  - 20 participants: Visual first, then Auditory
  - 20 participants: Auditory first, then Visual

Analysis: Include order as a factor to check for effects

title: Counterbalancing
text:
R Code Example
# Create counterbalanced design
set.seed(42)
n <- 40
participants <- 1:n

# Assign to orders
orders <- rep(c("AB", "BA"), each = n/2)
orders <- sample(orders)  # Randomise assignment

design <- tibble(
  participant_id = participants,
  order = orders,
  first_condition = ifelse(order == "AB", "Visual", "Auditory"),
  second_condition = ifelse(order == "AB", "Auditory", "Visual")
)

# Check balance
table(design$order)

# Analyse including order
model <- aov(dv ~ condition * order + Error(participant_id/condition), data = mydata)

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Checking for Order Effects
Always test whether order affected results:

Include order as a between-subjects factor
Test the condition × order interaction
If significant, order effects may be present

Correlation: A and B are related

Possible explanations:
1. A → B         A causes B
2. B → A         B causes A
3. C → A, B      Third variable causes both
4. Coincidence   No real relationship

CANNOT determine which is true!

text:

Rank both variables separately
Calculate Pearson’s r on the ranks
Result: Spearman’s rho

title: Spearman’s rho
text:
The Formula
\[\rho = 1 - \frac{6\sum d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)}\]
Where d = difference between ranks for each pair.

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Station Overview
The Frontal Lob station investigates metacognition — your ability to accurately predict your own performance. Before throwing ping pong balls at a target, participants rate their throwing ability. We then compare their self-rating to actual performance, calculating a calibration score that reveals whether people are overconfident, underconfident, or well-calibrated.

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
What Participants Do

Before throwing: Rate your throwing ability (1–10)
Stand at the marked line
Throw 10 ping pong balls at the basket (dominant hand)
Optionally: Throw 5 more with your non-dominant hand
Count your successes

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Research Questions

Is self-rated ability correlated with actual performance?


Are people generally overconfident or underconfident?


Does dominant vs non-dominant hand performance differ?

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Experimental Design



Element
Description




Design
Correlational (self-rating vs performance)


Predictor
Self-rated throwing ability (1–10)


Outcome
Actual throwing success (0–10)


Measure
Calibration = accuracy − rating

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Data Variables



Variable
Type
Description
Range




throw_self_rating
Ordinal
Self-rated ability (before)
1–10


throw_dom_success
Count
Dominant hand successes
0–10


throw_nondom_success
Count
Non-dominant hand successes
0–5


throw_dom_hand
Categorical
Dominant hand
Left, Right

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Calculated Variables








Variable
Formula
Interpretation




throw_accuracy_pct
(dom_success / 10) × 100
Performance as percentage


throw_calibration
accuracy_pct/10 - rating
Calibration score









ImportantCalibration Score Interpretation




Positive calibration: Performed better than predicted → underconfident
Negative calibration: Predicted better than performed → overconfident
Zero calibration: Perfect self-knowledge!

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Expected Results







Metric
Typical Finding




Mean success rate
~40–60% (4–6 out of 10)


Self-rating mean
Often slightly higher than actual


Calibration
Slight overconfidence (negative mean)


Correlation (rating vs performance)
Moderate positive (r ≈ 0.3–0.5)









NoteThe Dunning-Kruger Effect?



This task can reveal calibration biases. Research on metacognition shows that people are often poorly calibrated — we think we’re better at things than we actually are. However, the relationship is complex and depends on task difficulty and expertise.

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Suggested Analyses
Primary analyses:

Pearson’s r: Correlation between self-rating and success
Scatterplot: Visualise the relationship

Calibration analysis:

Calculate mean calibration score
One-sample t-test: Is mean calibration different from 0?

Exploratory analyses:

Compare dominant vs non-dominant hand performance
Correlate conscientiousness (TIPI) with calibration

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate calibration
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(
    throw_accuracy_pct = (throw_dom_success / 10) * 100,
    throw_calibration = (throw_accuracy_pct / 10) - throw_self_rating
  )

# Correlation between self-rating and performance
cor.test(datalab$throw_self_rating, datalab$throw_dom_success)

# Mean calibration (are people overconfident?)
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_calibration = mean(throw_calibration, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_calibration = sd(throw_calibration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# One-sample t-test: Is calibration different from 0?
t.test(datalab$throw_calibration, mu = 0)

# Scatterplot
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = throw_self_rating, y = throw_dom_success)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#275882") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#EA8439") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(
    x = "Self-Rated Ability (1-10)",
    y = "Actual Success (out of 10)",
    title = "Self-Prediction vs Actual Performance",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect calibration"
  ) +
  coord_fixed()

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
Station Overview
The Mind Palace station tests short-term memory using a classic word list paradigm. Participants study a list of 10 words, complete a distractor task, then recall as many words as possible. This station demonstrates the serial position effect — the tendency to remember words at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list better than those in the middle.
Additionally, this station implements a between-groups manipulation: Lab 304A sees abstract words with background music, while Lab 304B sees concrete words in silence.

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
What Participants Do

STUDY (30 seconds): Memorise 10 words shown on screen
DISTRACT (60 seconds): Complete simple maths problems
RECALL (90 seconds): Write down as many words as remembered on paper
RECORD: Enter results in Qualtrics — total recalled, which positions, intrusions

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
Research Questions

Do participants recall more words from the beginning and end of the list (serial position effect)?


Do concrete words lead to better recall than abstract words (between-labs comparison)?


Does background music affect memory performance?

Element
Description




Design
Between-groups (lab room) + Within-subjects (serial position)


IV 1
Word type: Abstract (Lab 304A) vs Concrete (Lab 304B)


IV 2
Serial position (positions 1–10)


DV
Number of words correctly recalled


Controls
Same presentation time, same distractor task

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Compare total recall between labs
datalab |>
  group_by(lab_room) |>
  summarise(
    mean_recall = mean(mem_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_recall = sd(mem_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )

# Independent t-test
t.test(mem_total ~ lab_room, data = datalab)

# Serial position analysis
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Convert position data to long format
position_data <- datalab |>
  select(participant_id, lab_room, mem_pos1:mem_pos10) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("mem_pos"),
    names_to = "position",
    values_to = "recalled"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    position = parse_number(position),
    recalled = if_else(recalled == "Yes", 1, 0)
  )

# Calculate proportion recalled at each position
serial_curve <- position_data |>
  group_by(position) |>
  summarise(prop_recalled = mean(recalled, na.rm = TRUE))

# Plot serial position curve
ggplot(serial_curve, aes(x = position, y = prop_recalled)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#275882", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = "#EA8439", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    x = "Serial Position",
    y = "Proportion Recalled",
    title = "Serial Position Curve"
  )

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Station Overview
The Sixth Sense station tests whether people can detect when someone is staring at them from behind. This classic psychology experiment creates a signal detection paradigm where we can calculate hit rates, false alarm rates, and test performance against chance (50%). Spoiler: most research finds no evidence for “gaze detection” beyond chance!

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
What Participants Do

Sit back-to-back with your partner (~1m apart)
STARER: Flip a coin

Heads = Stare intently at partner’s head
Tails = Look away (at the floor or wall)

Hold for 15 seconds
TARGET: Say “Staring” or “Not staring”
Rate your confidence (1 = guessing, 5 = certain)
Complete 6 trials as target, then swap roles

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Research Questions

Can people detect when they are being stared at better than chance (50%)?


Is confidence related to accuracy?


Do believers in psychic phenomena perform differently?

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Experimental Design



Element
Description




Design
Signal detection paradigm


Signal
Partner staring (coin = Heads)


Noise
Partner not staring (coin = Tails)


Response
“Staring” or “Not staring”


Measure
Accuracy, confidence, hit rate, false alarm rate

text:
Data Variables









Variable
Type
Description
Values




stare_t1_actual – stare_t6_actual
Categorical

Staring, Not staring


stare_t1_guess – stare_t6_guess
Categorical
What you guessed
Staring, Not staring


stare_t1_conf – stare_t6_conf
Ordinal
Confidence rating
1 (Guessing) – 5 (Certain)


stare_solo
Categorical

Yes, No

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Calculated Variables



Variable
Description
Expected Value




stare_correct_total
Correct detections (0–6)
~3 (chance)


stare_hit_rate
P(say “staring” | actually staring)
~0.5


stare_fa_rate
P(say “staring” | not staring)
~0.5

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Signal Detection Theory



Outcome
Actual: Staring
Actual: Not Staring




Guess: Staring
Hit ✓
False Alarm


Guess: Not Staring
Miss
Correct Rejection ✓









NoteTesting Against Chance



With 6 trials and 50% chance, we expect participants to get 3 correct by guessing randomly. We use a one-sample t-test to compare the group mean to 3 (or equivalently, test if proportion correct differs from 0.5).

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Expected Results



Metric
Expected Value




Mean correct
~3 out of 6 (50%)


Hit rate
~0.5


False alarm rate
~0.5


Confidence
Often higher than accuracy warrants









WarningThe Null Hypothesis



The null hypothesis for this task is that people cannot detect gaze better than chance. Published research consistently fails to reject this null — there’s no reliable evidence for “sixth sense” gaze detection!

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Suggested Analyses
Primary analysis:

One-sample t-test: Is mean correct different from 3?
Alternatively: Binomial test against 50%

Signal detection analysis:

Calculate hit rate and false alarm rate
Compare d’ (sensitivity) across conditions

Exploratory analyses:

Correlation between confidence and accuracy
Compare believers vs sceptics

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate correct total (need to create from individual trials)
# Assuming trial data is in separate columns

# One-sample t-test: Is mean different from chance (3)?
t.test(datalab$stare_correct_total, mu = 3)

# Descriptive statistics
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_correct = mean(stare_correct_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_correct = sd(stare_correct_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_above_chance = mean(stare_correct_total > 3, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Hit rate and false alarm rate (per participant)
# Would need trial-level data manipulation

# Visualise distribution
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = stare_correct_total)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#275882", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    x = "Number Correct (out of 6)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Sixth Sense Performance",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = chance performance (3/6)"
  )

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Connection to Other Concepts
This station demonstrates:

Null Hypothesis — testing the claim that gaze cannot be detected
P-value — probability of results if null is true
Effect Size — how far performance is from chance

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Tips for Facilitators

Partners should sit truly back-to-back — no peeking!
The starer must commit fully to staring OR looking away
Coin flips should be hidden from the target
Confidence ratings are valuable — encourage honest self-assessment
If working solo, participants can use an online random generator

Hypothes.is Annotation
This module uses Hypothes.is for collaborative annotation. Think of it as a shared highlighter and sticky-note system that lives on top of web pages. You can highlight passages, add comments and questions, and see what other students have noticed or wondered about.
Why use it?

Active reading - Annotation helps you engage with material rather than passively skimming
Shared learning - See what confuses or interests your classmates (you’re probably not alone!)
Ask questions in context - Flag something unclear right where it appears, rather than trying to describe it later
Build a revision resource - Your annotations become a personalised study guide

title: Project Toolkit
text:
🐒 LittleMonkeyLab



Group Project Toolkit


PS50008A — Everything you need to prepare for data collection



Research Methods & Experimental Design · Goldsmiths, University of London



What is this page? This is your one-stop shop for preparing your group project. It contains a week-by-week timeline, a document checklist with guidance on each document, a complete worked example study for reference, and blank templates you can download and adapt for your own project. Bookmark this page — you’ll come back to it often.
📚 Suggested readings for all projects are available in the Project Articles folder on Learn.gold.


Week-by-Week Timeline
Use this to track what you should be working on each week. Documents don’t all need to be finished at once — the timeline shows when each piece fits in.




Week
Dates
Focus
Key tasks




16
24–28 Feb
Form groups & choose project
Form your group of 4–5. Read the Project Options. Agree on a project and design (between or within). Submit your Research Plan (Fri 27 Feb, 12 noon).

Draft: Participant Information Sheet, Consent Form, Debrief Form, Participant Instructions. Start your Researcher Procedure.

1–3 Apr
Data collection
Run your study! Collect data in the lab session. Research Report deadline (Fri 1 Apr, 12 noon).






Document Checklist
Your group needs to prepare 9 documents before data collection day. Click each one for details on what it is, who sees it, and tips for getting it right.


📋



Participant Information Sheet


Given to participant Both designs



▶


What it is: A formal document explaining the study to potential participants before they agree to take part. Required for informed consent.
Who sees it: Every participant — they read this before deciding whether to participate. They keep a copy.
When needed: Draft by Week 17, finalised by Week 19.

Tips

Describe the study in general terms — do not reveal your hypothesis
Include: purpose, what participation involves, time required, risks/benefits, confidentiality, right to withdraw
Keep the language accessible — no jargon
The template has the standard boilerplate sections; you mainly need to customise the “purpose” and “what will happen” sections






✅



Consent Form


Given to participant Ethics requirement



▶


What it is: A checklist the participant signs to confirm they understand the study and agree to take part. A legal and ethical requirement.
Who sees it: Every participant signs one. You keep the signed copies securely.
When needed: Draft by Week 17, finalised by Week 19.

Tips

You mostly just need to update the study title — the checklist items are standardised
Make sure the study title matches across all your documents
Print plenty of spare copies (aim for 30)






📝



Debrief Form


Given to participant Both designs



▶


What it is: A document given to participants after the study explaining its true purpose, including the hypothesis and relevant theory.
Who sees it: Every participant — they receive this after completing the study.
When needed: Draft by Week 17, finalised by Week 19.

Tips

Unlike the Information Sheet, you can (and should) reveal the hypothesis here
Briefly explain the theory behind your study (e.g., dual coding, anchoring)
Include the data withdrawal instructions and support service contacts
Keep it to about one page






🗣️



Recruitment Script


Researcher use Both designs



▶


What it is: A short script your group uses to approach potential participants and invite them to take part.
Who sees it: Researchers only — you read or paraphrase this when recruiting.
When needed: Finalise by Week 19.

Tips

Keep it brief and friendly — 3–4 sentences
Mention: who you are, what the study involves (briefly), how long it takes, where to go, and any incentive (snacks!)
Print several copies so multiple group members can recruit simultaneously






📊



Data Recording Sheet


Researcher use Both designs



▶


What it is: A table where you record each participant’s data (condition, DV score, optional demographics).
Who sees it: Researchers only — you fill this in after scoring each participant.
When needed: Draft by Week 18, finalised by Week 19.

Tips

Include columns for: participant number, condition (if between-subjects), DV score, and any optional demographics
Include a scoring guide so all group members score consistently
The template has tables for both between- and within-subjects designs — delete the one you don’t need
This is where your raw data comes from, so accuracy matters!






🧪



Stimulus Materials


Used in study Study-specific



▶


What it is: The actual materials participants interact with during the study — word lists, images, passages, rating sheets, questionnaires, etc.
Who sees it: Participants (during the study) and researchers.
When needed: Draft by Week 17, finalised by Week 18.

Tips

This varies hugely by project — see the Project Options for what your chosen project needs
Make sure materials are matched across conditions (word frequency, difficulty, length, etc.)
The example study uses word lists; your project might need photos, passages, anagrams, or rating scales
Test your materials on each other before data collection day






📄



Participant Instructions


Given to participant Both designs



▶


What it is: A clear, step-by-step sheet telling the participant exactly what they will do during the study.
Who sees it: Every participant reads this before the study begins.
When needed: Draft by Week 17, finalised by Week 18.

Tips

Write in plain, simple language — no jargon or technical terms
Use numbered steps
Do not reveal the hypothesis or what you expect to find
Keep it short — half a page is usually enough
If your between- and within-subjects variants have different procedures, you may need separate instruction sheets






📓



Researcher Procedure


Researcher use Design-specific



▶


What it is: A detailed step-by-step guide for the researcher running the study. Includes exact wording, timing, and the full procedure.
Who sees it: Researchers only — this is your “recipe” for running the study identically every time.
When needed: Draft by Week 17–18, finalised by Week 19.

Tips

Be extremely detailed — include exact words to say to participants (in italics or quotes)
Include timing for each phase (study period, distractor, recall, etc.)
Include the checklist of materials to prepare before testing begins
Any group member should be able to run the study from this document alone
You will need a different procedure document for between-subjects vs within-subjects designs






🛒

text:
TipBefore You Begin



This is your first reading for PS50008A. Take your time with it. The concepts introduced here form the foundation for everything else in this module.




You chose psychology because you want to understand people. Why do we remember some things and forget others? What drives someone to help a stranger—or to hurt them? How do our early experiences shape who we become? These questions drew you here, and they’re genuinely worth exploring.
Then you look at your timetable and see “Research Methods and Experimental Design.”
If your heart sinks a little, you’re not alone - but I’m going to try to turn this around. This material has a reputation, and not a glamorous one. But there are real reasons it’s central to your degree—not because we enjoy watching you suffer, but because it changes what you’re capable of doing. It’s powerful stuff!

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
text:
You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
Right now, if someone asked you “Does social media cause anxiety?”, you might have an opinion. Everyone has one of those. But psychology isn’t about opinions—it’s about evidence. And evidence doesn’t just land in your lap. Someone has to design a way to gather it, collect it carefully, and work out what it actually shows.
That’s what you’re learning to do. By the end of your degree, you won’t just think social media might cause anxiety—you’ll be able to design a study that could actually test the idea, spot the weaknesses in existing research, and understand why the answer might be more complicated than the headlines suggest.

Think about that for a second… You don’t have to rely on anecdote or opinion anymore. You can create knowledge.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
You’ll See Through the Nonsense
We’re surrounded by claims about human behaviour. Adverts tell us certain products will make us more confident. Influencers promote supplements that supposedly sharpen your mind. News stories announce that scientists have “proved” all sorts of things about personality, intelligence, or relationships. 9 out of 10 adverts are dubious! (not a real stat!)
Most of these claims are, at best, oversimplified. Many are outright wrong. Understanding research methods gives you the ability to look at a study and ask:

How many people did they actually test?
Could something else explain these results?
Is this finding likely to replicate?

This isn’t just academic scepticism. It’s protection against being manipulated by people who use the language of science without the rigour, without the appropriate ‘methods’.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
These Skills Travel
Psychology graduates end up in all sorts of places: clinical training, education, marketing, human resources, policy research, user experience design, data analysis, all sorts of entrepreneurial activities I don’t understand. What connects these fields is that they all involve understanding people and making decisions based on evidence. It’s just thinking scientifically.
The ability to gather data systematically, analyse it honestly, and communicate what it means is valuable almost everywhere. It’s also incredibly rare. Many people can express opinions confidently; fewer can actually interrogate those opinions with evidence.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
And One More Thing
Some of you will genuinely enjoy this. Not everyone, and probably not immediately, but there’s real satisfaction in solving methodological puzzles: working out how to test something that seems untestable, spotting a flaw in an argument, seeing a pattern emerge from data you collected yourself.
I’m not promising you’ll love every moment. But we are promising that this material is worth taking seriously—and that taking it seriously might surprise you.






ImportantThis Week



Since Week 11 has no lecture, use this reading to prepare for the term ahead. But above all, be curious!








Note



Sophie von Stumm (formerly from Goldsmiths!) and colleagues (2011) sought to identify the best predictors of academic performance. Unsurprisingly perhaps, a person’s intelligence was the best predictor. However, they also found that this was matched by the combined predictive power of effort and intellectual curiosity. They conclude that succeeding in academic fields (such as psychology) is not just a question of being smart and trying hard, it is also about having a hungry mind!

Von Stumm, S., Hell, B., & Chamorro-Premuzic, T. (2011). The hungry mind: Intellectual curiosity is the third pillar of academic performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6, 574-588.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
Why Do Psychologists Do Research?
Psychology aims to understand human behaviour and mental processes. But how do we move from casual observation to scientific knowledge?

The Problem with Common Sense
We often think we understand human behaviour based on everyday experience - my mum certainly thinks so. But “common sense” has limitations (sorry, mum!):

Hindsight bias: Events seem obvious after they occur (“I knew it all along”)
Confirmation bias: We notice evidence that supports our beliefs and ignore contradicting evidence
Anecdotal evidence: Individual cases can mislead — your friend’s experience isn’t representative of everyone

Consider these “common sense” claims:

“Opposites attract” — But also “Birds of a feather flock together”
“Too many cooks spoil the broth” — But also “Many hands make light work”
“Absence makes the heart grow fonder” — But also “Out of sight, out of mind”

Common sense can justify almost any conclusion. Research methods provide systematic tools to overcome these biases and determine which claims actually hold up under scrutiny.


Why Intuitions About Behaviour Are Often Wrong
Our intuitions fail us for several reasons:

We don’t see our own blind spots — We’re unaware of the biases affecting our judgement
Memory is reconstructive — We misremember events to fit our current beliefs
We overgeneralise from small samples — One or two examples feel like proof
We confuse correlation with causation — Two things happening together doesn’t mean one caused the other

For example, studies consistently show that:

People are poor at predicting what will make them happy
Eyewitness testimony is far less reliable than we assume
“Venting” anger often increases rather than decreases aggression

These findings contradict common intuitions — which is precisely why we need systematic research.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
What Makes a Claim Scientific?

The Difference Between Opinion and Science
An opinion is a personal belief that may or may not be supported by evidence: > “I think social media makes people unhappy.”
A scientific claim is testable, based on systematic evidence, and open to being proven wrong: > “In a study of 1,000 adults, those who used social media for more than 3 hours daily reported lower life satisfaction scores (M = 5.2) than those who used it less than 1 hour (M = 6.8), t(998) = 4.32, p < .001.”


Four Hallmarks of Scientific Claims


Empirical basis — Based on observable, measurable evidence, not just reasoning or authority
Systematic collection — Data gathered using consistent, documented methods
Falsifiability — The claim could, in principle, be proven wrong by evidence
Transparency — Methods are described clearly enough that others could repeat them




What “Replicable” Means
A finding is replicable if other researchers, following the same procedures, get the same results.
Why does this matter?

A single study might have flaws we don’t notice
Random chance can produce misleading results
Researcher bias might influence findings

When multiple independent teams find the same result, we can be more confident it’s real.






NoteThe Replication Crisis



Psychology has faced a “replication crisis” — many classic findings failed to replicate when researchers tried to repeat them. This has led to better practices: larger samples, pre-registration of hypotheses, and more transparency. You’ll learn about this in Week 17.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
The Scientific Method
Researchers typically follow these steps:

1. Identify a Question
Start with curiosity. What do you want to understand?

“Do people remember information better if they test themselves rather than just re-reading?”



2. Review Existing Knowledge
What have others already discovered? Build on previous work rather than starting from scratch.


3. Formulate a Hypothesis
Make a specific, testable prediction.

“Students who use self-testing will recall more information after one week than students who re-read the material.”



4. Design a Study
Plan exactly how you’ll test your hypothesis: - Who will you study? - What will you measure? - How will you control for other explanations?


5. Collect Data
Gather observations systematically, following your planned procedures.


6. Analyse Results
Use statistics to determine whether your findings are meaningful or could have occurred by chance.


7. Draw Conclusions
What do your results mean? Do they support your hypothesis? What are the limitations?


8. Report Findings
Share your methods and results so others can evaluate and build on your work.
You’ll work through all these steps in your group project this term.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
Variables: Things That Vary
A variable is anything that can take different values.

Examples of Variables



Variable
Possible Values




Height
150cm, 165cm, 180cm…


Reaction time
200ms, 350ms, 420ms…


Mood
Happy, sad, anxious, neutral…


Number of words recalled
0, 1, 2, 3… 20


Exam score
0-100





Why Variables Matter
Research is fundamentally about understanding how variables relate to each other:

Does study time affect exam performance?
Does sleep quality predict reaction time?
Is age related to memory capacity?

In DataLab, you’ll measure several variables and see how they differ between people and across conditions.


Types of Variables
Continuous variables can take any value within a range: - Height (175.3cm) - Reaction time (287.4ms) - Temperature (36.8°C)
Categorical variables fall into distinct categories: - Gender (male, female, non-binary) - Experimental condition (control, treatment) - Handedness (left, right, ambidextrous)
Discrete variables are countable whole numbers: - Number of items recalled (7) - Number of errors (3) - Number of children (2)
Understanding variable types helps you choose appropriate statistical analyses — something you’ll learn throughout this module.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour
text:
How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour

Moving Beyond Speculation
Without data, debates about human behaviour often go in circles. Everyone has opinions, but how do we know whose is correct?
Empirical evidence allows us to:

Test competing theories — Instead of arguing, we can design studies to see which prediction holds
Discover unexpected findings — Data often reveals patterns we wouldn’t have predicted
Quantify effects — Not just “X affects Y” but “X increases Y by approximately this much”
Identify boundary conditions — Under what circumstances does a finding hold or not hold?



An Example: Does Punishment Deter Crime?
Common sense might suggest that harsher punishments reduce crime. But what does the evidence show?
Research has found: - Certainty of punishment matters more than severity - Very harsh sentences may actually increase recidivism in some cases - Deterrent effects vary by crime type and offender characteristics
Without systematic data collection, we’d have no way to discover these nuances.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
Connecting to DataLab

Your Data, Your Learning
In Thursday’s lab, you’ll experience research from both perspectives:

As a participant — completing cognitive tasks
As a tester — administering tasks and recording data

This dual perspective helps you understand:

Why standardised procedures matter (you’ll see what happens when instructions vary)
How measurement introduces variability (the same person gives different responses across trials)
What it feels like to generate data that will be analysed

The data you generate will be used throughout the term. When we discuss distributions in Week 12, we’ll look at the distribution of YOUR reaction times. When we learn about t-tests in Week 14, we’ll compare performance between Room A and Room B. This is your data, and you’ll learn statistics by exploring it.

Memory Test: Mind Palace





What survives the interference?
We complete the memory test together as a group. Two word lists will appear on screen — List A on the LEFT and List B on the RIGHT. Your instructor will tell you which side to look at.

The Procedure

STUDY (30 sec): Look at YOUR word list and memorise as many as you can

RECORD: Enter your results in Qualtrics

text:
Task 1: Reflex Test





How fast is your nervous system?
Measure your reaction time using a ruler-drop task.

What You’ll Do

Partner A holds the ruler at the 30cm mark, letting it hang vertically
Partner B positions thumb and finger at the 0cm mark — don’t touch!
Partner A drops the ruler without warning (within 5 seconds)
Partner B catches it as fast as possible
Read the cm mark at the top of your thumb
Complete 5 trials, then swap roles



What You’ll Record

Which hand you used (dominant or non-dominant)
The distance caught on each trial (in cm)
Any trials you missed

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 2: Time Warp





Your brain’s internal clock
Explore how accurately you perceive time and physical dimensions.

Part A: 60-Second Estimation

Close your eyes
When you hear “Start”, sense time passing
Say “Stop” when you think 60 seconds have passed
Record the actual time



Part B: Visual Estimation (Lines)

Look at Line Card A — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with Line Card B



Part C: Tactile Estimation (Strings)

Feel String 1 with eyes closed — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with String 2



What You’ll Record

Your 60-second estimate (actual seconds)
Line estimates (cm)
String estimates (cm)
Whether you counted

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 3: Sixth Sense





Can you tell when someone is watching you?

What You’ll Do

Sit back-to-back with your partner (~1m apart)
STARER: Flip the coin

Heads = Stare at partner’s head
Tails = Look away

Hold for 15 seconds
TARGET: Say “Staring” or “Not staring”
Rate your confidence (1 = guess, 5 = certain)
Complete 6 trials as target, then swap



What You’ll Record

For each trial: actual, guess, confidence
Total correct out of 6

What Is This Module?
Research Methods & Experimental Design
How psychologists:

Ask questions about the mind and behaviour
Design studies to answer those questions
Collect and analyse data
Draw valid conclusions


Emphasise this is a practical, skills-based module. Not just theory — they will DO research.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Problem with Common Sense

“Opposites attract”
“Birds of a feather flock together”
Both can’t be true… can they?



Common sense often gives contradictory answers. Science provides a systematic way to find out what’s actually true.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Everyday Thinking vs Scientific Thinking


Everyday Thinking

Based on personal experience
Influenced by biases
Accepts anecdotes as evidence
Confirmation bias
“I just know”


Scientific Thinking

Based on systematic observation
Controls for biases
Requires replicable evidence
Seeks disconfirmation
“Let’s test it”

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:

Evaluate claims you encounter daily
Understand how psychological knowledge is created
Essential for your dissertation
Transferable skills for any career
Required for postgraduate study

text:
From Question to Knowledge





flowchart LR
    Q[Research Question] --> H[Hypothesis]
    H --> D[Design Study]
    D --> C[Collect Data]
    C --> A[Analyse Data]
    A --> I[Interpret Results]
    I --> Q

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 1: The Research Question
Where do research questions come from?

Curiosity about behaviour
Gaps in existing research
Real-world problems
Theory testing
Unexpected observations


Example: Do people lie more when texting than face-to-face?

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 2: The Hypothesis

A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about what you expect to find.

Good hypothesis:

“Participants will tell more lies per conversation when communicating via text message compared to face-to-face.”

Not a hypothesis:

“I wonder if texting affects lying.”

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 3: Design the Study
Key decisions:

Who will you study? (participants)
What will you measure? (variables)
How will you measure it? (methods)
What comparisons will you make? (design)


We’ll spend most of this module on this step.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 4: Collect Data

Follow your plan precisely
Treat participants ethically
Record everything carefully
Minimise errors and bias

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 5: Analyse Data

Statistics are tools for finding patterns in data and determining whether those patterns are meaningful.

This is where R comes in — and what you’ll learn in the labs.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 6: Interpret Results

What do the findings mean?
Do they support the hypothesis?
What are the limitations?
What questions remain?


Then the cycle continues…

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries

The Mean: What’s Average?

Mean (\(\bar{x}\)) = Sum of all values ÷ Number of values
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries

That’s what I mean!

But Wait… Same Mean, Different Stories


Same mean, but Group B is much more variable!

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
We Need to Measure Spread

Standard Deviation (SD) = How spread out the data are from the mean


Low SD = Scores clustered together (consistent)
High SD = Scores spread out (variable)


For your memory scores: SD = 2.14 words

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Key Insight






Remember This


A difference between means only matters if it’s big relative to the spread.

Signal = difference between means
Noise = variability within groups
The question: Is the signal bigger than the noise?

Now Let’s Introduce the Terminology

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or controls
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures — the outcome



In the memory experiment:

IV = Word type (abstract vs concrete)
DV = Number of words recalled (0-10)

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Design Type: Between-Subjects

Between-subjects design: Different participants in each condition




Lab A people only saw abstract words
Lab B people only saw concrete words
You couldn’t be in both labs!



Why? Between = different people in each group

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Writing a Hypothesis

Experimental hypothesis (H₁): Predicts an effect or difference
Null hypothesis (H₀): Predicts no effect or no difference


For the memory experiment:

H₁: Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words
H₀: There will be no difference in recall between word types

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed: Predicts the direction of the effect
Two-tailed: Predicts a difference but not which direction



One-tailed: “Concrete words will be better than abstract” (predicts direction)
Two-tailed: “Word type will affect memory” (no direction)

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Pre-Post Mood Survey
Remember you rated your mood at the start AND end of the session?

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
This Is Within-Subjects Design

Within-subjects design: The same participants measured in all conditions



Pre-mood and post-mood came from the same person
You’re being compared to yourself

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Why Is This Powerful?






The Power of Within-Subjects


Each person is their own control!




Individual differences are controlled:

If your pre-mood was 5 and post-mood was 7…
You improved by 2 points
We don’t need to worry about other people’s baseline moods

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text: Correlational design (15 min)

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Self-Rating vs Actual Performance
Before the throwing task, you rated how good you thought you’d be.
Question: Do people know themselves?

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
This Is Correlational Design

Correlational design: Measuring the relationship between two variables — no manipulation



Variable 1: Self-rating (1-10)
Variable 2: Actual accuracy (%)









Key Point


There is no IV in a correlational design!

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Critical Warning






Say It With Me


Correlation ≠ Causation
Finding a relationship does NOT mean one variable causes the other.




Even if self-ratings predict performance, we can’t say self-ratings cause good performance.

You tried to detect if someone was staring at you.

6 trials

The Question


Does getting 5 or 6 right mean you have a sixth sense?




Not necessarily!


If you flip a coin 6 times, sometimes you get 5 or 6 heads just by luck.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Null Hypothesis

Null hypothesis (H₀): The result is due to chance, not a real effect.


For the sixth sense:

H₀: People are just guessing (performance = 50%)
H₁: People can detect staring (performance ≠ 50%)

title: Week 12 Preview Video

Key Concepts Preview

The Big Question
How do we go from raw data to meaningful summaries?
When you collected reaction times in DataLab, you generated dozens of individual measurements. This week, we learn how to compress that information into statistics that tell a clear story.


Central Tendency
Where is the “centre” of the data?

Mean: The arithmetic average — add everything up, divide by how many
Median: The middle value when sorted — resistant to outliers
Mode: The most common value — useful for categories



Variability
How spread out is the data?

Range: Maximum minus minimum — simple but limited
Standard deviation: How far, on average, values are from the mean



Distribution Shape
What does the data look like?

Normal: Symmetric, bell-shaped
Skewed: Tail on one side (positive = right, negative = left)
Bimodal: Two peaks

Debrief: Time Perception
Finding: Most people underestimate 60 seconds (say it’s up before it actually is).
Why? When engaged in a task, time seems to pass faster.
Design: This is testing against a known value (60 seconds) - a one-sample design.
Null hypothesis: Mean estimate will equal 60 seconds (no systematic bias).

Debrief: Memory Design
IV: Word type (abstract vs concrete)
DV: Number of words recalled (0-10)
Design: Between-subjects (different people in each lab)
Hypotheses:

H1 (one-tailed): Concrete words will be recalled better than abstract words.

title: Design Detectives: DataLab
text:
Why Concrete Words?
Dual Coding Theory (Paivio, 1971)
Concrete words can be stored TWO ways:

Verbal code (the word itself)
Visual code (a mental image)

Abstract words only have the verbal code.
Two codes > One code = Better memory

title: Design Detectives: DataLab
section: Debrief: Chance and the Null Hypothesis
text:
Debrief: Chance and the Null Hypothesis
H0: Performance equals chance (50% - just guessing)
H1: Performance differs from chance
Key insight: Some people will get 5/6 or 6/6 just by luck, even with no real ability.
With 28 people flipping coins, SOMEONE will get 5+ heads. That doesn’t mean the coin is biased.
This is why we need statistics - to separate signal from noise.

title: Design Detectives: DataLab
text:
Task 5: Sleep & Memory

The Question
Before the session, you told us how many hours you slept last night. We also measured how many words you recalled.
Is there a relationship between sleep and memory?


Your Results











Group Discussion Questions
Q5.1 Is there an IV in this study?
Yes - sleep hoursYes - memory scoreNo - we measured both variables, we didn’t manipulate eitherYes - the participant
Q5.2 What design type is this? (See correlational design)
Between-subjectsWithin-subjectsCorrelationalExperimental
Q5.3 What does a positive correlation mean here?
Sleep causes better memoryPeople who slept more tended to recall more wordsPeople who slept less recalled more wordsThere is no relationship
Q5.4 Can we say that sleep causes better memory based on this data?
TRUEFALSE
Q5.5 Why can’t we make causal claims from correlational data?
The sample was too smallThe correlation wasn’t strong enoughThird variables might explain the relationship (e.g., health, motivation)Correlations are always meaningless






WarningThe Critical Point: Correlation ≠ Causation



Even if we find a relationship between sleep and memory, we cannot say sleep causes better memory. Why?

Maybe healthier people sleep more AND have better memory
Maybe motivated students prepare better (sleep AND study)
Maybe stress reduces both sleep AND memory

This is why experiments (with manipulation) are needed to establish causation.

What You Did

If just guessing randomly: You’d expect to get 3 out of 6 correct (50%).


Your Results











Group Discussion Questions
Q6.1 If someone got 5 out of 6 correct, does that prove they have a sixth sense?
TRUEFALSE
Q6.2 Why not?
5/6 is impossibleSome people will get 5/6 just by luck, even without any real abilityThe experiment was designed wrongSixth sense definitely doesn’t exist
Q6.3 What does 50% accuracy suggest?
They definitely have a sixth senseThey definitely don’t have a sixth sensePerformance is at chance level - consistent with random guessingThe task was too hard
Q6.4 What is the null hypothesis for this study?
People can detect staringPeople cannot detect staringDetection accuracy equals 50% (chance level)There is no null hypothesis






TipWhy Statistics Matter





With 28 people, some will get lucky just by chance. If everyone flipped a coin 6 times, someone would get 5 or 6 heads - but that doesn’t mean their coin is biased!
Statistics help us ask: Is this result more extreme than we’d expect from chance alone?

title: Building Your Research
text: Operationalisation (~25 min)

title: Building Your Research
text:
What is Operationalisation?

Operationalisation: The process of turning an abstract concept into a concrete, measurable variable.


Your Research Plan requires you to specify:

Exactly how you’ll manipulate the IV
Exactly how you’ll measure the DV

title: Building Your Research
text:
Why Does It Matter?

Vague variables = unmeasurable research
Other researchers need to replicate your study
Poor operationalisation = confounded results
Reviewers (and markers!) will critique weak operationalisation



Bad: “We measured happiness”
Good: “Participants rated their current happiness on a 1-10 scale, with 1 = extremely unhappy and 10 = extremely happy”

title: Building Your Research
text:
Topic 1: Font Difficulty → Memory

The claim: Reading in hard-to-read fonts creates “desirable difficulty” that enhances learning
Source: Diemand-Yauman et al. (2011)


Questions to answer:

What counts as “difficult to read”?
How different should the fonts be?
What “memory” outcome do we measure?

title: Building Your Research
text:
Operationalising “Font Difficulty”
Option 1: Fluent (Arial 12pt) vs Disfluent (Comic Sans 12pt, 75% grey)
Option 2: Fluent (Times New Roman 14pt) vs Disfluent (Haettenschweiler 12pt)
Option 3: Fluent (standard) vs Disfluent (Italicised, smaller font)







Note


The key is CLEAR CONTRAST between conditions that isolates font readability while keeping content identical.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Operationalising “Memory”

Free recall: How many facts can participants remember?
Recognition test: Multiple choice on material content
Cued recall: Provide category, ask for specific items


Each measures slightly different aspects of memory. Your choice must be justified.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Topic 2: Hydration → Cognitive Performance

The claim: Being hydrated improves cognitive function
Source: Edmonds & Burford (2009)


Questions to answer:

What does “hydration” mean operationally?
What cognitive task(s) measure “performance”?

title: Building Your Research
text:
Operationalising “Hydration”
Option 1: Water group drinks 500ml; control group drinks nothing
Option 2: Water group drinks 250ml; control group sips (no swallowing)
Option 3: Measure time since last drink (observational)







Potential Confound


If water group believes water helps cognition, expectation effects may drive results. Consider a placebo control?

title: Building Your Research
text:
Operationalising “Cognitive Performance”

Attention task: Reaction time, sustained attention
Working memory: Digit span, n-back task
Processing speed: Symbol substitution
Combined score: Multiple tasks averaged

title: Building Your Research
text:
Topic 3: Eye Contact → Trustworthiness

The claim: Eye contact increases perceptions of trustworthiness
Source: Argyle & Dean (1965); subsequent research on gaze and trust


Questions to answer:

How do you manipulate eye contact?
How do you measure “perceived trustworthiness”?

title: Building Your Research
text:
Operationalising “Eye Contact”
Option 1: Video of person with direct gaze vs averted gaze
Option 2: Photo with eyes meeting camera vs eyes looking away
Option 3: Duration manipulation: 2 seconds vs 6 seconds of eye contact







Note


Videos/photos provide control. Live interaction adds realism but introduces variability.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Operationalising “Trustworthiness”

Rating scale: “How trustworthy does this person seem?” (1-7)
Behavioural proxy: “Would you lend this person money?” (Yes/No)
Investment game: How much would you invest with this person?
Multiple items: Composite trustworthiness scale (Likert items)

title: Building Your Research
text:
Common Operationalisation Pitfalls

Vague language: “We changed the IV” — HOW exactly?
Confounded manipulation: Changing multiple things at once
Unreliable measures: Single-item scales, ceiling/floor effects
Missing details: Another researcher couldn’t replicate



Test yourself: Could a stranger run your study exactly from your description?

title: Building Your Research
text: One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed (~20 min)

title: Building Your Research
text:
Review: H₀ and H₁

Null Hypothesis (H₀): There is no effect or no difference
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): There IS an effect or difference


We test H₀. If the data is very unlikely under H₀, we reject it and accept H₁.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Two Types of H₁


Two-Tailed (Non-directional)
H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂
“There IS a difference”
Direction not specified

One-Tailed (Directional)
H₁: μ₁ > μ₂ OR H₁: μ₁ < μ₂
“Group 1 is higher/lower than Group 2”
Direction IS specified

title: Building Your Research
text:
When to Use Each

Two-Tailed: When you’re uncertain about direction, or the effect could reasonably go either way
One-Tailed: When strong theory or prior evidence supports a specific direction

title: Building Your Research
text:
One-Tailed: Pros and Cons
Advantages:

More statistical power to detect effect in predicted direction
More precise research question

Disadvantages:

Must JUSTIFY the direction (prior literature)
Cannot claim significance if effect goes the OTHER way
Some journals/reviewers are skeptical

title: Building Your Research
text:
Two-Tailed: Pros and Cons
Advantages:

Safe choice when direction is uncertain
Can detect effects in either direction
More widely accepted

Disadvantages:

Less statistical power
Less precise prediction

title: Building Your Research
text:
Font Difficulty: Writing Hypotheses

Two-tailed:

H₀: There is no difference in recall between fluent and disfluent font conditions
H₁: Recall scores differ between fluent and disfluent font conditions

One-tailed:

H₀: Disfluent font does not improve recall
H₁: Participants in the disfluent font condition will recall more words than those in the fluent font condition

title: Building Your Research
text:
Justifying Your Direction
For your Research Plan, if you choose one-tailed:

Cite prior research supporting the direction
Explain the theoretical mechanism
Acknowledge what you’ll conclude if the effect is opposite








Assessment Requirement


Your Research Plan MUST include justification for your hypothesis choice.

title: Building Your Research
text: Between vs Within (~25 min)

title: Building Your Research
text:
The Fundamental Choice

Between-Subjects: Different people in each condition
Within-Subjects: Same people in all conditions


Both test the SAME hypothesis. The difference is HOW you assign participants.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Between-Subjects Design


How it works:

Participant 1-30: Condition A
Participant 31-60: Condition B
Compare group means


Advantages:

No order effects
No practice/fatigue
Simpler procedure

Disadvantages:

Individual differences add noise
Need more participants

title: Building Your Research
text:
Within-Subjects Design


How it works:

All 30 participants do BOTH conditions
Each person is their own control
Compare within-person differences


Advantages:

Controls individual differences
More statistical power
Fewer participants needed

Disadvantages:

Order effects
Practice/fatigue
Demand characteristics

title: Building Your Research
text:
Decision Tree for Our Topics

Font difficulty → Memory

Between: Group A reads fluent, Group B reads disfluent
Within: Everyone reads BOTH (counterbalanced)

Which is better? What are the trade-offs?

title: Building Your Research
text:
Font Study: Design Analysis
Within-subjects concerns:

If same content twice → memory for first reading confounds second
If different content → is content equivalent?
Order effects: Which font first?

Between-subjects concerns:

Some people have better memory naturally
Need twice as many participants








Tip


Typical choice: Between-subjects for memory studies with identical content

title: Building Your Research
text:
Hydration Study: Design Analysis

Think: What would between-subjects vs within-subjects look like?
What are the trade-offs for each?



Within: Same person tested hydrated and dehydrated

Problem: Requires multiple sessions or dehydration manipulation

Between: Different people in water vs no-water groups

Problem: Individual differences in cognitive ability

title: Building Your Research
text:
Eye Contact Study: Design Analysis

Vote: For the eye contact → trustworthiness study, which design would you choose?

Between-subjects (different photos/videos for each participant)
Within-subjects (same participant rates BOTH gaze conditions)



Within-subjects is common here: Each participant can rate multiple stimuli, and we compare their ratings across conditions.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Practical Constraints
Your design choice isn’t just about statistics. Consider:

Time: How long can you test each participant?
Participants: How many can you realistically recruit?
Ethics: Any concerns with repeated testing or manipulation?
Materials: Can you create equivalent stimuli?

title: Building Your Research
text: The Critical Link (~15 min)

title: Building Your Research
text:
Why Design Determines Test

The data structure from your design determines which statistical test is appropriate.


Different designs produce different types of data relationships. The test must match.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Between-Subjects → Independent t-test

Design: 30 people in Font A, 30 different people in Font B
Data: Two independent groups of scores
Test: Independent samples t-test
Assumptions: Scores in Group A are independent of scores in Group B

title: Building Your Research
text:
Within-Subjects → Paired t-test

Design: 30 people rate trustworthiness for BOTH gaze conditions
Data: Paired scores (same person, two measurements)
Test: Paired samples t-test
Assumptions: Pairs of scores are related (same individual)

title: Building Your Research
text:
The Match Matters






Critical Point


Using the WRONG test gives you WRONG results.

Independent t-test on paired data → loses power, wrong df
Paired t-test on independent data → violates assumptions

title: Building Your Research
text:
For Your Research Plan

You MUST:

State your design (between or within)
State your test (independent or paired t-test)
EXPLAIN why this test matches your design



This is the “justify your choice of test” requirement.

title: Building Your Research
text:
Example Justification

“This study uses a between-subjects design with different participants randomly assigned to each font condition. Because the data consist of scores from two independent groups, an independent samples t-test is the appropriate statistical test. This test compares the mean recall scores between the fluent and disfluent font groups to determine whether any observed difference is statistically significant.”

title: Building Your Research
text: What Goes Where (~15 min)

title: Building Your Research
text:
The Four Subsections
A Method section typically includes:

Design: What type? What are the IV and DV?
Participants: Who? How many? How recruited?
Materials: What stimuli, measures, equipment?
Procedure: What happened, step by step?

title: Building Your Research
text:
Design Subsection

Example:
“The word list consisted of 20 common concrete nouns (e.g., ‘table’, ‘flower’). In the fluent condition, words were presented in 16-point Arial font. In the disfluent condition, words were presented in 12-point Comic Sans MS at 75% greyscale. A blank recall sheet was provided for participants to write remembered words.”

Example:
“Participants were tested individually. After providing informed consent, they were presented with the word list for 60 seconds and instructed to memorise as many words as possible. The screen then went blank for 30 seconds (retention interval), followed by a 2-minute recall period during which participants wrote down all remembered words. Participation took approximately 10 minutes.”


Include: Step-by-step what happened, timing, instructions given

title: Research Plan Workshop
text:
Activity 1: Operationalisation Workshop (30 min)

Choose Your Topic
The Research Plan requires you to investigate ONE of these three questions:

Font difficulty → Memory: Does reading in a harder-to-read font improve retention?
Hydration → Cognitive performance: Does drinking water improve cognitive task performance?
Eye contact → Perceived trustworthiness: Does eye contact affect how trustworthy someone seems?







NoteYour Topic



Write down which topic you’ve chosen (or are leaning towards) before continuing.




Understanding Operationalisation






TipWhat is Operationalisation?



Turning an abstract concept into a concrete, measurable variable. Your description must be specific enough that another researcher could replicate your study exactly.


1. Which of these is a well-operationalised IV?
Stress levelAmount of exercise20 minutes of moderate cycling (heart rate 120-140 bpm) vs 20 minutes of seated restHigh vs low anxiety
2. Which of these is a well-operationalised DV?
Memory performanceHow well they did on the testNumber of words correctly recalled from a 20-word list (range: 0-20)Whether they remembered things


Learning from Examples
Here’s how operationalisation works with topics different from your assessment:
Example: Caffeine → Alertness

IV: Caffeine consumption with two levels:

Condition 1: 200mg caffeine capsule (equivalent to ~2 cups of coffee)
Condition 2: Placebo capsule (identical appearance, no caffeine)

DV: Alertness measured by:

Task: Psychomotor Vigilance Test (10-minute sustained attention task)
Scoring: Mean reaction time to stimuli (milliseconds)
Range: Continuous, typically 200-500ms


Notice the specificity: exact dosage, how conditions are matched, what task, what metric.
Example: Background Music → Concentration

IV: Audio condition with two levels:

Condition 1: Instrumental background music (60-70 dB, classical piano)
Condition 2: Silence (ambient noise only, <30 dB)

DV: Concentration measured by:

Task: Proofreading task — identify spelling errors in a 500-word passage
Scoring: Number of errors correctly identified
Range: 0-15 (15 errors embedded)




Apply to Your Topic
3. For your chosen topic, complete this IV template:

“The independent variable is _____________ with two levels:
Condition 1: _____________________________________________
Condition 2: _____________________________________________”

4. For your chosen topic, complete this DV template:

“The dependent variable is _____________ measured by:
Task/Measure: ___________________________________________
Scoring: _______________________________________________
Range: ________________________________________________”



Check Your Operationalisation
5. The “replicability test” asks whether:
Your study is interesting enough to replicateAnother researcher could run the exact same study from your descriptionThe results would be the same if repeatedYour participants could do the task again






WarningSelf-Check



Read your operationalisation aloud. Could a stranger run your exact study from this description alone? If not, add the missing details.

title: Research Plan Workshop
text:
Activity 2: Hypothesis Writing Practice (25 min)

Writing Your Null Hypothesis
The null hypothesis (H₀) states there is NO effect or NO difference.
1. A null hypothesis predicts:
The effect you expect to findNo difference or no effect between conditionsThe direction of the effectWhat you hope will happen
2. Write a null hypothesis for YOUR topic:
H₀: _________________________________________________


One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
3. A one-tailed hypothesis:
Tests for any differencePredicts a specific direction of effectIs always more appropriateRequires no justification
4. A two-tailed hypothesis:
Predicts a difference without specifying directionPredicts no effectIs never appropriate in psychologyIs only used for correlations


Making the Decision
5. When should you use a one-tailed hypothesis?
Whenever you want more statistical powerWhen you’re not sure what will happenWhen prior research consistently supports a specific directionAlways - it’s better practice
Example justification for direction:

“I have chosen a one-tailed hypothesis predicting that caffeine will decrease reaction times because:

McLellan et al. (2016) meta-analysis found caffeine consistently improved reaction time across 21 studies
The adenosine-blocking mechanism provides theoretical basis for increased alertness
No studies have found caffeine impairs reaction time in healthy adults”



“I have chosen a two-tailed hypothesis because:

While some studies show music improves concentration (Rauscher et al., 1993), others show it impairs performance (Perham & Vizard, 2011)
The effect may depend on task type, music type, and individual differences
I cannot confidently predict which direction the effect will go”




Write Your Hypotheses
Two-tailed version:
H₁: _________________________________________________
One-tailed version (if you can justify it):
H₁: _________________________________________________
Your justification:

“I have chosen a [one-tailed / two-tailed] hypothesis because:
_________________________________________________________”



Quick Checks
True or False: A one-tailed hypothesis gives you more statistical power to detect an effect in the predicted direction. TRUEFALSE
True or False: If your effect goes in the opposite direction to your one-tailed prediction, you can still claim statistical significance. TRUEFALSE

text:
Activity 3: Design & Analysis Matching (25 min)

Choosing Your Design
1. In a between-subjects design, participants:
Experience only ONE condition eachExperience ALL conditionsAre matched in pairs across conditionsDrop out before completing the study
2. In a within-subjects design, participants:
Experience only one condition eachExperience ALL conditionsAre tested only onceCannot be counterbalanced


Evaluating Trade-offs
3. The main advantage of between-subjects designs is:
More statistical powerFewer participants neededNo order effects, practice effects, or carryoverSimpler randomisation
4. The main advantage of within-subjects designs is:
Each participant serves as their own control, increasing powerNo need for counterbalancingParticipants prefer themFaster data collection
5. The main disadvantage of within-subjects designs is:
Less statistical powerMore participants neededOrder effects, practice effects, and demand characteristicsCannot use t-tests


Apply to Your Topic
6. Describe what a between-subjects version of YOUR study would look like:

“Group A (n = ): ______________________________________
Group B (n = ): ______________________________________”

7. Describe what a within-subjects version of YOUR study would look like:

“All participants (n = ) would: _________________________
Order would be counterbalanced by: __________________________”

8. For YOUR topic, identify one specific trade-off:

“A key consideration for my study is: _________________________
This makes [between / within] subjects more appropriate because: ___”



Matching Design to Test
9. A between-subjects design with two groups requires:
Paired samples t-testIndependent samples t-testOne-sample t-testCorrelation
10. A within-subjects design with two conditions requires:
Paired samples t-testIndependent samples t-testOne-sample t-testChi-square test
11. Why does design determine the statistical test?
Statistical software requires you to specifyIt’s a tradition in psychologyDifferent designs produce different data structures that require different analysesBoth tests give the same answer anyway


Write Your Complete Justification

“This study will use a [between-subjects / within-subjects] design because:
Given this design, I will use a [independent / paired] samples t-test because [how the data structure matches the test]: _______________”

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

Explain the logic of null hypothesis significance testing
Interpret p-values correctly (and avoid common misconceptions)
Understand confidence intervals as ranges of plausible values
Calculate and interpret Cohen’s d
