title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: Return to Week 12

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Remember the DataLab Results?

Lab A (abstract words): M = 5.4 words recalled
Lab B (concrete words): M = 6.8 words recalled
Difference: 1.4 words



The questions we need to answer:

Is this difference REAL, or just chance?
How CERTAIN are we about these estimates?
How BIG is this effect in practical terms?

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Three Questions

Today we learn to answer:

Is it real? → Hypothesis testing & p-values
How certain? → Confidence intervals
How big? → Effect sizes (Cohen’s d)



You need ALL THREE for your Research Report.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: NHST (~25 min)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Fundamental Question
When we observe a difference in our data…

Is it a real effect, or just random chance?



The 1.4 word difference could reflect:

A genuine effect of word type on memory
OR just random variation in who was in each lab

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST)

NHST: A statistical framework that tests whether observed data are consistent with a null hypothesis of “no effect.”


We assume there’s nothing going on, then ask: “How surprising is our data?”

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Two Hypotheses


Null Hypothesis (H₀)

Assumes no effect/difference
The “skeptic’s position”
What we test against

“Word type has no effect on memory.”

Alternative Hypothesis (H₁)

Assumes there IS an effect
The researcher’s prediction
What we hope to support

“Word type does affect memory.”

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: Summary

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Logic: Proof by Contradiction

Assume H₀ is true (no real effect)
Calculate how likely our data would be under H₀
If our data would be very unlikely…
Reject H₀ and accept H₁



Like a court trial: Assume innocence (H₀) until evidence (data) proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: What It Really Means (~20 min)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
What is a p-value?

p-value: The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.


It answers: “If there were truly no effect, how often would we see data this extreme just by chance?”

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Example: Memory Data

If our memory comparison has p = 0.03, this means:
“If word type truly had no effect on memory, we would observe a difference this large (or larger) in only 3% of experiments, just by chance.”


Because 3% is rare, we conclude H₀ is probably wrong.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Significance Threshold (α)

Alpha (α): The predetermined threshold for rejecting H₀. Conventionally set at 0.05 (5%).





p-value
Decision




p < .05
Reject H₀ (“significant”)


p ≥ .05
Fail to reject H₀ (“not significant”)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: A visual demonstration

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
What p-values Do NOT Mean






Common Misconceptions


The p-value is NOT:

The probability that H₀ is true
The probability the results occurred by chance
The probability of replication
A measure of effect size





A p-value only tells you how surprising your data would be IF H₀ were true.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
section: Type I and Type II Errors
text:
Type I and Type II Errors




H₀ True
H₀ False




Reject H₀
Type I Error (false positive)
Correct!


Fail to reject H₀
Correct!
Type II Error (false negative)





Type I error rate = α (usually .05)
Type II error rate = β (related to power)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: 10 minutes

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: Effect Sizes & Confidence Intervals (~25 min)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Beyond “Is There an Effect?”






The Limitation of p-values


A p-value tells us IF an effect probably exists.
It does NOT tell us:

How BIG the effect is
How PRECISE our estimate is





We need additional tools: effect sizes and confidence intervals.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Effect Sizes: How Big?

Cohen’s d: A standardised measure of the difference between two means, expressed in standard deviation units.
\[d = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{s_{pooled}}\]


Key insight: Effect sizes are independent of sample size. A tiny effect can be “significant” with huge n.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Cohen’s Benchmarks



d value
Interpretation
Visual Overlap




0.2
Small
85% overlap


0.5
Medium
67% overlap


0.8
Large
53% overlap










Note


These are rough guidelines. Context matters! In some fields, d = 0.3 is impressive.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: Visualising Effect Sizes

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
DataLab Example: Cohen’s d

Our memory data:

Lab A: M = 5.4, SD = 1.8
Lab B: M = 6.8, SD = 2.0

\[d = \frac{6.8 - 5.4}{1.9} = \frac{1.4}{1.9} = 0.74\]
This is a medium-to-large effect.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Confidence Intervals: How Certain?

Confidence Interval (CI): A range of values that is likely to contain the true population parameter.


Instead of saying “the mean is 6.8”, we say:
“The mean is 6.8, 95% CI [6.07, 7.53]”
This shows our precision.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Interpreting 95% CIs






Common Misconception


A 95% CI does NOT mean “there’s a 95% probability the true value is in this interval.”










Correct Interpretation


If we repeated this study many times and calculated a 95% CI each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true value.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
CIs and Significance

The CI rule: If the 95% CI for a difference does not include zero, the difference is statistically significant at p < .05.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Complete Picture

Report all three pieces:

p-value: Is the effect real?
Effect size (d): How big is it?
95% CI: How precise is our estimate?



Example: “The difference was significant, t(58) = 2.86, p = .006, d = 0.74, 95% CI [0.42, 2.38]”

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: Independent vs Paired (~25 min)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Two Types of t-test

Independent samples t-test: Compares means from two different groups
Paired samples t-test: Compares means from the same people measured twice


The choice depends on your design (Week 13!).

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: One or Two Tailed

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Independent t-test: When?
Use when you have:

Two separate groups of participants
Each participant in only ONE condition
Between-subjects design



DataLab example: Lab A (abstract) vs Lab B (concrete)
Different students in each lab → Independent t-test

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Independent t-test: The Formula
\[t = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{SE_{difference}}\]

The t-statistic is the ratio of:

Signal: The difference between group means
Noise: The standard error of that difference

Larger t = more evidence against H₀

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Paired t-test: When?
Use when you have:

The same participants in both conditions
Each participant measured twice
Within-subjects design



DataLab example: Pre-session mood vs Post-session mood
Same students measured at both times → Paired t-test

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
Paired t-test: The Formula
\[t = \frac{\bar{D}}{SE_{\bar{D}}}\]

Where \(\bar{D}\) is the mean of the difference scores.
We’re testing: Is the average change within each person significantly different from zero?

title: Is Your Effect Real?
section: Why Paired Tests Are More Powerful
text:
Why Paired Tests Are More Powerful

Controls for individual differences
Each person serves as their own control
Reduces “noise” in the data
Can detect smaller effects with same sample size








Tip


This is why Week 13’s design decision matters! Within-subjects = more power.

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
The Design → Test Link (Recap)



Your Design
Data Structure
Your Test




Between-subjects
Two independent groups
Independent t-test


Within-subjects
Paired scores
Paired t-test










Warning


Using the wrong test gives invalid results!

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: In short

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: Signal wins

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text: APA Reporting (~15 min)

title: Is Your Effect Real?
text:
What to Report

APA format for t-tests:
t(df) = X.XX, p = .XXX, d = X.XX, 95% CI [X.XX, X.XX]


All five pieces:

Test statistic (t)
Degrees of freedom (df)
p-value (exact, unless p < .001)
Effect size (Cohen’s d)
Confidence interval

title: Is Your Effect Real?

text:
Part 1: Understanding the Two Designs
The first choice you make is crucial: What type of design is your study?

Between-Subjects Design
In a between-subjects (or “between-groups”) design:

Different people are in each condition
Each participant only experiences ONE level of the IV
We compare Group A to Group B

Examples:

Comparing test scores between students who used Method A vs Method B
Comparing anxiety levels in people who received therapy vs a control group
Comparing memory for abstract words (Lab A) vs concrete words (Lab B)



Within-Subjects Design
In a within-subjects (or “repeated measures”) design:

The SAME people are in both conditions
Each participant experiences BOTH levels of the IV
We compare each person’s score at Time 1 to their score at Time 2

Examples:

Measuring mood before AND after a relaxation exercise
Testing reaction time with AND without distractions
Comparing performance on Monday vs Friday (same students)




Self-Check: Design Types

1. A researcher randomly assigns 30 students to learn with flashcards and 30 different students to learn with practice tests, then compares their exam scores.
Between-subjectsWithin-subjects
2. A researcher measures participants’ stress levels before a meditation session, then measures the SAME participants’ stress levels after the session.
Between-subjectsWithin-subjects
3. In Lab A, students memorised abstract words. In Lab B, different students memorised concrete words. This is:
Between-subjectsWithin-subjects
4. The same participants rate how attractive faces look when smiling vs when neutral.
Between-subjectsWithin-subjects

Summary






ImportantKey Takeaways



Choosing the right test:

Different people in each group → Independent samples t-test
Same people measured twice → Paired samples t-test

What affects significance (p-value):

Larger difference between means → easier to detect
Smaller SDs (less noise) → easier to detect
Larger sample size → easier to detect

What affects effect size (Cohen’s d):

Larger difference between means → larger d
Smaller SDs → larger d
Sample size does NOT affect d

Why we report both:

p-value tells us IF the effect is real
Effect size tells us HOW BIG the effect is
A significant result isn’t always a meaningful result!

Learning Outcomes
By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

Create and interpret scatterplots

title: Correlation
text:
Beyond Group Differences


So far: comparing groups (t-tests)
Now: examining relationships between variables
Both variables are measured, not manipulated



Question: Is there a relationship between study hours and exam scores?

title: Correlation
text:
What is Correlation?


Correlation: A statistical measure that quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables.

title: Correlation
text:
Direction of Relationships



Positive: As X ↑, Y ↑
Example: Height and weight

Negative: As X ↑, Y ↓
Example: Stress and sleep quality

title: Correlation
text: Strength of Relationships

title: Correlation
text:
Types of Relationships







Warning


Correlation measures LINEAR relationships only. The curvilinear data has a strong pattern but r ≈ 0!

title: Correlation
text:
Visualising Relationships

Scatterplot: A graph displaying the relationship between two continuous variables, with each observation represented as a point.



X-axis: One variable (often predictor)
Y-axis: Other variable (often outcome)
Each point: One observation

title: Correlation
text:
Creating Good Scatterplots

Label axes clearly (with units)
Use appropriate scales
Include a trend line (with caution)
Look for patterns, outliers, clusters

title: Correlation
section: Example: Study Hours vs Exam Scores
text: Example: Study Hours vs Exam Scores

title: Correlation
text:
What to Look For

When examining a scatterplot, ask:

Is there a relationship? (or random scatter?)
What direction? (positive/negative)
How strong? (tight/loose clustering)
Is it linear? (or curved?)
Any outliers? (unusual points)

title: Correlation
text:
The Impact of Outliers







Warning


A single outlier dramatically changed r from 0.70 to 0.35! Always visualise first.

title: Correlation
text:
Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient


Pearson’s r: A measure of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. Ranges from -1 to +1.

\[r = \frac{\sum(X - \bar{X})(Y - \bar{Y})}{(n-1)s_X s_Y}\]

title: Correlation
text:
Interpreting Pearson’s r




r value
Interpretation




+/- 1.0
Perfect correlation


+/- 0.7 to 0.9
Strong


+/- 0.4 to 0.6
Moderate


+/- 0.1 to 0.3
Weak


0
No linear relationship










Note


These are rough guidelines. Context and field norms matter!

title: Correlation
text:
Coefficient of Determination (r^2)


r^2 (r-squared): The proportion of variance in Y that is explained by X. Found by squaring r.



If r = 0.6, then r^2 = 0.36
“36% of the variance in exam scores is explained by study hours.”

title: Correlation
text:
Assumptions of Pearson’s r


Both variables are continuous
Linear relationship (check scatterplot!)
Bivariate normality (roughly)
No extreme outliers
Independence of observations

title: Correlation
text:
When Pearson’s r Fails







Warning


Pearson’s r is inappropriate when:

Data are ordinal (ranked)
Relationship is non-linear
There are extreme outliers
Data are severely non-normal

title: Correlation
text:
Spearman’s Rho (rho)


Spearman’s rho: A non-parametric correlation based on ranks rather than raw values. More robust to outliers and non-linearity.



Converts data to ranks
Then calculates Pearson’s r on ranks
Ranges from -1 to +1 (same interpretation)

title: Correlation
text:
Pearson vs Spearman



Use Pearson’s r when:

Both variables continuous
Linear relationship
Roughly normal data
No major outliers


Use Spearman’s rho when:

Ordinal data
Non-linear but monotonic
Non-normal data
Outliers present

title: Correlation
text:
Testing Significance


Null hypothesis: r = 0 (no correlation in population)
Test: Is our observed r significantly different from 0?
Report: r(df) = value, p = value

title: Correlation
text:
The Third Variable Problem


Third Variable (Confound): An unmeasured variable that causes both X and Y, creating a spurious correlation between them.



Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated.
Third variable: Hot weather causes both!

title: Correlation
text:
Directionality Problem


Correlation shows X and Y are related
But which causes which?
X -> Y?
Y -> X?
Or both directions?



Depression and social isolation are correlated.
Does depression cause isolation, or isolation cause depression, or both?

title: Correlation
text:
Famous Spurious Correlations


Real correlations that aren’t causal:

Number of pirates and global temperature (r = -0.9)
Nicolas Cage films and pool drownings (r = 0.87)
Cheese consumption and death by bedsheet (r = 0.95)



tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations

title: Correlation
text:
When CAN We Infer Causation?


Temporal precedence: Cause before effect
Covariation: They vary together
Elimination of alternatives: No confounds








Tip


Experimental designs (with random assignment) can establish causation. Correlational designs cannot.

title: Correlation
text:
Reporting Correlations


APA format:
“There was a strong positive correlation between study hours and exam scores, r(48) = .72, p < .001. Study time explained 52% of the variance in exam performance.”

title: Correlation
text:
Key Takeaways

Correlation measures strength and direction of linear relationships
Scatterplots visualise relationships - always look first!
Pearson’s r for continuous, linear, normal data
Spearman’s rho for ordinal, non-linear, or non-normal data
Correlation NEVER proves causation (third variables, directionality)

text: Pearson’s r and Spearman’s rho (~30 min)

title: Correlation in R
text:
Pearson’s r

Use Pearson’s r when:

Both variables are continuous
Relationship is approximately linear
No extreme outliers

cor.test(x, y, method = "pearson")

title: Correlation in R
text:
Spearman’s rho

Use Spearman’s rho when:

Data are ordinal (ranks)
Relationship is monotonic but not linear
Outliers are a concern

cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")

When You Have Many Variables

Correlation matrix shows correlations between ALL pairs of variables at once.
Useful for exploring DataLab data with multiple measures.

title: Correlation in R

The R Code
# Select numeric variables
cor_data <- select(data, var1, var2, var3)

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor(cor_data, use = "complete.obs")

title: Correlation in R
text:
Reading a Correlation Matrix
Key points:

Diagonal is always 1.00 (variable with itself)
Matrix is symmetric (top-right = bottom-left)
Look for strong correlations (> .50 or < -.50)

text: Writing Up Correlations (~20 min)

title: Correlation in R
text:
APA Format

Template: r(df) = .XX, p = .XXX
Example: r(48) = .42, p = .003

Note: df = n - 2 for correlations.

title: Correlation in R
text:
Example Write-Up

“There was a significant positive correlation between confidence and accuracy, r(48) = .42, p = .003. Participants who reported higher confidence tended to perform better on the memory task.”

title: Correlation in R
text:
Correlation vs Causation






Key Point


Correlation does NOT imply causation!
Students must avoid causal language:

NO: “Confidence causes better performance”
YES: “Confidence was associated with better performance”

text:
Activity 1: Creating Scatterplots (15 min)

Visualising Relationships
Before calculating correlations, we should always visualise the relationship with a scatterplot.











Understanding Scatterplots
1. In a scatterplot, each point represents:
A variableA groupOne participantAn average
2. The x-axis typically shows:
The predictor or first variableThe outcome variableThe sample sizeThe correlation coefficient
3. What does the line of best fit show?
The average of all pointsThe predicted relationship between the variablesWhere most points should fallThe maximum possible score


Reading Scatterplot Patterns
4. If points cluster tightly around an upward-sloping line, this suggests:
A strong positive correlationA strong negative correlationNo correlationA weak relationship
5. If points are scattered randomly with no clear pattern, this suggests:
A strong positive correlationA strong negative correlationNo correlation (r close to 0)A curvilinear relationship
6. If points cluster around a downward-sloping line, this suggests:
A strong positive correlationA strong negative correlationNo correlationThe data is wrong
True or False: We should always create a scatterplot before calculating a correlation. TRUEFALSE
True or False: Scatterplots can reveal non-linear relationships that correlation coefficients might miss. TRUEFALSE

title: Correlation in R
text:
Activity 2: Calculating Correlations (15 min)

Pearson’s r
The Pearson correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables.


Properties of r
1. Pearson’s r ranges from:
0 to 1-1 to 0-1 to +10 to 100
2. An r value of 0 means:
A perfect positive relationshipA perfect negative relationshipNo linear relationshipThe calculation failed
3. An r value of -0.8 indicates:
A weak positive relationshipA strong negative relationshipA weak negative relationshipNo relationship


R Syntax
In R, we calculate correlation using cor() or cor.test():
# Simple correlation
cor(variable1, variable2)

# Correlation with p-value and CI
cor.test(variable1, variable2)
4. What is the key difference between cor() and cor.test()?
cor() is fastercor.test() provides a p-value and confidence intervalcor() gives more decimal placesThey calculate different types of correlation


Reading R Output
Here’s example output from cor.test():
    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  self_rating and accuracy
t = 3.45, df = 28, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.24  0.75
sample estimates:
      cor
0.55
5. What is the correlation coefficient (r)?
3.450.002280.55
6. Is this correlation statistically significant at alpha = 0.05?
Yes, because p = 0.002 < 0.05No, because the correlation is positiveCan’t tellNo, because df = 28
7. The 95% CI is [0.24, 0.75]. What does this tell us?
The correlation is exactly 0.55We’re 95% confident the true r is between 0.24 and 0.75The p-value is between 0.24 and 0.75The sample size should be 24 to 75

TipInterpretation Tips






Strong correlations (|r| > 0.5): Points cluster tightly around the line
Moderate correlations (|r| = 0.3-0.5): Clear trend but more scatter
Weak correlations (|r| < 0.3): Trend barely visible, lots of scatter
Near-zero correlations: No discernible pattern at all
Negative correlations: Line slopes downward (one goes up, other goes down)

title: Correlation in R
text:
Activity 3: Interpreting r Values (15 min)

Cohen’s Guidelines
Jacob Cohen provided rough guidelines for interpreting correlation strength:




r




0.10 - 0.29
Small/weak


0.30 - 0.49
Medium/moderate


0.50 - 1.00
Large/strong





Practice Interpretation
1. r = 0.25 would be considered:
Small/weakMedium/moderateLarge/strongNegligible
2. r = -0.65 would be considered:
Small/weakMedium/moderateLarge/strongNot applicable - it’s negative
3. r = 0.42 would be considered:
Small/weakMedium/moderateLarge/strongNegligible


Coefficient of Determination (r-squared)
Squaring r tells us the proportion of variance explained.
4. If r = 0.50, then r-squared (r^2) equals:
0.500.250.752.5
5. r^2 = 0.25 means:
25% of the variance in Y is explained by XThe correlation is 25%75% of participants show the relationshipThe effect is 25% larger than expected
6. If r = 0.70, what percentage of variance is explained?
70%49%30%100%


Critical Thinking
7. A statistically significant correlation of r = 0.15 suggests:
A strong, important relationshipA real but very weak relationship - likely not practically meaningfulThe data is unreliableWe need to use a different test
True or False: A significant p-value tells us the correlation is strong. TRUEFALSE
True or False: Correlation does not imply causation. TRUEFALSE
True or False: A negative correlation is weaker than a positive correlation of the same magnitude. TRUEFALSE

Activity 4: Correlation in YOUR Data (10 min)

Applying to DataLab
Let’s think about correlational questions we could ask with the DataLab data.


Question 1: Self-Rating and Performance
In the Frontal Lob task, participants rated their throwing ability before throwing.
If high self-ratings are associated with better performance, what type of correlation would we expect?
Positive correlationNegative correlationNo correlationCannot determine
Is there an IV and DV in this analysis?
Yes - self-rating is IV, performance is DVYes - performance is IV, self-rating is DVNo - correlational designs have no IV/DV, just two variablesDepends on the hypothesis


Question 2: Sleep and Memory
Imagine we correlate hours of sleep the night before with memory test performance.
What would a negative correlation (r = -0.30) mean?
More sleep = better memoryMore sleep = worse memoryNo relationshipSleep causes memory problems
Could we conclude that lack of sleep causes poor memory?
Yes, the correlation proves itNo, correlation doesn’t establish causationOnly if p < 0.05Yes, if r is negative


Question 3: Third Variables
Sleep quality might be related to both coffee consumption AND memory performance.
This illustrates:
A direct causal relationshipA potential third variable (confound)That coffee improves memoryThat the correlation is invalid
If coffee consumption is related to both variables, it could:
Create a spurious correlation between sleep and memoryProve that coffee causes poor sleepHave no effect on the correlationMake the correlation negative

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Why Does Format Matter?

Psychology uses a standardised format for reporting research
Readers know exactly where to find information
Allows critical evaluation of methods and findings
You will use this format for your Research Report (due 1 April)



APA Format: The publication style of the American Psychological Association. Used worldwide in psychology for journal articles, lab reports, and dissertations.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
section: The Sections of a Lab Report
text:
The Sections of a Lab Report

Every APA lab report follows the same structure:

Title Page
Abstract
Introduction
Method
Results
Discussion
References



Think of it as telling a story — background, what you did, what you found, and what it means.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
The Hourglass Shape

The hourglass

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Details

Introduction — Broad to narrow

Start with the big picture
Narrow to your specific study
End with your hypothesis



Method & Results — The narrow middle

Precise and specific
Exactly what you did and found



Discussion — Narrow to broad

Start with your findings
Broaden to implications
End with the big picture

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
section: When Will You Write Each Section?
text:
When Will You Write Each Section?



Section
What it does
When you’ll write it




Title Page
Identifies the study
Week 20 onwards


Abstract
~150-word summary
Write last


Introduction
Background + hypothesis
Weeks 17-18


Method
What you did
Weeks 17-18

Week 19-20

Week 20 onwards

Tip


You don’t write it all at once. We build it section by section over the coming weeks.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 1: Title Page

Purpose: Identify the study, the author, and the institution.


Title: Concise and informative — include your key variables
Your name and student number
Module code: PS50008A



Good title: “The Effect of Word Type on Free Recall Performance”
Bad title: “My Psychology Experiment”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 2: Abstract

Purpose: A brief summary of the entire study (~150 words). Written last.


One or two sentences on background/rationale
One sentence on method (design, participants, task)
One or two sentences on key results (with statistics)
One sentence on conclusion/implications








Pro Tip


Write the abstract after everything else. It’s a summary, not a preview.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 3: Introduction

Purpose: Provide background, establish rationale, state your hypothesis.

The funnel structure:

Broad context — What is the general topic area?
Key research — What have other researchers found?
Gap or question — What hasn’t been addressed?
Your study — What are you investigating and why?
Hypothesis — Your specific, testable prediction

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Introduction: What NOT to Do

Which of these is a problem in an Introduction?
A. Starting with a dictionary definition
B. Citing relevant research to build an argument
C. Including your results
D. Both A and C








Warning


Answer: D — Don’t start with “The dictionary defines…” and never reveal your results in the Introduction. Build a logical argument from the literature.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 4: Method

Purpose: Describe what you did in enough detail that someone could replicate your study.








Sound Familiar?


The Method section has four subsections — the same ones you’ve been writing in your Research Plan. Let’s use your Research Plan as a worked example.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 5: Results

Purpose: Report what you found — descriptive and inferential statistics.


Descriptive statistics — means, SDs (often in a table)
Inferential test — the t-test result with full APA notation
Effect size — Cohen’s d with 95% confidence interval
Brief verbal description — what the numbers mean in words








Note


We’ll cover Results reporting in detail in Week 19.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 6: Discussion

Purpose: Interpret your findings, acknowledge limitations, suggest future directions.


Restate key findings (in words, not statistics)
Interpret — what do the results mean?
Relate to literature — support or contradict previous research?
Limitations — what could have been done differently?
Future directions — what should researchers do next?
Conclusion — take-home message








Note


We’ll cover Discussion writing in detail in Week 20.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Section 7: References

Purpose: Full reference list in APA format for every source cited.


Journal article format:
Walker, I., & Hulme, C. (1999). Concrete words are easier to recall than abstract words: Evidence for a semantic contribution to short-term serial recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 25(5), 1256–1271.








Tip


Use a reference manager (e.g., Zotero — it’s free!) to format references automatically.

The Key Insight






Your Research Plan Practises Method Writing


The Research Plan you’re submitting this Friday is a standalone assessment on its own topic. But the skills are identical — it’s structured exactly like a Method section.




When you write your Research Report later (on a different topic, with your group), you’ll use the same structure. Let’s walk through it now.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Method Section Structure








A Method section needs…
In your Research Plan…
In your Research Report…




Hypothesis
Your chosen topic
Your group project topic


Design + justification
Design subsection
Design subsection


Who takes part
Participants subsection
Participants subsection


What you use
Materials subsection
Materials subsection


Step-by-step process
Procedure subsection
Procedure subsection


Statistical test
Named + justified
Named + justified

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Method Subsection 1: Design

What to include:

Type of design (between-subjects or within-subjects)
Independent variable and its levels
Dependent variable and how it’s measured






Weak:
“We used a between-subjects design.”



Strong:
“A between-subjects design was used. The independent variable was word type with two levels: concrete words and abstract words. The dependent variable was the number of words correctly recalled out of 15.”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Method Subsection 2: Participants

What to include:

Total number (and per condition if between-subjects)
Recruitment method
Key demographics (age range, mean age, gender)
Inclusion/exclusion criteria




Good example:
“Twenty participants (15 female, 5 male; Mage = 21.3, SD = 2.1) were recruited via opportunity sampling from the student population at Goldsmiths, University of London. All were native English speakers aged 18 or over. Ten participants were randomly allocated to each condition.”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Method Subsection 3: Materials

What to include:

Stimuli (word lists, images, questionnaires)
How they were created or sourced
Key properties (e.g., word frequency, length)
Equipment used (if relevant)




Good example:
“Two word lists were constructed, each containing 15 words. The concrete list contained words referring to physical objects (e.g., hammer, bicycle, elephant). The abstract list contained words referring to concepts or qualities (e.g., freedom, honesty, courage). Lists were matched for word frequency and syllable count.”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Method Subsection 4: Procedure

What to include:

Chronological account of what happened
What participants experienced step by step
Timing of each phase
Standardised instructions (summarised)
Ethical safeguards (consent, debrief)




Good example:
“Participants were tested individually. After providing informed consent, they were presented with their assigned word list and given two minutes to study the words. The list was then removed and participants counted backwards from 100 for one minute as a distractor task. They were then given two minutes to write down as many words as they could recall, in any order. Finally, participants were debriefed and thanked.”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Common Method Mistakes

Too vague: “Participants did a memory test” — what kind? How long? How scored?
Including results: Method describes what you did, not what you found
Missing justification: State your design AND explain why you chose it
Wrong tense: Method uses past tense (“participants were asked…”)
Forgetting ethics: Always mention consent and debriefing

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
section: What Makes a Good Research Plan?
text:
What Makes a Good Research Plan?

Your Research Plan will be assessed on:

Clarity and appropriateness of hypothesis
Justification of design choices
Feasibility and detail of procedure
Appropriate selection and justification of statistical test
Overall coherence and scientific reasoning









Tip


The word justify keeps appearing. Don’t just say what you’d do — explain why.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text: The Rules of the Game

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Tense


Past tense — for what was done


“Participants were randomly allocated…”
“The study used a between-subjects design…”
“Results showed a significant difference…”



Present tense — for established facts


“Research suggests that concrete words…”
“Dual coding theory proposes that…”
“The concreteness effect is well-documented…”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Person and Voice

Third person preferred in most sections

“Participants were asked to…” (not “I asked participants to…”)
“The study aimed to…” (not “We aimed to…”)

Passive voice is acceptable in Method and Results

“Words were presented for two minutes”

Active voice for clarity when describing others’ work

“Walker and Hulme (1999) found that…”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Statistical Notation

Key rules:

Italicise statistical symbols: t, F, r, p, M, SD, d, n, N
Leading zero for statistics that CAN exceed 1: M = 0.45
No leading zero for statistics that CANNOT exceed 1: p = .023, r = .72




t-test result in APA format:
t(18) = 2.45, p = .025, d = 0.87, 95% CI [0.12, 1.61]

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
section: Reporting a t-test: Step by Step
text:
Reporting a t-test: Step by Step

Step 1: Descriptives
“The concrete word group recalled more words (M = 11.2, SD = 2.4) than the abstract word group (M = 8.7, SD = 2.1).”



Step 2: Inferential test
“An independent-samples t-test revealed a significant difference, t(18) = 2.48, p = .023.”




Step 3: Effect size
“The effect was large, d = 1.11, 95% CI [0.17, 2.03].”

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
The Complete Results Paragraph

“Participants in the concrete word condition recalled significantly more words (M = 11.2, SD = 2.4) than those in the abstract word condition (M = 8.7, SD = 2.1). An independent-samples t-test confirmed this difference was statistically significant, t(18) = 2.48, p = .023, d = 1.11, 95% CI [0.17, 2.03]. This suggests that word concreteness has a large effect on free recall performance.”








Note


You don’t need to write results yet — but this is what you’re building toward.

title: APA Report Writing & Your Research Project
text:
Quick Reference: APA Checklist

Before you submit anything, check:

Past tense in Method and Results?
Third person throughout?
Statistical symbols italicised?
No leading zero before p and r?
Every claim supported by a citation or data?
Reference list matches in-text citations?

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 1: Hypothesis
A clear, testable hypothesis is the foundation of your Research Plan.
1. Does your hypothesis name the independent variable?
Yes — the IV is clearly statedNo — I need to add thisI’m not sure what the IV is
2. Does your hypothesis name the dependent variable?
Yes — the DV is clearly statedNo — I need to add thisI’m not sure what the DV is
3. Is your hypothesis directional (one-tailed) or non-directional (two-tailed)?
One-tailed — I predict a specific directionTwo-tailed — I predict a difference but not the directionI have stated which it is and explained why
4. Is your hypothesis testable with the statistical test you’ve chosen?
Yes — my hypothesis maps onto my testI think so but I’m not certainNo — I need to revise

Self-Check

A good hypothesis should:
Name both the IV and DV: TRUEFALSE
Include the word “significant”: TRUEFALSE
State a predicted direction (if one-tailed): TRUEFALSE
Be based on previous research or theory: TRUEFALSE
Include statistical values: TRUEFALSE

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 2: Design
Your design section should tell the reader exactly how the study is structured.
1. Have you stated the type of design?
Yes — between-subjects or within-subjects is clearly statedI’ve mentioned the design but not the typeI haven’t included this yet
2. Have you justified your design choice?
Yes — I’ve explained WHY this design was chosenI’ve stated the design but not explained whyI haven’t thought about justification
3. Have you identified the IV with its levels?
Yes — IV named with both/all levels specifiedI’ve named the IV but not the levelsI need to add this
4. Have you identified the DV and how it’s measured?
Yes — DV named with measurement methodI’ve named the DV but not how it’s measuredI need to add this

Common Design Mistakes
Which of these is a problem?
Stating that a between-subjects design avoids order effectsStating the design type without explaining why it was chosenMentioning potential confounding variablesIncluding both IV and DV
“A between-subjects design was used” is:
A complete design sectionMissing justification, IV, DV, and levelsToo detailedOnly missing the DV
True or False: You should explain why your design is appropriate, not just name it. TRUEFALSE
True or False: A within-subjects design always requires counterbalancing. TRUEFALSE

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 3: Participants
Your participants section tells the reader who would take part and how they’d be recruited.
1. Have you stated the total number of participants?
Yes — with numbers per condition if between-subjectsI’ve given a total but not per conditionI haven’t specified a number
2. Have you described the recruitment method?
Yes — e.g., opportunity sampling from the student populationI’ve mentioned sampling but not the methodI haven’t included this
3. Have you included demographic information?
Yes — age range, mean age, gender breakdownI’ve included some demographicsI haven’t included demographics
4. Have you mentioned inclusion/exclusion criteria?
Yes — e.g., native English speakers, aged 18+I’ve thought about it but not written itI haven’t considered this

Self-Check
A Participants subsection should be written in:
Present tensePast tense (or future tense for a plan)First personBullet points
Which is better?
20 people took partTwenty participants (12 female, 8 male; M_age = 20.5, SD = 1.8) were recruited via opportunity sampling from the student population at Goldsmiths, University of LondonWe tested some students from our class
True or False: You should justify your sample size if possible. TRUEFALSE
True or False: “Some people” is an acceptable description of participants. TRUEFALSE

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 4: Materials
Your materials section describes everything you need to run the study.
1. Have you described your stimuli (e.g., word lists, images, questionnaires)?
Yes — with examples of specific itemsI’ve mentioned materials but without examplesI haven’t described materials yet
2. Have you explained how materials were created or selected?
Yes — I’ve explained the source or construction methodI’ve listed materials but not their originI haven’t included this
3. Have you mentioned any key properties of your materials?
Yes — e.g., number of items, matching for word frequency/lengthSome properties are mentionedI haven’t included properties

Self-Check
Which materials description is stronger?
We used a word listA list of words was prepared for the experimentTwo word lists were constructed, each containing 15 words. The concrete list contained words referring to physical objects (e.g., hammer, bicycle). Lists were matched for word frequency using the MRC Psycholinguistic Database.
True or False: You should give examples of your stimuli (e.g., sample words from a list). TRUEFALSE
True or False: “We used some materials” is sufficient for this section. TRUEFALSE

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 5: Procedure
Your procedure is a chronological account of what participants would experience.
1. Is your procedure written in chronological order?
Yes — step by step from start to finishMostly, but some steps are out of orderI need to reorganise
2. Have you included timing for each phase?
Yes — e.g., ‘2 minutes to study’, ‘1 minute distractor task’Some timings are mentionedI haven’t included timings
3. Have you mentioned informed consent?
Yes — participants provide consent before the study beginsI’ve implied it but not stated itI haven’t mentioned consent
4. Have you mentioned debriefing?
Yes — participants are debriefed at the endI’ve implied itI haven’t mentioned debriefing
5. Is there enough detail for someone to replicate your study?
Yes — another researcher could follow my procedureMostly, but some details are vagueProbably not — I need more detail

Common Procedure Mistakes
Which of these is a problem in a Procedure section?
Including the timing of each phaseIncluding the results of the studyMentioning the distractor taskDescribing how consent was obtained
“Participants did the experiment and then we collected the data” is:
AdequateFar too vague — needs step-by-step detailAppropriate for a Research PlanOnly missing one detail
True or False: The Procedure should mention ethical safeguards (consent and debrief). TRUEFALSE
True or False: You should include your actual results in the Procedure section. TRUEFALSE

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 6: Statistical Test
Your Research Plan should name and justify the statistical test you plan to use.
1. Have you named the specific statistical test?
Yes — e.g., independent-samples t-test or paired-samples t-testI’ve said ‘t-test’ but not which typeI haven’t named a test
2. Have you justified why this test is appropriate?
Yes — I’ve linked it to my design, IV levels, and DV measurementI’ve named the test but not justified itI haven’t thought about justification
3. Does your test match your design?
Yes — between-subjects → independent t-test, within-subjects → paired t-testI think soI’m not sure which test matches which design

Self-Check
An independent-samples t-test is used when:
The same participants are in both conditionsDifferent participants are in each conditionThere are more than two conditionsThe data is categorical
A paired-samples t-test is used when:
The same participants are in both conditionsDifferent participants are in each conditionYou want to compare three groupsThe DV is nominal
True or False: You should explain why your chosen test is appropriate for your design. TRUEFALSE
True or False: A t-test can compare more than two groups. TRUEFALSE

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Section 7: Writing Quality
Finally, check the quality of your writing.
1. Is your Research Plan written in past tense (or planned future tense)?
Yes — consistent tense throughoutMostly, but some present tense slips inI’m not sure about tense
2. Is it written in third person?
Yes — ‘Participants were asked…’ not ‘I asked…’Mostly, but I’ve used ‘I’ or ‘we’ in placesI’ve written in first person throughout
3. Is it within the word count (1,000–1,200 words)?
Yes — I’ve checkedI’m close but haven’t checked exactlyI’m over or under
4. Have you proofread for spelling and grammar?
Yes — I’ve read through it carefullyI’ve done a quick checkNot yet

Final Check
True or False: “I will ask participants to…” should be “Participants will be asked to…” TRUEFALSE
True or False: Statistical symbols like t, p, and M should be italicised. TRUEFALSE
True or False: You should include a reference list if you cite any sources. TRUEFALSE

text:
Final Checklist

Hypothesis: Specific, testable, names IV and DV, states direction
Design: Type stated and justified, IV with levels, DV with measurement

title: Research Plan Self-Assessment
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






WarningDon’t Do These




No justification — “A between-subjects design was used” without explaining why
Too vague — “Some people did a test” instead of precise details
Wrong tense — “Participants will sit down and I give them the words”
Including results — the Method describes what you plan to do, not what you found
Missing ethics — forgetting to mention consent and debriefing
No examples — “A word list was used” without saying what kind of words
Wrong test — choosing an independent t-test for a within-subjects design
First person — “I decided to use…” instead of “An X design was employed because…”

title: Week 16 Lab Reading
text:
Forming Your Project Group
In Thursday’s lab, you’ll form groups of 3–4 students. Each group will work together on a research project, collecting data that every member will then use to write their own individual Research Report (due mid-late April).

How Groups Work

Group data, individual reports — you collect data together, but every person writes their own Research Report independently
Same data, different reports — do not share written drafts or copy from group members
3–4 students per group — form your own group in the lab







ImportantYou Must Attend Thursday’s Lab



If you do not attend the Week 16 lab and have not signalled your intent to participate, you will be allocated to a group on Monday of Week 17. It is much better to choose your own group.




What Makes an Effective Group?
Research on group work consistently shows that effective groups share a few characteristics:

Reliability — members who show up and do what they say they will
Communication — agreeing early on how you’ll stay in touch (WhatsApp group, email, etc.)
Shared expectations — discussing how much effort you each plan to put in
Complementary schedules — being able to find times to meet and collect data together

You don’t need to be best friends. You need to be dependable.

title: Week 16 Lab Reading
text:
Literature Searching
Once your group has a project topic, you’ll need to find relevant published research. This is the foundation of your Introduction section.

Where to Search

PsycINFO (via Goldsmiths Library)

Psychology-specific database
Only peer-reviewed sources
Allows filtering by methodology, age group, population
Best for targeted psychological research

Google Scholar (scholar.google.com)

Broader coverage across disciplines
Good for finding highly cited papers
“Cited by” feature helps you find related work
Set up Library Links to Goldsmiths for full-text access




How to Search Effectively
Start with your key variables. If your project is about the effect of word type on memory, your initial search terms might be:

"concrete words" AND "abstract words" AND recall
"word concreteness" AND memory
imageability AND "free recall"

Use Boolean operators:



Operator
What it does
Example




AND
Both terms must appear
memory AND emotion


OR
Either term can appear
recall OR recognition


NOT
Excludes a term
memory NOT "working memory"


” “
Exact phrase
"dual coding theory"



Narrow your search if you get too many results:

Add more specific terms
Filter by date (e.g., last 15 years)
Filter by peer-reviewed only
Look within a specific journal

Broaden your search if you get too few results:

Use synonyms or related terms
Remove one search term
Try Google Scholar as well as PsycINFO



What to Look For
Prioritise these types of sources:

Peer-reviewed journal articles — the gold standard in psychology
Recent publications (last 10–15 years) — for current evidence
Highly cited foundational papers — classic studies everyone references
Review articles or meta-analyses — for broad overviews of a topic

Avoid: Wikipedia, blog posts, newspaper articles, non-peer-reviewed sources. These are fine for initial background reading but should not appear in your reference list.

title: Week 16 Lab Reading
text:
Evaluating Sources
Not every paper you find will be useful. Read strategically.

The Quick Evaluation
When you find a paper, read in this order:

Title — Is it clearly relevant to your research question?
Abstract — What did they do and find? Is it related to your study?
Introduction — What’s their argument? Do they cite papers you should read too?
Method — Is their design similar to yours? (This helps with your own Method section)
Discussion — What do they conclude? What limitations do they note?

You do not need to read every paper from start to finish. Strategic reading saves time and helps you find the most relevant information quickly.


Assessing Quality
Ask yourself:

Is it peer-reviewed? (Published in an academic journal?)
Is it relevant? (Does it address your specific variables or topic?)
Is it recent enough? (Or is it a classic that’s still widely cited?)
Is the sample appropriate? (Similar population to your study?)
Are the findings clear? (Can you summarise what they found?)



How Many Sources?
For your Research Report introduction, aim for 5–8 quality sources. A mix of:

1–2 foundational/classic papers
3–4 recent studies directly relevant to your topic
1–2 broader theoretical or review papers

Quality matters more than quantity. Five well-chosen, well-integrated sources are better than ten papers listed without connection.

title: Week 16 Lab Reading
text:
Building a Literature Review
A literature review is not a list of summaries. It builds an argument that leads logically to your research question and hypothesis.

Structure Your Argument
Think of your literature review as answering a sequence of questions:

What is the general area? (1–2 sentences introducing the broad topic)
What do we know? (Key findings from existing research, with citations)
What don’t we know? (Gaps, inconsistencies, or unanswered questions)
What are we going to do about it? (Your study and hypothesis)



Synthesise, Don’t Summarise

Poor (list of summaries): “Smith (2020) found that concrete words were recalled better. Jones (2021) found that imagery helped memory. Brown (2019) found that abstract words were harder to recall.”


Good (synthesised argument): “Research has consistently demonstrated that concrete words are recalled more easily than abstract words (Brown, 2019; Smith, 2020). This advantage may be explained by dual coding theory, which proposes that concrete words are encoded both verbally and visually (Paivio, 1971). Supporting this, Jones (2021) found that imagery instructions specifically benefited recall of abstract words, suggesting that the availability of visual encoding is the key mechanism.”

The second version connects findings, identifies a mechanism, and builds toward a coherent argument.


Handling Conflicting Findings
Research doesn’t always agree. When you find conflicting results:

Acknowledge the disagreement — don’t ignore inconvenient findings
Consider possible explanations — different methods? Different populations? Different measures?
Use it to motivate your study — conflicting findings create a gap your research can address

title: Week 16 Lab Reading
text:
APA Referencing Basics

In-Text Citations








Situation
Format
Example




One author
Author (Year)
Walker (1999) found…


Two authors
Author & Author (Year)
Walker and Hulme (1999) demonstrated…


Three or more
First Author et al. (Year)
Smith et al. (2022) reported…


Parenthetical
(Author, Year)
…in free recall tasks (Walker & Hulme, 1999).


Multiple sources
(Author, Year; Author, Year)
…is well-established (Brown, 2019; Smith, 2020).





Reference List
Every source cited in-text must appear in the reference list, and vice versa. References are listed alphabetically by first author surname.

Journal article: Walker, I., & Hulme, C. (1999). Concrete words are easier to recall than abstract words: Evidence for a semantic contribution to short-term serial recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 25(5), 1256–1271. https://doi.org/10.1037/0278-7393.25.5.1256
Book: Paivio, A. (1971). Imagery and verbal processes. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.



Reference Managers
A reference manager saves you hours of manual formatting. Install one now:

Zotero (free) — integrates with Word and Google Docs, browser extension captures references directly from journal websites
Mendeley (free) — good PDF organiser
EndNote (available via Goldsmiths) — powerful but steeper learning curve







TipStart Now



Create a shared folder in Zotero or Mendeley for your project group. Add papers as you find them. When you write your Research Report, the reference list will be generated automatically.

If your heart sinks a little, you’re not alone - but I’m going to try to turn this around. This material has a reputation, and not a glamorous one. But there are real reasons it’s central to your degree—not because we enjoy watching you suffer, but because it changes what you’re capable of doing. It’s powerful stuff!

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: 2 You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
text:
2 You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
Right now, if someone asked you “Does social media cause anxiety?”, you might have an opinion. Everyone has one of those. But psychology isn’t about opinions—it’s about evidence. And evidence doesn’t just land in your lap. Someone has to design a way to gather it, collect it carefully, and work out what it actually shows.
That’s what you’re learning to do. By the end of your degree, you won’t just think social media might cause anxiety—you’ll be able to design a study that could actually test the idea, spot the weaknesses in existing research, and understand why the answer might be more complicated than the headlines suggest.

Think about that for a second… You don’t have to rely on anecdote or opinion anymore. You can create knowledge.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
3 You’ll See Through the Nonsense
We’re surrounded by claims about human behaviour. Adverts tell us certain products will make us more confident. Influencers promote supplements that supposedly sharpen your mind. News stories announce that scientists have “proved” all sorts of things about personality, intelligence, or relationships. 9 out of 10 adverts are dubious! (not a real stat!)
Most of these claims are, at best, oversimplified. Many are outright wrong. Understanding research methods gives you the ability to look at a study and ask:

How many people did they actually test?
Could something else explain these results?
Is this finding likely to replicate?

This isn’t just academic scepticism. It’s protection against being manipulated by people who use the language of science without the rigour, without the appropriate ‘methods’.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
4 These Skills Travel
Psychology graduates end up in all sorts of places: clinical training, education, marketing, human resources, policy research, user experience design, data analysis, all sorts of entrepreneurial activities I don’t understand. What connects these fields is that they all involve understanding people and making decisions based on evidence. It’s just thinking scientifically.
The ability to gather data systematically, analyse it honestly, and communicate what it means is valuable almost everywhere. It’s also incredibly rare. Many people can express opinions confidently; fewer can actually interrogate those opinions with evidence.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
5 And One More Thing
Some of you will genuinely enjoy this. Not everyone, and probably not immediately, but there’s real satisfaction in solving methodological puzzles: working out how to test something that seems untestable, spotting a flaw in an argument, seeing a pattern emerge from data you collected yourself.
I’m not promising you’ll love every moment. But we are promising that this material is worth taking seriously—and that taking it seriously might surprise you.






ImportantThis Week



Since Week 11 has no lecture, use this reading to prepare for the term ahead. But above all, be curious!








Note



Sophie von Stumm (formerly from Goldsmiths!) and colleagues (2011) sought to identify the best predictors of academic performance. Unsurprisingly perhaps, a person’s intelligence was the best predictor. However, they also found that this was matched by the combined predictive power of effort and intellectual curiosity. They conclude that succeeding in academic fields (such as psychology) is not just a question of being smart and trying hard, it is also about having a hungry mind!

Von Stumm, S., Hell, B., & Chamorro-Premuzic, T. (2011). The hungry mind: Intellectual curiosity is the third pillar of academic performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6, 574-588.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
6 Why Do Psychologists Do Research?
Psychology aims to understand human behaviour and mental processes. But how do we move from casual observation to scientific knowledge?

6.1 The Problem with Common Sense
We often think we understand human behaviour based on everyday experience - my mum certainly thinks so. But “common sense” has limitations (sorry, mum!):

Hindsight bias: Events seem obvious after they occur (“I knew it all along”)
Confirmation bias: We notice evidence that supports our beliefs and ignore contradicting evidence
Anecdotal evidence: Individual cases can mislead — your friend’s experience isn’t representative of everyone

Consider these “common sense” claims:

“Opposites attract” — But also “Birds of a feather flock together”
“Too many cooks spoil the broth” — But also “Many hands make light work”
“Absence makes the heart grow fonder” — But also “Out of sight, out of mind”

Common sense can justify almost any conclusion. Research methods provide systematic tools to overcome these biases and determine which claims actually hold up under scrutiny.


6.2 Why Intuitions About Behaviour Are Often Wrong
Our intuitions fail us for several reasons:

We don’t see our own blind spots — We’re unaware of the biases affecting our judgement
Memory is reconstructive — We misremember events to fit our current beliefs
We overgeneralise from small samples — One or two examples feel like proof
We confuse correlation with causation — Two things happening together doesn’t mean one caused the other

For example, studies consistently show that:

People are poor at predicting what will make them happy
Eyewitness testimony is far less reliable than we assume
“Venting” anger often increases rather than decreases aggression

These findings contradict common intuitions — which is precisely why we need systematic research.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
7 What Makes a Claim Scientific?

7.1 The Difference Between Opinion and Science
An opinion is a personal belief that may or may not be supported by evidence: > “I think social media makes people unhappy.”
A scientific claim is testable, based on systematic evidence, and open to being proven wrong: > “In a study of 1,000 adults, those who used social media for more than 3 hours daily reported lower life satisfaction scores (M = 5.2) than those who used it less than 1 hour (M = 6.8), t(998) = 4.32, p < .001.”


7.2 Four Hallmarks of Scientific Claims


Empirical basis — Based on observable, measurable evidence, not just reasoning or authority
Systematic collection — Data gathered using consistent, documented methods
Falsifiability — The claim could, in principle, be proven wrong by evidence
Transparency — Methods are described clearly enough that others could repeat them




7.3 What “Replicable” Means
A finding is replicable if other researchers, following the same procedures, get the same results.
Why does this matter?

A single study might have flaws we don’t notice
Random chance can produce misleading results
Researcher bias might influence findings

When multiple independent teams find the same result, we can be more confident it’s real.






NoteThe Replication Crisis



Psychology has faced a “replication crisis” — many classic findings failed to replicate when researchers tried to repeat them. This has led to better practices: larger samples, pre-registration of hypotheses, and more transparency. You’ll learn about this in Week 17.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
8 The Scientific Method
Researchers typically follow these steps:

8.1 1. Identify a Question
Start with curiosity. What do you want to understand?

“Do people remember information better if they test themselves rather than just re-reading?”



8.2 2. Review Existing Knowledge
What have others already discovered? Build on previous work rather than starting from scratch.


8.3 3. Formulate a Hypothesis
Make a specific, testable prediction.

“Students who use self-testing will recall more information after one week than students who re-read the material.”



8.4 4. Design a Study
Plan exactly how you’ll test your hypothesis: - Who will you study? - What will you measure? - How will you control for other explanations?


8.5 5. Collect Data
Gather observations systematically, following your planned procedures.


8.6 6. Analyse Results
Use statistics to determine whether your findings are meaningful or could have occurred by chance.


8.7 7. Draw Conclusions
What do your results mean? Do they support your hypothesis? What are the limitations?


8.8 8. Report Findings
Share your methods and results so others can evaluate and build on your work.
You’ll work through all these steps in your group project this term.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
9 Variables: Things That Vary
A variable is anything that can take different values.

9.1 Examples of Variables



Variable
Possible Values




Height
150cm, 165cm, 180cm…


Reaction time
200ms, 350ms, 420ms…


Mood
Happy, sad, anxious, neutral…


Number of words recalled
0, 1, 2, 3… 20


Exam score
0-100





9.2 Why Variables Matter
Research is fundamentally about understanding how variables relate to each other:

Does study time affect exam performance?
Does sleep quality predict reaction time?
Is age related to memory capacity?

In DataLab, you’ll measure several variables and see how they differ between people and across conditions.


9.3 Types of Variables
Continuous variables can take any value within a range: - Height (175.3cm) - Reaction time (287.4ms) - Temperature (36.8°C)
Categorical variables fall into distinct categories: - Gender (male, female, non-binary) - Experimental condition (control, treatment) - Handedness (left, right, ambidextrous)
Discrete variables are countable whole numbers: - Number of items recalled (7) - Number of errors (3) - Number of children (2)
Understanding variable types helps you choose appropriate statistical analyses — something you’ll learn throughout this module.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: 10 How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour
text:
10 How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour

10.1 Moving Beyond Speculation
Without data, debates about human behaviour often go in circles. Everyone has opinions, but how do we know whose is correct?
Empirical evidence allows us to:

Test competing theories — Instead of arguing, we can design studies to see which prediction holds
Discover unexpected findings — Data often reveals patterns we wouldn’t have predicted
Quantify effects — Not just “X affects Y” but “X increases Y by approximately this much”
Identify boundary conditions — Under what circumstances does a finding hold or not hold?



10.2 An Example: Does Punishment Deter Crime?
Common sense might suggest that harsher punishments reduce crime. But what does the evidence show?
Research has found: - Certainty of punishment matters more than severity - Very harsh sentences may actually increase recidivism in some cases - Deterrent effects vary by crime type and offender characteristics
Without systematic data collection, we’d have no way to discover these nuances.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
11 Connecting to DataLab

11.1 Your Data, Your Learning
In Thursday’s lab, you’ll experience research from both perspectives:

As a participant — completing cognitive tasks
As a tester — administering tasks and recording data

This dual perspective helps you understand:

Why standardised procedures matter (you’ll see what happens when instructions vary)
How measurement introduces variability (the same person gives different responses across trials)
What it feels like to generate data that will be analysed

The data you generate will be used throughout the term. When we discuss distributions in Week 12, we’ll look at the distribution of YOUR reaction times. When we learn about t-tests in Week 14, we’ll compare performance between Room A and Room B. This is your data, and you’ll learn statistics by exploring it.

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
2 Part 1: The Building Blocks — Variables

2.1 What Is a Variable?
A variable is anything that can vary — any characteristic, number, or quantity that can take different values.
In the DataLab:

Memory scores varied (some people remembered 4 words, others 8)
Mood ratings varied (some felt 3/10, others 8/10)
Reaction times varied (some caught the ruler quickly, others slowly)



2.2 Independent and Dependent Variables
In experimental research, we distinguish between two types of variables:

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or controls — the presumed cause.
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures — the outcome that may be affected.

The DV depends on the IV. We’re asking: Does the outcome depend on the condition?


2.3 DataLab Example: Memory Task
In the memory experiment:

IV: Word type (abstract vs concrete)
DV: Number of words recalled (0-10)

Lab A saw abstract words (justice, freedom, wisdom). Lab B saw concrete words (chair, river, mountain). The researcher manipulated which words you saw — that’s the IV.
What we measured — how many words you recalled — is the DV. We wanted to know if recall depended on the word type.


2.4 When There Is No IV
Not all research involves manipulation. Sometimes we simply measure two things and look at their relationship.
In the Frontal Lob task, you rated how good you thought you’d be at throwing (1-10), and then we measured your actual accuracy. Neither was manipulated — we just measured both.






ImportantKey Insight



When there’s no manipulation, there’s no IV. This is called a correlational design, and we’ll cover it shortly.




2.5 Data Types
The DV can be measured in different ways:








Data Type
Description
Example




Continuous
Can take any value (including decimals)
Reaction time (245.3ms)


Discrete
Whole numbers only (counts)
Words recalled (7)


Categorical
Categories with no numerical order
Lab group (A or B)


Ordinal
Categories with an order
Rating (1-10 scale)



In the DataLab:

Memory score is discrete (you can’t recall 6.5 words)
Reaction time is continuous (could be 245.3ms or 245.4ms)
Mood rating is ordinal (1-10 scale with order, but intervals may not be equal)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
3 Part 2: Design Types
The design refers to how participants are assigned to conditions.

3.1 Between-Subjects Design

Between-subjects design: Different participants in each condition.

In the memory experiment, you were in either Lab A (abstract words) or Lab B (concrete words) — never both. Different people were in each condition.
Why “between”? We’re comparing between groups — Lab A people versus Lab B people.
Advantage: No order effects (practice, fatigue, boredom)
Disadvantage: Individual differences may affect results (maybe Lab B just happened to have better memorisers)


3.2 Within-Subjects Design

Within-subjects design: The same participants measured in all conditions.

In the pre-post mood survey, you rated your mood before and after the session. The same person provided both data points.
Why “within”? We’re comparing within the same person — your pre-mood versus your post-mood.
Advantage: Each person is their own control! Individual differences are controlled because we’re comparing you to yourself.
Disadvantage: Order effects possible (practice, fatigue)


3.3 Within-Subjects Examples from DataLab



Task
Same Person Compared




Pre/Post mood
Before vs after session


Pre/Post energy
Before vs after session


Pre/Post stress
Before vs after session


Frontal Lob
Dominant vs non-dominant hand





3.4 Matched Pairs Design

Matched pairs design: Participants are paired on a key characteristic, then one from each pair goes to each condition.

This is a hybrid — different people in each condition (like between-subjects), but they’re matched to be similar (reducing individual difference problems).
Example: Match students by the amount of sleep they reported the night before. Let’s say two participants reported five hours and two participants reported 10 hours. One from each pair gets abstract words, the other gets concrete words. This would allow me to control for sleep quantity (five or ten hours), as I would have each level represented in each group. It means I would have to ask about sleep before allocating to condition, and so is a little bit more complicated in everyday life.


3.5 Correlational Design

Correlational design: Measuring the relationship between two variables — no manipulation.

When we measured self-rating and actual throwing performance, we didn’t manipulate either. We simply measured both and asked: Are they related? This could be the same for hours of sleep and memory performance, or any of the personality traits we measured and any other outcome variable.






WarningCritical Point



In correlational designs, there is NO IV. Neither variable is the “cause” — we’re just measuring a relationship.




3.6 Summary: Design Types








Design
Key Feature
Example

Lab A vs Lab B


Within-subjects

Participants paired, one per condition
Matched by ability


Correlational

Self-rating vs performance

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
4 Part 3: Writing Hypotheses
A hypothesis is a prediction about what you expect to find.

4.1 Experimental vs Null Hypothesis

Experimental hypothesis (H₁ or Ha): Predicts an effect or difference will exist.
Null hypothesis (H₀): Predicts no effect or no difference.

For the memory experiment:

H₁: Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words.
H₀: There will be no difference in recall between word types.

Statistical testing works by assuming H₀ is true, then checking if the data is surprising enough to reject that assumption.


4.2 One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed hypothesis: Predicts the direction of the effect.
Two-tailed hypothesis: Predicts a difference but not which direction.

One-tailed examples:

“Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words” (predicts concrete > abstract)
“Mood will improve after the session” (predicts post > pre)
“Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant hand” (predicts dominant > non-dominant)

Two-tailed examples:

“Word type will affect memory” (could be better or worse)
“Mood will change after the session” (could go up or down)
“There will be a difference in accuracy between hands” (no direction predicted)



4.3 When to Use Which?
Use one-tailed when:

Previous research strongly suggests a direction
Your theory predicts a specific direction
You only care about effects in one direction

Use two-tailed when:

You’re uncertain about the direction
Effects in either direction would be interesting
You’re being conservative (harder to reach significance)



4.4 Hypotheses for Each DataLab Task



Task
One-tailed Hypothesis




Memory
Concrete words will be recalled better than abstract words


Pre-Post Mood
Mood will improve after the session


Frontal Lob
Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant


Sixth Sense
Detection accuracy will be greater than chance (50%)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
5 Part 4: Descriptive Statistics
Before running statistical tests, we need to describe our data. Descriptive statistics summarise the key features.

5.1 The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average — the most common measure of central tendency.
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]
Calculating by hand:

Add up all values (Σx)
Divide by the number of values (n)

Example: Memory scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9

Sum: 5 + 7 + 6 + 8 + 9 = 35
Count: 5
Mean: 35 ÷ 5 = 7



5.2 The Standard Deviation
The mean alone doesn’t tell the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look very different:

Group A: 6, 6, 7, 7, 8 (Mean = 6.8)
Group B: 2, 5, 7, 9, 11 (Mean = 6.8)

Group B is much more spread out. We need to measure this variability.

Standard Deviation (SD) measures how spread out the data is from the mean.

Low SD = scores clustered together (consistent)
High SD = scores spread out (variable)




5.3 Calculating SD by Hand
Formula:
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}\]
Steps:

Calculate the mean
Subtract the mean from each value (deviation)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by (n-1)
Take the square root

Example: Scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9 (Mean = 7)



Score
Deviation (x - mean)
Squared

Variance = 10 ÷ (5-1) = 2.5
SD = √2.5 = 1.58



5.4 Why n-1?
We divide by (n-1), not n, because we’re estimating the population SD from a sample. This “degrees of freedom” correction makes our estimate unbiased.


5.5 Interpreting SD
For normally distributed data:

~68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean
~95% fall within 2 SDs
~99.7% fall within 3 SDs

If the mean memory score is 7 with SD = 1.58:

About 68% of people scored between 5.4 and 8.6
About 95% scored between 3.8 and 10.2



5.6 The Key Insight






ImportantSignal vs Noise



A difference between means only matters if it’s big relative to the spread.

Signal = difference between group means
Noise = variability within groups (SD)
The key question: Is the signal bigger than the noise?

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
6 Part 5: Reporting Descriptive Statistics
When writing up research, report descriptives clearly using APA format.

6.1 Basic Format
Report both mean AND standard deviation:

(M = value, SD = value)

Example:

Participants’ memory scores were moderate (M = 6.8, SD = 1.58).



6.2 Comparing Groups
When comparing conditions, report descriptives for each:

Lab A participants (M = 5.8, SD = 1.4) recalled fewer words than Lab B participants (M = 6.5, SD = 1.3).



6.3 APA Conventions

Use italics for statistical symbols: M, SD, t, p, r, d
Report two decimal places
No leading zero for values that cannot exceed 1 (e.g., p = .023, not p = 0.023)
